questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: What condition is an absolute contraindication for breastfeeding?
questions.explanation: While breastfeeding is almost always the ideal nutritional source, there are a few rare absolute contraindications. Classic Galactosemia in the infant (Option B) is an absolute contraindication because the baby lacks the enzyme to metabolize galactose, a component of the lactose found in breast milk. Continued breastfeeding in these infants leads to liver failure, cataracts, and mental retardation. HIV-positive status in the mother (Option A) is a contraindication in developed nations, but in developing countries, the WHO recommends breastfeeding with antiretroviral therapy if safe alternatives are unavailable. Hepatitis C (Option C) is not a contraindication provided nipples are not cracked or bleeding. For Tuberculosis (Option D), breastfeeding is only temporarily suspended until the mother is non-infectious; it is not an absolute, lifelong contraindication for that child. Therefore, galactosemia is the only infant-related metabolic condition listed that requires the absolute cessation of all breast milk

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 38-year-old patient presents with tachycardia, hypertension, and hypokalemia. Laboratory tests show elevated serum aldosterone with suppressed plasma renin activity. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The classic clinical triad of hypertension, hypokalemia, and the biochemical finding of high serum aldosterone with suppressed renin is diagnostic for primary hyperaldosteronism, also known as Conn's syndrome. This is typically caused by an aldosterone-secreting adrenal adenoma. The excess aldosterone leads to sodium retention (causing hypertension) and excessive potassium excretion in the kidney (causing hypokalemia). Cushing disease (Option B) results from excess cortisol and presents with a "moon face" and central obesity. Pheochromocytoma (Option C) presents with episodic paroxysmal hypertension, headaches, and palpitations, with high metanephrine levels. Diabetes Mellitus (Option D) involves hyperglycemia and is unrelated to this hormonal profile. Conn's syndrome is a common cause of resistant hypertension. Diagnosis is supported by an elevated aldosterone-to-renin ratio and confirmed by salt-loading suppression tests. Treatment involves surgical removal of the adenoma or medical management with aldosterone antagonists like spironolactone or eplerenone. Accurate diagnosis allows for a potential surgical cure for hypertension
questions.learning: The classic clinical triad of hypertension, hypokalemia, and the biochemical finding of high serum aldosterone with suppressed renin is diagnostic for primary hyperaldosteronism, also known as Conn's syndrome.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: For a woman who already has a 2-year-old child and received all the recommended vaccines during her previous pregnancy, what immunization advice should be given for her current pregnancy?
options: Give a booster dose of TT
Give a booster dose of Td
questions.explanation: According to the National Immunization Schedule in India, if a woman becomes pregnant within 3 years of a previous pregnancy where she received the complete primary series of vaccinations, she requires only a single booster dose for the current pregnancy. In modern practice, the Tetanus-diphtheria (Td) vaccine has replaced the older Tetanus Toxoid (TT) vaccine (Options A and C) to provide added protection against diphtheria in the adult population. Giving two doses (Option D) is necessary if the previous pregnancy was more than 3 years ago or if her immunization status is unknown. The booster dose ensures high levels of circulating maternal antibodies, which are transferred across the placenta to provide passive immunity to the newborn against neonatal tetanus—a potentially fatal condition. Clinical guidelines emphasize using the Td formulation for all doses during pregnancy. For this patient with a 2-year-old child and a documented complete history, a single Td booster is the correct evidence-based recommendation
questions.learning: According to the National Immunization Schedule in India, if a woman becomes pregnant within 3 years of a previous pregnancy where she received the complete primary series of vaccinations, she requires only a single booster dose for the current pregnancy.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text:
An elderly patient on a vegetarian diet presenting with easy fatigability and pallor was investigated. Peripheral smear showed findings of macrocytic anemia. What is the probable cause of anemia in this patient? Other lab findings are as follows:

Hemoglobin - 9 g/dL

Mean corpuscular volume (MCV) - 112 fL

Serum homocysteine - Elevated

Serum methylmalonic acid - Normal
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Folate deficiency

The probable cause of anemia in this patient of folate deficiency.

The given clinical scenario of macrocytic anemia in a vegetarian with elevated homocysteine levels is due to megaloblastic anemia, which can be caused by the deficiency of vitamin B12 or folic acid. Vitamin B12 deficiency is associated with raised serum methylmalonic acid (MMA) levels, which are normal in this patient; hence, folic acid deficiency is the cause of megaloblastic anemia in this patient.

Folic acid deficiency is associated with the following clinical and laboratory findings:

• Raised MCV (normal range: 80–100 fL) - macrocytosis
• Normal MCHC (normal range: 33–36 g/dL)
• Increased MCH
• Elevated RDW
• Decreased reticulocyte count - due to destruction of abnormal erythroid precursors
• Elevated homocysteine level
• Normal MMA level

where MCV, mean corpuscular volume; MCHC, mean corpuscular hemoglobin concentration; mean corpuscular hemoglobin, MCH; RDW, red cell distribution width

In vitamin B12 deficiency, neurological abnormalities, elevated homocysteine, and elevated MMA levels are seen.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Urate crystals are described as having the following shape:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Long and needle-like

Monosodium urate (MSU) crystals are the diagnostic hallmark of gout. On polarized light microscopy, they appear as long, slender, needle-shaped crystals showing strong negative birefringence. In contrast, calcium pyrophosphate dihydrate (CPPD) crystals seen in pseudogout are rhomboid-shaped and exhibit weak positive birefringence.

Why are the other options incorrect?

• A. Short and stout: Not the characteristic morphology of urate crystals.
• C. Small and triangular: Not seen in crystal-induced arthropathies.
• D. Large and rhomboid: Rhomboid crystals are characteristic of CPPD deposition disease (pseudogout), not gout.
questions.learning: Long and needle-like Monosodium urate (MSU) crystals are the diagnostic hallmark of gout. On polarized light microscopy, they appear as long, slender, needle-shaped crystals showing strong negative birefringence.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: Match the following: A. ERCP B. MRCP C. HIDA D. PTC
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. A-3, B-1, C-4, D-2

• A. ERCP → 3
• B. MRCP → 1
• C. HIDA Scan → 4
• D. Percutaneous Transhepatic Cholangiography (PTC) → 2

Educational Objective:

Different imaging modalities are used to evaluate the hepatobiliary and pancreatic system, each with distinct indications and techniques.

• ERCP (Endoscopic Retrograde Cholangiopancreatography) is an endoscopic fluoroscopic procedure used for both diagnosis and therapy (stone extraction, sphincterotomy, biliary stenting).
• MRCP (Magnetic Resonance Cholangiopancreatography) is a non-invasive MRI technique that provides excellent visualization of the biliary and pancreatic ducts without contrast injection or radiation.
• HIDA (Hepatobiliary Iminodiacetic Acid) scan is a nuclear medicine study that evaluates gallbladder function and biliary patency.
• Percutaneous Transhepatic Cholangiography (PTC) is an invasive fluoroscopic procedure in which contrast is injected directly into the intrahepatic bile ducts through a percutaneous transhepatic needle, commonly used when ERCP is not feasible.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: Which of the following is incorrect regarding myelodysplastic syndrome?
options: Treatment induced MDS is not dependent on age
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. More commonly seen in females

Myelodysplastic syndrome (MDS) is more commonly seen in males than females.

The MDS is a heterogeneous group of hematologic disorders characterized by both cytopenias due to bone marrow failure and a high risk of development of acute myeloid leukemia. Anemia due to ineffective erythropoiesis, often with thrombocytopenia and neutropenia, is seen.

MDS is a disease of the elderly; the mean age at onset is older than 70 years (option C). There is a slight male predominance (option A). Secondary or therapy-related MDS is not age-related (option B). It occurs as a late toxicity of cancer treatment; radiation (option D) and the radiomimetic alkylating agents such as busulfan, nitrosourea, or procarbazine (with a latent period of 5–7 years); or the DNA topoisomerase inhibitors (2-year latency). Acquired aplastic anemia, Fanconi anemia, and other constitutional marrow failure diseases can evolve into MDS.

Anemia dominates the early course. Most symptomatic patients complain of the gradual onset of fatigue and weakness, dyspnea, and pallor. Platelets also are large and lack granules. In functional studies, they may show marked abnormalities, and patients may have bleeding symptoms despite seemingly adequate numbers. Neutrophils are hypo-granulated; have ringed, or abnormally segmented nuclei; contain Döhle bodies; and may be functionally deficient. Circulating myeloblasts usually correlate with marrow blast numbers, and their quantity is important for classification and prognosis.

The bone marrow is usually normal or hypercellular, but in about 20% of cases, it is sufficiently hypocellular to lead to confusion with aplastic anemia. The following are commonly observed: dyserythropoietic changes (especially nuclear abnormalities) and ringed sideroblasts in the erythroid lineage; hypogranulation and hyposegmentation in granulocytic precursors, with an increase in myeloblasts; and megakaryocytes showing reduced numbers of or disorganized nuclei.

Only hematopoietic stem cell transplantation offers a cure for MDS. The hypomethylating agents azacitidine and decitabine are frequently used in bone marrow failure clinics. Lenalidomide, a thalidomide derivative with a more favorable toxicity profile, is particularly effective in reversing anemia in MDS patients with 5q– syndrome.

questions.text: Luminescent stools are associated with which of the following?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Phosphorus

Luminescent stools are seen in acute phosphorus poisoning. The vomitus and stools will be luminous in the dark.

The stools may give rise to faint fumes, constituting the smoky stool syndrome.

questions.subject: Psychiatry
questions.text: What is the most likely diagnosis in a girl who has normal language development but predominantly focuses on watching her own hands and shows minimal social interaction with others?
questions.explanation: Rett's Syndrome is the correct diagnosis. A girl with normal early development who subsequently shows hand-wringing/hand-watching stereotypies and social withdrawal is the classic presentation of Rett's syndrome — an X-linked neurodevelopmental disorder occurring exclusively in females. Key Diagnostic Features: 1. Occurs exclusively in females 2. Normal early development followed by regression 3. Characteristic hand stereotypies — wringing, watching, mouthing 4. Social withdrawal and loss of purposeful hand use 5. Language may be preserved initially then regresses Why other options are wrong: (A) ADHD is incorrect because ADHD presents with inattention, hyperactivity, impulsivity — not hand stereotypies or social withdrawal. No characteristic hand-focusing behavior occurs in ADHD. (B) Autism is incorrect because while autism shows social withdrawal, it occurs in both sexes, lacks the characteristic hand-watching stereotypies and normal early developmental period followed by regression specific to Rett's. (C) Asperger's Syndrome is incorrect because Asperger's presents with normal intelligence, social difficulties, and restricted interests — no hand stereotypies, regression, or gender specificity as seen in Rett's syndrome. **************

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text:
A 16-year-old girl with primary amenorrhea has the following features. What is the most probable diagnosis?

• Normal stature
• Thelarche - absent
• FSH, LH - high
• Karyotype - 46 XX
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Gonadal dysgenesis

The scenario of a 16-year-old girl with absent secondary sexual characters, normal stature, with XX karyotype and high FSH and LH is suggestive of pure gonadal dysgenesis.

46 XX and 46 XY gonadal dysgenesis without the phenotype of Turner's syndrome (short stature, webbed neck) is described as pure gonadal dysgenesis. It is characterized by the presence of primary amenorrhea with or without normal secondary sexual characteristics.

Option A: Testicular feminizing syndrome occurs in karyotype XY. Secondary sexual characters are present and the uterus is absent.

Option C: Kallmann syndrome is a form of hypogonadotropic hypogonadism. GnRH synthesis is reduced, therefore FSH and LH are low, and secondary sexual characters are absent.

Option D: Turner syndrome is associated with short stature and karyotype X0. Secondary sexual characters and the uterus is present, but the ovaries are streaked.
questions.learning: Gonadal dysgenesis — The scenario of a 16-year-old girl with absent secondary sexual characters, normal stature, with XX karyotype and high FSH and LH is suggestive of pure gonadal dysgenesis.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Analyzing the statements given about cystic masses of the neck, identify the false statement:
options: Type 3 branchial fistula has its internal orifice on the cricopharyngeus
Cystic hygroma is filled with clear lymph
Thyroglossal cyst moves upwards on swallowing and tongue protrusion
Fluctuation is positive in branchial cysts
questions.explanation: The statement claiming that a Type 3 branchial fistula opens on the cricopharyngeus is false (Option A). Anatomically, a second branchial fistula opens into the tonsillar fossa, while a third branchial fistula (and fourth) has its internal orifice located in the pyriform fossa of the larynx. The cricopharyngeus is a muscle of the esophagus and is not the standard site for these embryological remnants. All other statements are true: Cystic hygroma is a lymphatic malformation filled with clear lymph (Option B). A Thyroglossal cyst is unique because it is attached to the hyoid bone, meaning it moves upwards with both swallowing and tongue protrusion (Option C). A branchial cyst is a fluid-filled lesion, so the clinical fluctuation test is positive (Option D). Therefore, based on the specific anatomical tracts of branchial anomalies, the description of the internal opening in Option A is the definitive error

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.text: A 30-year-old pregnant woman presents to the dermatology outpatient department with the skin condition shown. Based on her pregnancy status and the clinical appearance, what is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The clinical image shows blotchy, brownish hyperpigmentation on the cheeks and forehead of a pregnant woman, which is the pathognomonic presentation of Chloasma (Option D). Also known as melasma or the "mask of pregnancy," it is a common physiological skin change occurring in up to 70% of pregnant women. It is caused by the stimulatory effect of pregnancy hormones (estrogen, progesterone, and MSH) on melanocytes, exacerbated by sun exposure. Systemic lupus erythematosus (Option A) presents with a "malar rash" that is typically erythematous and spares the nasolabial folds, unlike the brown pigmentation seen here. Viral infections (Option B) and rosacea (Option C) would present with redness, pustules, or systemic symptoms rather than isolated pigmentation. Therefore, chloasma is the most probable diagnosis. It is benign and usually fades after delivery as hormone levels normalize
questions.learning: The clinical image shows blotchy, brownish hyperpigmentation on the cheeks and forehead of a pregnant woman, which is the pathognomonic presentation of Chloasma (Option D).

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: Which of the following is not a feature of keratoconus?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Haab's striae

The incorrect about keratoconus is Haab's striae. Haab's striae are seen in cases of buphthalmos where the intraocular pressure is raised and the eyeball is enlarged as a whole. The enlarged cornea is associated with tears in Descemet's membrane called Haab's striae.

Keratoconus or the conical cornea is a bilateral non-inflammatory progressive condition of the axial part of the cornea. Central or paracentral thinning of the cornea and apical protrusion of the anterior cornea are pathognomonic. This is attributed to mucopolysaccharide and collagen tissue synthesis defects.

Clinical features of the condition include defective vision due to progressive myopia and irregular astigmatism. Light sensitivity and ocular irritation may also be present. Complications include acute hydrops following the rupture of Descemet's membrane.

Slit-lamp examination reveals Fleischer's ring at the base of the cone formed. Deep, vertical stromal striae (Vogt lines) that disappear with external pressure are characteristic. Retinoscopy shows a scissoring reflex. The bulging of the lower lid in the downgaze, called Munson's sign, is shown in the image below.

The severity of the condition is graded based on keratometry. Corneal topography is a diagnostic modality with the highest sensitivity for early cases.

Intacs or intracorneal ring segments are useful in moderate cases due to their flattening effect. Rigid gas-permeable contact lenses, corneal collagen cross-linking with riboflavin, and keratoplasty are the other treatment modalities.
questions.learning: Haab's striae — The incorrect about keratoconus is Haab's striae. Haab's striae are seen in cases of buphthalmos where the intraocular pressure is raised and the eyeball is enlarged as a whole.

The highlighted region is anterior and inferior, not posterior. 3. questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.text: A 30-year-old male presents with following finding. Which of the following clinical tests will aid in diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Grattage Test

The image depicts silvery white scaly plaques on the back which is a charateristic feature of Psoriasis. Grattage test will aid in its diagnosis.

Grattage Test:

* Scratching (grattage) scales in psoriasis makes the scale appear more silver in colour by introducing air–keratin interfaces.

* When the scales are completely scraped off, the stratum mucosum (basement membrane) is exposed and is seen as a moist red surface (membrane of Bulkeley) through which dilated capillaries at the tip of elongated dermal papillae are torn, leading to multiple bleeding points.This classical pinpoint bleeding is known as Auspitz sign.

* Auspitz sign is due to the elongated, dilated, tortuous vessels in the dermal papilla along with supra papillary thinning of epidermis.

However Auspitz sign is neither sensitive nor specific for Psoriasis.

* It is not seen in Pustular, Guttate, Erythrodermic or Inverse psoriasis.

* It is also seen in non-psoriatic scaling disorders like Darier's disease and Actinic Keratosis.

Psoriasis is a group of common chronic inflammatory and proliferative conditions of the skin, associated with systemic manifestations in many organ systems. The most characteristic lesions consist of red, scaly, sharply demarcated, indurated plaques, present particularly over the extensor surfaces and scalp.

Other Options:

Option B: Nikolsky's sign: Firm tangential sliding pressure with a finger will separate normal‐looking epidermis from dermis, producing an erosion. Lateral pressure on the normal skin around the blister results in separation between the layers of epidermis and the epidermis moves under the finger and shears off.

Nikolsky's sign is positive in the following:

* Pemphigus

* Staphylococcal Scalded Skin Syndrome(SSSS)

* Pemphigus foliaceus

The following image shows Nikolsky's sign, where the application of gentle lateral pressure causes sliding of the epidermis.

Option C: The Asboe-Hansen sign is a dermatological test that involves applying pressure to a blister to see if it spreads to the surrounding skin. It's used to help diagnose blistering diseases like pemphigus vulgaris and toxic epidermal necrolysis (TEN).

Option D: The standard patch test units are applied in two sets (on either side of the spine) and kept covered. One set of patches is removed and exposed to UVA. After irradiation, the other set of patches are also removed and both the sites are covered again for 48 hours. A positive reaction on the irradiated side only is an indication of photoallergy. Negative reaction is seen in phototoxic reaction.

Pearl PF1213: Nail changes in psoriasis

Nail changes in psoriasis are present in about 40% of the cases at any point in time. Nail psoriasis is associated with more extensive psoriasis, longer disease duration, family history of psoriasis, and the presence of psoriatic arthritis.

Subungal oil drop sign or Salmon Patch is a highly specific pathognomonic sign seen in Nail psoriasis. It is a yellow-red discoloration in the nail bed resembling a drop of oil.

Nail pitting however is the most frequent sign. Individual pits are uniformly sized, deep and irregular in nature. These nail pits are also known as Thimble pits and are due to the involvement of the proximal nail matrix.

Nail Bed disease also causes subungual hyperkeratosis, splinter hemorrhages, and distal onycholysis.

Leuconychia may also be present.

Trachonychia or Twenty Nail dystrophy may be present in severe cases.

Image :  Pitting is the commonest manifestation of nail psoriasis.

Image: oil drops visible in the nail bed.

Image: pitting and salmon patches in fingernails.

Image: Leukonychia in a patient with psoriasis.

Features of Nail Psoriasis – Mnemonic

“Nail – POLISH”

* P – Pitting

* O – Oil drop sign, Onycholysis

* L – Leuconychia

* I – Irregular pitting pattern

* S – Splinter Hemorrhage

* H – Hyperkeratosis (Subungual)

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.text: A farmer presents with a swelling on the palm that developed several months after sustaining a thorn prick injury. What is the most likely medical diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The clinical history of a palm swelling following a penetrating injury (like a thorn prick) is the "textbook" presentation of an implantation dermoid cyst. This occurs when a fragment of surface epithelium is driven into the deeper subcutaneous tissues during trauma. Over time, this trapped tissue grows and desquamates keratin, forming a cyst. Farmers are particularly susceptible due to occupational exposure to thorns and splinters. Ameloblastoma (Option A) is a tumor of the jaw. Embryogenic (Option B) and sequestration dermoids (Option C) are congenital cysts that occur along embryonic fusion lines (e.g., the midline or outer angle of the eye) rather than resulting from trauma. Implantation dermoids are typically firm, non-tender, and move with the skin. Surgical excision is the definitive treatment. Therefore, the traumatic origin in the palm confirms the diagnosis of an implantation dermoid
questions.learning: The clinical history of a palm swelling following a penetrating injury (like a thorn prick) is the "textbook" presentation of an implantation dermoid cyst.

questions.text: Which of the following muscles are supplied by the deep branch of the ulnar nerve? 1. 3rd lumbrical 2. 4th Dorsal interossei 3. Opponens digiti minimi 4. Flexor carpi ulnaris

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A hypertensive patient is taking three antihypertensive drugs including diuretics but the blood pressure is not controlled. He also has hypokalemia. Which of the following drug should be used to manage this patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Spironolactone

Resistant hypertension on three drugs including a diuretic suggests aldosterone-mediated volume excess.

Associated hypokalemia further supports hyperaldosteronism.

Hypokalemia strongly suggests: Excess aldosterone

Aldosterone causes:

• Na⁺ retention → hypertension
• K⁺ loss → hypokalemia

This condition is known as:

Primary hyperaldosteronism (Conn syndrome)

Spironolactone, an aldosterone antagonist, is the drug of choice in resistant hypertension.

It controls BP and corrects hypokalemia, unlike loop diuretics or potassium supplements alone.
questions.learning: Spironolactone Resistant hypertension on three drugs including a diuretic suggests aldosterone-mediated volume excess. Associated hypokalemia further supports hyperaldosteronism.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: Which of the following statements accurately describes the Little's area?
options: Keisselbach's plexus is present in the Little' area
It is situated at the postero-inferior part of the nasal septum
Anastomoses of 7 major arteries occur here
questions.explanation: Little's area is a clinically significant region located on the antero-inferior part of the nasal septum (Option B is incorrect). It is famous for the presence of Kiesselbach’s plexus (Option A), which is a dense network of anastomosing vessels. This area is the most common site for epistaxis (nosebleeds), accounting for approximately 90% of cases, due to its vascularity and exposure to trauma and dry air (Option C is incorrect). The plexus is formed by the anastomosis of four (not seven) major arteries: the Anterior ethmoidal, Sphenopalatine, Greater palatine, and Superior labial arteries. Recognizing Little's area is essential for clinicians as it is the primary target for anterior nasal packing or chemical cautery with silver nitrate to stop common nosebleeds. Therefore, the presence of the Kiesselbach's plexus is the definitive anatomical hallmark of this region. Accurate localization helps in directing effective emergency treatment for pediatric and adult patients alike
questions.learning: Little's area is a clinically significant region located on the antero-inferior part of the nasal septum (Option B is incorrect). It is famous for the presence of Kiesselbach’s plexus (Option A), which is a dense network of anastomosing vessels.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Five days after a common bile duct injury, there is a leak, and the patient presents with fever and abdominal pain . What will be the next line of management ?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Ultrasound-guided aspiration

In the case of a common bile duct injury with a leak and patient presenting with signs of localized peritonitis, the next step of management is ultrasound-guided aspiration, followed by ERCP and stenting.

Common bile duct injury: The most common cause of bile duct injury is laparoscopic cholecystectomy.

Management

* If detected on table with

* Duct injury less than 3 mm or those draining less than single segment of the liver: Ligation

* Lateral injury—Duct injury more than 4 mm or those draining multiple hepatic segments: Repair using T-tube.

* Transection with minimal loss of duct length: Repair using T-tube is used; in case of extensive loss of duct length, billiary enteric anastomosis is performed.

* Cystic duct leaks can be treated by the percutaneous drainage of intra-abdominal collection and endoscopic biliary drainage.

* Post-operative detection of leak: Major biliary leakage is usually seen 2 to 10 days after cholecystectomy. Patients usually present with pain in the abdominal region, fever, and, in some cases, bilious ascitic fluid.

* Jaundice is usually mild. Leukocytosis and abnormal liver function tests, particularly elevations in the serum levels of alkaline phosphatase and gamma-glutamyl transferase, are common.

* Radiological workup: Upon presentation, transabdominal ultrasonography is initially performed to define the extent of possible bile leak.

* For definitive leaks, ultrasound-guided aspiration is performed; alternatively, the collection is drained and a transhepatic biliary drain is placed. After 6–8 weeks, the definitive repair is ascertained.

* Ultrasonography confirmation and aspiration of the leak is followed by endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreatography and stenting.
questions.learning: Ultrasound-guided aspiration — In the case of a common bile duct injury with a leak and patient presenting with signs of localized peritonitis, the next step of management is ultrasound-guided aspiration, followed by ERCP and stenting.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: While performing a caloric test, what type of nystagmus would you expect on cold water irrigation?
options: Horizontal nystagmus towards the same side
Vertical nystagmus towards the same side
Horizontal nystagmus towards the opposite side
Vertical nystagmus towards the opposite side
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Horizontal nystagmus towards the opposite side

In caloric testing, cold water irrigation produces horizontal nystagmus towards the opposite side of irrigation. The direction of nystagmus can be remembered by the mnemonic, COWS (cold–opposite, warm–same).

The mechanism for the nystagmus is the creation of a temperature gradient by the cold water, which pulls the cupula away from the utricle, causing nystagmus towards the oppsite side. As the horizontal semicircular canal is closer to the outer ear canal, most of the response comes from it and the nystagmus is horizontal.

The Fitzgerald–Hallpike test (bithermal caloric test) is done to assess this phenomenon. The patient lies in a supine position with head tilted forward at a 30° angle, ensuring the horizontal canal becomes vertical. Alternatingly, water at temperatures of 30°C and 44°C (7° below and above normal body temperature, respectively) is irrigated into the ears for a duration of 40 seconds each. The examiner closely observes the patient's eyes for the emergence of nystagmus until its endpoint is reached. The time taken from the start of irrigation to the endpoint of nystagmus is recorded and plotted on a calorigram.

If no nystagmus is evoked from either ear, the test is repeated with water at a temperature of 20°C for a duration of 4 minutes before labeling the labyrinth dead. A 5-minute interval should be allowed between testing each ear to ensure accurate results.
questions.learning: Horizontal nystagmus towards the opposite side — In caloric testing, cold water irrigation produces horizontal nystagmus towards the opposite side of irrigation.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A 6-month-old infant is brought with lethargy, vomiting, and poor feeding after a period of prolonged fasting. Labs show hypoglycemia with low ketone bodies (hypoketosis), suggesting a defect in fat metabolism. Which of the following is the most likely disorder?
options: Glycogen storage disease type I (Von Gierke disease)
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Medium-chain acyl-Coa dehydrogenase (MCAD) deficiency

Medium-chain acyl-CoA dehydrogenase (MCAD) deficiency is a fatty acid β-oxidation disorder in which the body cannot properly break down medium-chain fatty acids in mitochondria to generate energy during fasting.

In MCAD deficiency, impaired β-oxidation results in:

• Decreased energy production
• Reduced ketone body formation (hypoketosis)
• Hypoglycemia during fasting

This leads to symptoms such as lethargy, vomiting, poor feeding, and hypoketotic hypoglycemia, especially after prolonged fasting or illness.

Why other options are incorrect:

• Hers disease (GSD VI): Liver glycogen phosphorylase deficiency causing mild hypoglycemia and hepatomegaly, not hypoketotic hypoglycemia.
• Hereditary fructose intolerance: Presents after fructose ingestion with hypoglycemia and vomiting.
• Von Gierke disease (GSD I): Causes severe fasting hypoglycemia with hepatomegaly and lactic acidosis, but ketone production is not characteristically absent.
questions.learning: Medium-chain acyl-Coa dehydrogenase (MCAD) deficiency Medium-chain acyl-CoA dehydrogenase (MCAD) deficiency is a fatty acid β-oxidation disorder in which the body cannot properly break down medium-chain fatty acids in mitochondria to generate energy during…

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: The drug that decreases the size of prostate is:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Finasteride

Finasteride reduces prostatic size.

Finasteride:

• It is a competitive inhibitor of 5α-reductase enzyme, thus inhibiting the conversion of testosterone into its active form DHT(Dihydrotestosterone) which is responsible for androgenic action in Prostate gland.
• It produces effect on long term use (nearly 6 months) by reducing prostatic epithelial cell proliferation thereby reducing the size of prostate and improves urine flow.

Tamsulosin is an α 1 Selective Antagonist which dilates prostatic urethra and hence produces immediate symptom relief in BPH. It has no effect on reducing size of the prostate.

Sildenafil acts by inhibiting phosphodiesterase-5 (PDE-5) and is used in the treatment of erectile dysfunction.

Flutamide is a Nonsteroidal Androgen Receptor antagonist with no hormonal activity. They are used for treatment of metastatic prostatic cancer in conjunction with GnRH agonists.
questions.learning: Finasteride Finasteride reduces prostatic size. Finasteride: • It is a competitive inhibitor of 5α-reductase enzyme, thus inhibiting the conversion of testosterone into its active form DHT(Dihydrotestosterone) which is responsible for androgenic action in…

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.text: A patient presents with an anesthetic patch in the areas on the face as shown in the image below. Which of the following nerves is the most commonly involved in this condition?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Facial nerve

The clinical scenario points to a case of leprosy and the most commonly involved cranial nerve is the facial nerve.

Leprosy is a chronic granulomatous condition caused by Mycobacterium leprae. It affects the skin, cutaneous and peripheral nerves, and mucous membranes. The most commonly affected peripheral nerves are the posterior tibial nerve followed by ulnar, median, and lateral popliteal nerves. The most commonly involved cranial nerve is the facial nerve.

Leprosy has a long incubation period, usually ranging from 2 to 12 years. It commonly presents as an area of numbness on the skin or a visible skin lesion which could be a hypopigmented or erythematous macule. Lesions usually involve the face, extensor aspect of the limbs, trunks, and buttocks. The lesions have impaired nerve function and poor hair growth. The patients may also present with burns or ulcers of the anesthetic limb.

Classification systems of leprosy include:

• Ridley Jopling classification:

• Tuberculoid (TT)
• Borderline tubercular (BT)
• Borderline (BB)
• Borderline lepromatous (BL)
• Lepromatous (LL)

• WHO classification:

• Paucibacillary
• Multibacillary

The cardinal signs for the diagnosis of leprosy include:

• Characteristic skin lesions- hypopigmented or erythematous lesions with definite impairment of sensation.
• Peripheral nerve involvement- thickening of the nerve with sensory impairment. Nerve tenderness can also be seen.
• Detection of acid-fast bacilli in slit-skin smear, skin biopsy, or positive biopsy PCR.

The presence of two of the three signs can establish the diagnosis of leprosy. Other tests done for diagnosis of leprosy include nerve biopsy in pure neural leprosy and PGL-1 antibody in cases in low bacterial load.
questions.learning: Facial nerve — The clinical scenario points to a case of leprosy and the most commonly involved cranial nerve is the facial nerve. Leprosy is a chronic granulomatous condition caused by Mycobacterium leprae.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: What is the serial interval?
options: Time take to develop a Primary case
Time gap between entry of organism till maximum infectivity
Interval between Primary and secondary case
Time gap between onset till first detection
questions.explanation: In epidemiology, the serial interval is defined as the time interval between the onset of symptoms in a primary (index) case and the onset of symptoms in a secondary case that has been infected by the primary case. It reflects the speed at which an infectious disease spreads from one generation of cases to the next. Option A refers to the incubation period, which is the time between exposure to an infectious agent and the appearance of symptoms in the same individual. Option B describes the period of maximum infectivity or communicability, not the relationship between two cases. Option D refers to the diagnostic delay, which is unrelated to transmission dynamics. The serial interval is a crucial parameter in outbreak investigation and epidemic modeling. It is commonly used along with the basic reproduction number (R₀) to estimate transmission potential and epidemic growth. When the serial interval is shorter than the incubation period, it suggests pre-symptomatic transmission, which complicates disease control measures. Accurate estimation of the serial interval through contact tracing helps public health authorities design effective isolation, quarantine, and containment strategies
questions.learning: In epidemiology, the serial interval is defined as the time interval between the onset of symptoms in a primary (index) case and the onset of symptoms in a secondary case that has been infected by the primary case.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: An infectious disease has its incubation period as 5-14 days, with its median incubation period being 10 days. The quarantine of contacts traveling to a new country should be done for:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. 14 days

The quarantine period is based on the maximum incubation period of the disease to ensure that all infected contacts manifest symptoms, if present.

Even though the median incubation period is 10 days, some individuals may develop disease as late as 14 days.

Therefore, quarantining contacts for 14 days is necessary to effectively prevent transmission during travel or population movement.
questions.learning: 14 days The quarantine period is based on the maximum incubation period of the disease to ensure that all infected contacts manifest symptoms, if present.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: Where is the electrode placed in cochlear implant procedures?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Scala tympani

The electrode of a cochlear implant is placed in the scala tympani. It allows for the electrodes to be in close proximity to the ganglion cells and their dendrites which are located in the modiolus and bony spiral lamina of the cochlea.

A cochlear implant is an electronic device for severe to profound SNHL and who cannot benefit from a hearing aid. It converts sound to an electrical signal (transduction) and delivers this to the auditory nerve. Prerequisites include an intact cochlear nerve and higher auditory pathway.

In the auditory brainstem implant, the site of the implant is the lateral recess of the fourth ventricle. It is used when the cochlear nerve is not intact.
questions.learning: Scala tympani — The electrode of a cochlear implant is placed in the scala tympani. It allows for the electrodes to be in close proximity to the ganglion cells and their dendrites which are located in the modiolus and bony spiral lamina of the cochlea.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: In multiple myeloma, monoclonal immunoglobulin light chains combine with Tamm–Horsfall protein precipitate in the renal tubules which leads to the development of which one of the following conditions?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Cast nephropathy

In multiple myeloma, excessive production of monoclonal free immunoglobulin light chains (Bence Jones proteins) leads to their filtration through the glomerulus. In the distal nephron, these light chains bind to Tamm–Horsfall protein (uromodulin) and form obstructing light-chain casts. This causes tubular obstruction and direct tubular injury, producing myeloma cast nephropathy, also called myeloma kidney.

Why not the other options?

• A. IgA nephropathy: Caused by deposition of IgA-containing immune complexes in the mesangium; not due to light-chain/Tamm–Horsfall protein casts.
• C. Membranous glomerulonephritis: Characterized by subepithelial immune-complex deposition and diffuse glomerular basement membrane thickening.
• D. Interstitial nephritis: Usually caused by drugs, infections, or systemic diseases and produces interstitial inflammatory infiltrates, rather than light-chain casts.
questions.learning: Cast nephropathy — In multiple myeloma, excessive production of monoclonal free immunoglobulin light chains (Bence Jones proteins) leads to their filtration through the glomerulus.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A known hypertensive patient is brought to the ER with palpitations and breathlessness. On examination, his BP was 220/140 with signs of encephalopathy. Which of the following is used as a 1st line drug to manage this patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Nicardipine

The given scenario points towards a diagnosis of hypertensive emergency. The first-line drug in this scenario is IV nicardipine.

Hypertensive emergencies are situations in which grade 3 hypertension (BP>180/110 mmHg) is associated with acute hypertension-mediated organ damage (HMOD).

Treatment of hypertensive emergency depends on the type of end-organ damage present (as shown in the table below). It is treated with rapidly acting intravenous antihypertensive agents.

In hypertensive encephalopathy, the initial goal of therapy is to immediately reduce mean arterial blood (MAP) pressure by no more than 25%. Rapid reduction of blood pressure may lead to reduced cerebral blood flow and result in cerebral infarction.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: What is the most appropriate disposal mechanism for expired medications in biomedical waste management?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Incineration

Expired or discarded pharmaceuticals are preferably disposed of by high-temperature incineration, which ensures complete destruction of the drugs and prevents environmental contamination or misuse. It is the recommended method under Biomedical Waste Management Rules for pharmaceutical waste.

Why not the other options?

• A. Autoclaving: Used for infectious biomedical waste, not pharmaceutical waste.
• B. Deep burial: Reserved for specific anatomical or infectious waste in limited settings; not recommended for expired medicines.
• D. Landfill: Not preferred because pharmaceuticals may leach into soil and groundwater, posing environmental hazards.
questions.learning: Incineration Expired or discarded pharmaceuticals are preferably disposed of by high-temperature incineration, which ensures complete destruction of the drugs and prevents environmental contamination or misuse.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: A young male came to the hospital with a clean-cut wound without any bleeding. The patient received a full course of tetanus vaccination 10 years ago. What is the best management for this patient?
options: Human tetanus immunoglobulin and full course of vaccine
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Single-dose tetanus toxoid

The patient with a clean-cut wound without any bleeding, who received a full course of tetanus vaccination 10 years ago, should be given a single dose of tetanus toxoid vaccine and appropriate wound care.

Wound management involves cleaning the wound thoroughly to remove soil, foreign bodies, and necrotic tissue.

Note: In cases where combined immunization is necessary, the patient is given 250 units of human tetanus immunoglobulin in one arm and 0.5 mL of adsorbed tetanus toxoid (PTAP or APT) in the other arm or gluteal region. The antitoxin is given for immediate temporary protection, and the tetanus toxoid is given for long-lasting protection.
questions.learning: Single-dose tetanus toxoid — The patient with a clean-cut wound without any bleeding, who received a full course of tetanus vaccination 10 years ago, should be given a single dose of tetanus toxoid vaccine and appropriate wound care.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: Bony septal perforation occurs in:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Syphilis

Syphilis involves the perforation of the bony and cartilaginous parts.

Lupus, tuberculosis, and leprosy cause perforation only in the cartilaginous part.

Septal perforation can be caused by:

* Trauma

* Pathological:

* Septal abscess

* Nasal myiasis

* Rhinolith

* Chronic granulomatous disease

* Wegner's granulomatous disease

* Drug-related:

* Chronic use of steroid spray

* Cocaine abuse

* Arsenic/ chromium

* Idiopathic
questions.learning: Syphilis Syphilis involves the perforation of the bony and cartilaginous parts. Lupus, tuberculosis, and leprosy cause perforation only in the cartilaginous part.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Which of the following is not a prodrug?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Primidone

Among the given options primidone is not a prodrug.

Prodrugs are drugs that are in their pharmacologically inactive form. They are converted to their active forms by metabolism.

The prodrug may offer advantages over the active form in being more stable, having better bioavailability, or fewer side effects and toxicity. Some prodrugs are activated selectively at the site of action. The given options are examples of prodrugs:

• Sulindac is a sulfoxide prodrug used in inflammatory diseases including osteoarthritis, rheumatoid arthritis, acute gouty arthritis, ankylosing spondylitis.
• Proguanil is a prodrug and its active metabolite is cycloguanil. It is used in the treatment and prevention of malaria.
• Fluro-uracil is a prodrug having the active metabolite as fluorouridine monophosphate
questions.learning: Primidone Among the given options primidone is not a prodrug. Prodrugs are drugs that are in their pharmacologically inactive form.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Revised A young sheep farmer presents to the OPD with pain in the right upper part of the abdomen. On examination, there is tenderness and enlargement of the liver. Blood investigations show eosinophilia, elevated liver enzymes, and abdominal ultrasound is as below. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Hydatid cyst

The clinical vignette along with the ultrasound image showing multiple septations and rosette or honeycomb appearance is diagnostic of active hydatid cyst.

Hydatid cyst:

Echinococcus granulosus is the most common causative agent in hydatid cysts, while Echinococcus multilocularis and Echinococcus ligartus account for a small number of cases.

The hydatid cyst usually develops three weeks after the infection. The cyst is surrounded by a fibrous capsule called the pericyst that is derived from the host tissue.

The cyst wall is composed of two layers, ectocyst (outer gelatinous membrane), and endocyst (inner germinal membrane). Ectocyst is a laminated membrane, which is acellular. It helps in the passage of nutrients. The endocyst helps in producing the laminated membrane and scoleces.

The brood capsules are cellular masses in the hydatid fluid which consists of scoleces. In a definitive host, these scoleces develop into adult tapeworm while in the intermediate hosts these develop into new hydatid cysts. The brood capsules are attached to the endocyst by a pedicle or stalk. The brood capsules may mature and detach from the mother cyst and become the daughter cysts, which are an exact replica of the mother cysts.

The freed brood capsules and scoleces present in the hydatid fluid are called hydatid sand.

The image attached below shows the C.S of hydatid cyst.

Investigations:

Computed tomography (CT) scan is the best imaging modality for hydatid cyst. It shows the presence of a space-occupying lesion with a smooth outline with septa.

CT scan has an accuracy of 98% in the detection of hydatid cysts and higher sensitivity to demonstrate the daughter cysts and extra-hepatic cysts.
The indirect hemagglutination test and enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA) have a sensitivity of 80% overall and are the initial screening tests of choice.

Note:

* First/Initial imaging test: USG

* Best imaging test: CT scan

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 60-year-old man undergoes resection for sigmoid colon adenocarcinoma. Histology shows tumor extending through the serosa but with no regional lymph node metastases. According to Dukes classification for colorectal carcinoma, which stage and approximate 5-year survival best correspond to this disease?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Dukes B2, 5-year survival 75 %

The Dukes classification of colorectal carcinoma correlates tumor depth and nodal involvement with prognosis.

Dukes staging overview

• Dukes A: Tumor confined to mucosa/submucosa → 5-year survival \~90–95%

• Dukes B: Tumor extends through bowel wall but no lymph node metastasis

o B1: Extends into muscularis propria

o B2: Penetrates through serosa or beyond → 5-year survival \~70–75%

• Dukes C: Any depth with regional lymph node involvement → survival \~40–65%

• Dukes D: Distant metastasis → poor prognosis

Key concept in this question

Tumor extends through serosa but no nodal metastasis

→ corresponds to Dukes B2

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Deficiency of the enzyme tyrosine transaminase leads to the development of which of the following conditions?
questions.explanation: Type II Tyrosinemia (also known as Richner-Hanhart syndrome) is an autosomal recessive metabolic disorder caused by a deficiency of the enzyme tyrosine transaminase (also called tyrosine aminotransferase). This enzyme catalyzes the first step of tyrosine breakdown. Its deficiency leads to elevated levels of tyrosine in the blood and tissues, characteristically presenting with painful corneal erosions (pseudodendritic keratitis) and hyperkeratotic lesions on the palms and soles. Type I Tyrosinemia (Option A) is caused by a deficiency of fumarylacetoacetate hydrolase and is the most severe form, often leading to liver failure. Alkaptonuria (Option C) results from a deficiency of homogentisate oxidase, causing dark urine and ochronosis. Type III Tyrosinemia (Option D) is rare and caused by a deficiency of 4-hydroxyphenylpyruvate dioxygenase. Understanding these specific enzymatic defects in the tyrosine catabolic pathway is essential for diagnosing inborn errors of metabolism and initiating targeted dietary management to prevent systemic and ocular complications
questions.learning: Type II Tyrosinemia (also known as Richner-Hanhart syndrome) is an autosomal recessive metabolic disorder caused by a deficiency of the enzyme tyrosine transaminase (also called tyrosine aminotransferase).

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: An elderly woman reports difficulty in buttoning her shirt and increased clumsiness during daily activities. On examination, she is unable to make an 'O' shape by opposing her thumb and index finger. Which of the following muscles is most likely involved?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Abductor pollicis brevis

The difficulty in buttoning the shirt and the inability to make the "O" shape with fingers suggest the involvement of the abductor pollicis brevis muscle.

This is a case of anterior interosseous nerve (AIN) syndrome. The AIN is a purely motor branch of the median nerve that affects specific muscles in the forearm, the flexor pollicis longus and flexor digitorum profundus leading to difficulty in performing tasks requiring fine motor control, such as the "OK" sign. Among the options provided, the abductor pollicis brevis is uniquely and consistently innervated by the recurrent motor branch of the median nerve, making it susceptible to dysfunction in conditions affecting the median nerve.

Other options:

Option A: The opponens pollicis is innervated primarily by the lateral terminal branch of the median nerve, with some contributions from a branch of the deep terminal branch of the ulnar nerve. While it plays a role in thumb opposition, it is not consistently affected in anterior interosseous nerve (AIN) syndrome, which primarily impacts deeper flexor muscles like the flexor pollicis longus. Therefore, it is less likely to be the cause of the patient’s inability to perform the "OK" sign.

Option B: The palmar interossei muscles are innervated by the deep branch of the ulnar nerve. Because they do not receive any innervation from the median nerve, they are not implicated in AIN syndrome. Their primary function involves the adduction of the fingers.

Option C: The flexor pollicis brevis has dual innervation: the superficial head is supplied by the recurrent branch of the median nerve, while the deep head is innervated by the deep branch of the ulnar nerve. This dual supply makes it less likely to be solely affected in AIN syndrome.
questions.learning: Abductor pollicis brevis — The difficulty in buttoning the shirt and the inability to make the "O" shape with fingers suggest the involvement of the abductor pollicis brevis muscle.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: Which color-coded waste bag is used for the disposal of waste that is treated by incineration?
questions.explanation: Under the Biomedical Waste Management rules, color-coding is used to segregate waste for appropriate treatment and disposal. The "Yellow Bag" is designated for infectious waste intended for deep burial or high-temperature incineration. This includes human anatomical waste (organs, tissues), animal waste, soiled waste (blood-soaked cotton, dressings), and expired/discarded medicines. The "Red Bag" (Option B) is used for recyclable plastic waste (tubing, bottles, gloves) which is treated via autoclaving or microwaving rather than incineration. The "Blue Bag/Cardboard box" (Option C) is for glass waste and metallic body implants. The "Black Bag" (Option D) was historically used for general municipal waste but is now largely replaced by translucent or green/blue containers for non-infectious waste in clinical settings. Proper segregation in yellow bags ensures that highly infectious materials are completely destroyed, preventing environmental contamination and the spread of healthcare-associated infections through the safe process of controlled combustion
questions.learning: Under the Biomedical Waste Management rules, color-coding is used to segregate waste for appropriate treatment and disposal. The "Yellow Bag" is designated for infectious waste intended for deep burial or high-temperature incineration.

questions.subject: Anaesthesia
questions.text: Epidural anesthesia involves local anesthetic administration between
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Dura and ligamentum flavum

Epidural anesthesia involves local anesthetic administration between the dura and ligamentum flavum.

Subdural injection (seen in a failed spinal anesthesia) is between dura and arachnoid.

Spinal anesthesia (subarachnoid block, intrathecal block) involves local anesthetic administration between the pia and arachnoid mater.

In spinal anesthesia, the local anesthetic is injected into CSF, which bathes the nerve root. Hence, a relatively small dose and volume of local anesthetic is sufficient to achieve dense sensory and motor blockade.
questions.learning: Dura and ligamentum flavum Epidural anesthesia involves local anesthetic administration between the dura and ligamentum flavum. Subdural injection (seen in a failed spinal anesthesia) is between dura and arachnoid.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A 2-week-old infant is brought to the hospital with a reported history of a single fall. However, radiographic evaluation reveals multiple fractures at varying stages of healing. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The presence of multiple fractures at different stages of healing (both acute and chronic) in a 2-week-old infant is a classic hallmark of non-accidental injury, also known as Battered Baby Syndrome or child abuse. The reported history of a single fall is highly inconsistent with the severity and chronicity of the radiographic findings. Osteogenesis imperfecta (Option A) is a genetic disorder causing brittle bones, but it is typically accompanied by blue sclera and a family history. An accidental fall (Option B) cannot explain fractures that are already in various stages of callous formation. Birth trauma (Option D) would result in fractures that are all at the same, acute stage of healing. Therefore, the discrepancy between the parental account and the evidence of repetitive, timed injuries makes child abuse the most likely diagnosis
questions.learning: The presence of multiple fractures at different stages of healing (both acute and chronic) in a 2-week-old infant is a classic hallmark of non-accidental injury, also known as Battered Baby Syndrome or child abuse.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A patient presented with joint pain and on evaluation, urine turns black on standing. What is the likely enzyme deficiency?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Homogentisic acid 1, 2 - dioxygenase

The urine turning black in color, on exposure to air, along with joint pain is suggestive of alkaptonuria. It occurs due to the defect in the homogentisic acid 1, 2 - dioxygenase enzyme.

Alkaptonuria is an autosomal recessive disorder of tyrosine metabolism, that develops due to the defect in homogentisate oxidase/homogentisic acid 1, 2 - dioxygenase, which oxidizes homogentisate to maleylacetoacetate. The defect in this enzyme leads to the accumulation of homogentisate, which is then excreted in the urine.

Alkaptonuria is characterized by homogentisic aciduria, ochronosis, and arthropathy (joint pain).

Homogentisic aciduria is the black discoloration of urine on prolonged exposure to air caused due to oxidation of the excreted homogentisate.

Ochronosis is the accumulation of oxidized homogentisic acid pigment (alkaptone bodies) in connective tissues leading to bluish-black discoloration of tissues mostly involving ear cartilage, ocular tissue, the skin of the eyelids, forehead, cheeks, and hands, nail beds, and intervertebral discs. The compound that accumulates in the tissues in ochronosis is benzoquinone acetate.

Painful arthritis (arthropathy) may be seen from the fourth or fifth decade.

Diagnosis: Blackish discoloration of urine on standing is diagnostic of alkaptonuria (shown below). The ferric chloride test will be positive.

The image further below shows Ochronosis.

Treatment:  No specific treatment is required. Symptomatic treatment with analgesics, spinal surgery, and arthroplasty along with ascorbic acid and protein restriction can be considered. Nitisinone (p-hydroxyphenylpyruvic acid (pHPPA) oxidase inhibitor) reduces urinary excretion of homogentisic acid.

Other options:

Option B: Tyrosine transaminase deficiency causes type II tyrosinemia (Richner-Hanhart syndrome). Patients present with painful corneal erosions with photophobia, learning disability, and palmoplantar keratosis.

Option C: Fumarylacetoacetate hydrolase deficiency causes type I tyrosinemia (Tyrosinosis). Patients generally present with failure to thrive, neuropathy, boiled-cabbage urine, and liver failure secondary to cirrhosis.

Option D:  4-hydroxy-phenyl pyruvate dioxygenase deficiency causes type III tyrosinemia (neonatal tyrosinemia). Patients might rarely have a mental disability. The liver function is generally normal.

The steps of tyrosine metabolism are shown below.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: Which of the following has the least risk of perinatal transmission?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Rubella

Rubella has the least risk of perinatal transmission.

Rubella or German measles has an intrauterine transmission that causes serious infection in pregnancy which results in abortions or severe fetal defects if infection occurs in the first trimester. The classical triad of congenital rubella syndrome is deafness, cataract, and congenital heart disease.

Other options-

Option A: Herpes simplex infection can be acquired in utero, intrapartum/perinatally, or during the neonatal period. The intrauterine infection causes skin vesicles, eye findings (chorioretinitis, keratoconjunctivitis), and microcephaly/hydranencephaly. Intrapartum infection presents with either:

• Skin, eye, and mouth disease
• Encephalitis
• Disseminated disease with sepsis-like presentation

Option B: Cytomegalovirus, the most common congenital infection with perinatal transmission presents with hepatosplenomegaly, petechial rashes, jaundice, chorioretinitis, and microcephaly. One of the long-term sequelae is hearing loss.

Option D: Hepatitis B virus is associated with significant perinatal transmission. The most important risk factor that determines perinatal transmission is HBeAg.
questions.learning: Rubella Rubella has the least risk of perinatal transmission. Rubella or German measles has an intrauterine transmission that causes serious infection in pregnancy which results in abortions or severe fetal defects if infection occurs in the first trimester.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: “Leukemia”, as an occupational cancer, is most commonly related to the exposure to which one of the following industrial chemicals?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Benzol

Benzene (benzol) is a well-established occupational carcinogen associated particularly with leukemia, especially acute myeloid leukemia (AML).

Why not the other options?

• A. Mineral oil: Associated mainly with skin cancers after prolonged occupational exposure.
• B. Auramine: Associated with bladder cancer in occupational exposure.
• C. β-naphthylamine: Classically associated with urinary bladder carcinoma.

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.text: During forensic analysis of a semen sample obtained in a rape case, distinctive yellow, needle-shaped crystals are observed. Which specific test is used to confirm the presence of sperm?
questions.explanation: The identification of distinctive yellow needle-like crystals (spermine picrate) during a forensic semen analysis is the hallmark of the Barberio test. This is a preliminary chemical test used to identify spermine, a component of seminal fluid. The Florence test (Option D) also produces crystals, but they are brown, rhombic crystals of choline periodide. The Acid Phosphatase test (Option B) is a very sensitive colorimetric screening test for semen but does not involve crystal formation. A Papanicolaou (Pap) smear (Option C) is a staining technique used for cytological examination to visualize actual sperm cells under a microscope. While Barberio is a useful screening tool, the confirmatory test for semen in a rape investigation remains the microscopic visualization of spermatozoa. Understanding these forensic tests is critical for the medico-legal documentation of sexual assault and the identification of the perpetrator
questions.learning: The identification of distinctive yellow needle-like crystals (spermine picrate) during a forensic semen analysis is the hallmark of the Barberio test.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A 4-year-old boy develops bloody diarrhea and abdominal cramps. The bacteria isolated from the stool specimen fermented lactose and produced colorless colonies on sorbitol MacConkey agar. The most likely etiological agent in this case is?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Shiga toxin-producing E.Coli

The given clinical scenario of a boy with bloody diarrhea and abdominal cramps with the isolated bacteria fermenting lactose and forming colorless colonies on sorbitol MacConkey agar is suggestive of infection by Shiga toxin-producing E. coli (STEC) O157: H7, also known as Enterohemorrhagic E. coli (EHEC).

O157: H7 is the most common type of Shiga toxin-producing E. coli (STEC). Unlike most other E. coli serotypes, the STEC O157: H7 does not use sorbitol and produces clear colonies on the Sorbitol MacConkey agar. The non-STEC produces pink colonies. All species of E. coli are lactose fermenters and produce pink colonies.

They produce two antigenic forms of the cytotoxic toxin known as Shiga-like toxin 1 and Shiga-like toxin 2. Shiga-like toxin 1 is identical to the Shiga toxin of Shigella dysenteriae type 1. E. coli O157:H7 has a small infective dose (around 100 bacilli) and spreads easily from child to child by the feco-oral route.

It can cause mild non-bloody diarrhea to hemorrhagic colitis, or a severe form of diarrhea, with hemolytic uremic syndrome, a disease resulting in acute renal failure, microangiopathic hemolytic anemia, and thrombocytopenia. The most common cause of hemolytic uremic syndrome in the world is E.coli O157:H7. The most common cause of hemolytic uremic syndrome in India is Shigella dysenteriae type I.

Other options:

Option A: Campylobacter is a slender, spirally curved, gram-negative bacillus. They grow at a slower rate and thus require selective media containing antibiotics like Skirrow's media for culture.

Option B: Yersinia enterocolitica causes diarrhea with symptoms resembling appendicitis (pseudoappendicitis). The patients present with abdominal pain which can be localized to the right iliac fossa, thus mimicking appendicitis. Additionally, it is a non-lactose fermenter.

Option D: Shigella dysenteriae type 1 can produce the Shiga toxin and result in a clinical profile similar to EHEC. But Shigella is a non-lactose fermenting organism, unlike E. coli, and will form pale colonies on MacConkey agar.

Enterobacteriaceae family is classified based on their action on lactose present in MacConkey's medium as,

Lactose fermenters

Escherichia, Klebsiella,Enterobacter

Late lactose fermenters

Shigella sonnei, Serratia, Citrobacter, Erwinia

Non-lactose fermenters

Salmonella, Shigella, Proteus

Mnemonic to remember Non-lactose fermenters: SPY PSM

* Salmonella

* Proteus

* Yersinia

* Providencia - late fermenter

* Shigella (Except S sonnie which is a late lactose fermenter)

* Morganella

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Which of the following is the causative organism of vulval warts?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Human papilloma virus

The causative agent of vulval warts is the human papillomavirus (HPV).

Genital warts/venereal warts/condyloma acuminata are verrucous growths that affect the skin of the labia majora, perineum, perianal region and vulva. The lesions may be discrete or coalesce to form cauliflower-like growth. The disease is sexually transmitted. The growth of the warts is favoured by vaginal discharge, the use of oral contraceptives, and pregnancy.

HPV causes structural changes in the epithelial cells of the skin called koilocytes, and their presence is characteristic of HPV infection. The koilocytes have large hyperchromatic nuclei and a perinuclear halo, as shown below.

The diagnosis is made by colposcopic studies. The lesions on the vulva are stained by toluidine blue. The abnormal areas of the skin retain the blue dye. These areas are then biopsied for histopathological examination.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Identify the type of joint shown in the given image.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Syndesmosis

The type of joint shown in the given image is syndesmosis.

The radius and ulna are united with each other by three joints:

* Proximal (superior) radioulnar joint

* Middle radioulnar joint

* Distal (inferior) radioulnar joint

Proximal and distal radioulnar joints are uniaxial pivot joints (synovial) and are involved in pronation and supination movements of the forearm.

The middle radioulnar joint is a fibrous joint (syndesmosis). The radius and ulna, in the middle, are connected by two syndesmoses namely:

* The oblique cord - extends from the lateral side of the ulnar tuberosity to the radius, distal to the radial tuberosity.

* Interosseous membrane - a broad, thin collagenous structure, which runs perpendicular to the oblique cord. It extends distomedially between the interosseous borders of the radius and ulna.

Based on the structure, joints are classified into three types:

* Fibrous joints

* Sutures

* Syndesmosis

* Gomphosis

* Cartilaginous joints

* Primary cartilaginous joints or synchondrosis

* Secondary cartilaginous joints or symphysis

* Synovial joints

* Ball-and-socket or spheroidal joints

* Sellar or saddle joints

* Condylar or bicondylar joints

* Ellipsoid joints

* Hinge joints

* Pivot or trochoid joints

* Plane joints

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: A 51-year-old man complains of abdominal pain and blood-stained stools. The barium study of his intestines shows the following finding. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Intussusception

The given clinical scenario and the radiological images are suggestive of intussusception.

In intussusception, the occluding mass prolapsing into the lumen has been termed the coiled spring appearance (barium in the lumen of the intussusceptum and in the intraluminal space). In adults, it develops due to a tumor of the bowel.

The intussusception appears as a sausage-shaped mass in a longitudinal plane or a target mass in the transverse plane on CT and USG.

Ultrasound signs include:

• Target sign (also known as the doughnut sign)
• Pseudokidney sign- this is seen in the longitudinal section of the bowel

• the edematous bowel resembles renal parenchyma and
• the mesentery which is dragged into the intussusception resembles renal hilum

• Crescent in a doughnut sign.

Note: The colographic appearance of intussusception is also described as a claw sign, pincer defect, shouldering effect, and coiled-spring pattern.

Option B: Volvulus presents with constipation, abdominal bloating, nausea, and/or vomiting. It shows coffee bean sign

Option C: Diverticulitis presents with pain in the left iliac fossa

Option D: Ulcerative colitis causes backwash ileitis

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A child is brought with complaints of multiple lesions. On examination, numerous vesicular lesions are observed on the palms, soles, and oral mucosa. Which organism is the most likely etiological agent responsible for this condition?
questions.explanation: The presence of multiple vesicular lesions on the palms, soles, and oral mucosa in a child is pathognomonic for Hand, Foot, and Mouth Disease (HFMD). This condition is most commonly caused by Coxsackie virus A16, although other strains like A6 and A10 can be involved. Varicella-zoster virus (Option A) causes chickenpox, presenting with a generalized rash mostly on the trunk and face. Human herpesvirus 6 (Option B) causes roseola, characterized by high fever followed by a maculopapular rash rather than vesicles. While Enterovirus (Option C) is the broader genus that includes Coxsackie viruses, "Coxsackie virus" is the more specific and prototypical etiological agent for this classic clinical triad in pediatric practice. Therefore, based on the specific anatomical distribution of the vesicles, Coxsackie virus is the most likely diagnosis

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: The partogram is plotted in regular intervals after _ cm dilatation:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. 4 cm

The partograph is plotted in regular intervals after 4 cm dilatation.

In a partograph, the labor process is divided into

1. Latent phase ends when cervix dilated upto 4 cm
2. Active phase begins with cervical dilatation of ≥6 cm and ends at 10 cm dilatation at the rate of 1 cm/hour.

The latent phase of labour is slow and extremely variable, while the active phase of labour is fairly predictable in terms of duration. Even though the active phase of labor is from more than 6cm dilatation, partograph is marked from 4 cm dilatation.

questions.subject: Psychiatry
questions.text: What is the most likely diagnosis in a 39-year- old man who repeatedly washes his hands 15–20 times daily due to persistent fears of contamination, resulting in significant impairment in his occupational functioning?
questions.explanation: The patient’s behavior fulfills the core diagnostic criteria for Obsessive-Compulsive Disorder (OCD) (Option B). OCD is characterized by the presence of obsessions (intrusive, persistent thoughts of contamination) and compulsions (repetitive behaviors like excessive hand washing) aimed at reducing the distress caused by the obsessions. These symptoms are time-consuming and lead to significant impairment in social or occupational functioning. Bipolar disorder (Option A) involves cycles of depression and mania, while Mania (Option D) is characterized by elevated mood and racing thoughts, not contamination obsessions. Schizophrenia (Option C) involves hallucinations and delusions. Because the patient's symptoms are specifically centered on a contamination ritual that he feels compelled to perform to neutralize his anxiety, OCD is the definitive psychiatric diagnosis. Management typically involves selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs) and cognitive-behavioral therapy

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 45-year-old patient is incidentally found to have an asymptomatic Grade I meningioma on MRI, confirmed by histopathology. What is the most appropriate initial management approach for this patient?
questions.explanation: A 45-year-old patient with a confirmed Grade I meningioma via histopathology is best managed with surgical excision. The histopathological confirmation itself implies tissue acquisition, and at this age with a confirmed tumor, definitive treatment is warranted. Gross Total Resection (GTR) offers potential cure with minimal recurrence rates, making surgery the gold standard. Why Other Options Are Wrong: A. Reassurance : While watch-and-wait suits truly incidental, unbiopsied, small meningiomas in elderly patients, a histopathologically confirmed tumor in a young 45-year-old demands definitive treatment due to long life expectancy and cumulative growth risk. C. Chemotherapy : Meningiomas are notoriously chemoresistant. No chemotherapeutic agent has proven efficacy in Grade I meningioma. Completely inappropriate here. D. Radiotherapy : Reserved for Grade II/III, post-operative residual disease, or surgically inaccessible tumors. It is not a primary treatment for resectable Grade I meningioma

questions.text: A 2-month-old baby presented with the following symptoms. What is the ideal treatment for the child?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Immediate surgery

Congenital cataract in infants is a vision-threatening condition requiring urgent surgical intervention to prevent irreversible amblyopia.

• Leukocoria (white pupillary reflex) in a 2-month-old
• Bilateral involvement in this image

Management principle:

• Immediate cataract extraction (ideally within first few weeks–months of life)
• Followed by:

• Optical correction (aphakic glasses/contact lens/IOL later)
• Amblyopia therapy

Why urgency matters:

• Visual development is critical in early infancy
• Delay → permanent visual impairment (deprivation amblyopia)

Why not others:

• Medical management has no role
• Delayed surgery → poor visual outcome

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: The ureter is safe in which type of hysterectomy?
questions.explanation: In vaginal hysterectomy, the ureter is considered to be at the lowest risk of injury compared to other surgical approaches. This is because the procedure is performed through the vaginal canal with minimal dissection near the ureters and fewer abdominal manipulations. In contrast, laparoscopic (Option B) and robotic (Option C) hysterectomies carry a higher risk of ureteric injury due to potential thermal damage from electrocautery and traction. Open laparotomy (Option A) also involves significant risk during the ligation of the uterine vessels or the cardinal ligaments where the ureter passes close by. While no surgery is entirely without risk, the anatomical approach used in vaginal hysterectomy provides the greatest degree of ureteric safety. Therefore, for patients without contraindications, the vaginal route is preferred for minimizing pelvic urinary tract complications

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A patient presenting with bleeding gums and easy bruisability was diagnosed with scurvy. This is due to ______.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Defective collagen formation

Bleeding gums and easy bruisability seen in scurvy are due to defective collagen formation.

Scurvy results from the deficiency of vitamin C, which is required for the hydroxylation of prolyl and lysyl residues of collagen reactions. Hence, deficiency of vitamin C results in a defective prolyl hydroxylase activity, leading to defective collagen formation and resulting in generalized bleeding tendencies.

Hemorrhagic manifestations of scurvy include petechiae, purpura, ecchymoses at pressure points, epistaxis, gum bleeding, and characteristic perifollicular hemorrhages. Other manifestations are poor wound and fracture healing, hyperkeratosis of hair follicles, arthralgia, and muscle weakness. It also results in defective osteoid formation. Costo-chondral separation leads to the formation of tender nodules that are sharply angulated and are also known as the scorbutic rosary.

The cutaneous manifestations of scurvy include

• Phrynoderma over posterolateral arms which can then generalize over the back and thighs and legs.
• Corkscrew hairs -  fractured and coiled hairs due to impaired keratin cross‐links by disulfide bonds
• Perifollicular hemorrhage and purpura
• Lower limb edema
• Splinter hemorrhages

It is treated with vitamin C supplementation.

Other options:

Option A: Low calcium levels do not cause scurvy; they may contribute to other clinical conditions like osteoporosis or muscle cramps.

Option C: Inhibition of clotting factors is not responsible for scurvy. Vitamin K deficiency, however, can lead to the inhibition of clotting factors and cause bleeding tendencies.

Option D: Increased keratinization of epithelium is not the cause of scurvy. Vitamin A deficiency, on the other hand, can result in hyperkeratoses and epithelial changes, such as xerosis and Bitot's spots.
