questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: Identify the swelling shown in the image below:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Ranula

A ranula is a mucus retention/extravasation cyst arising from the sublingual gland, presenting as a bluish, translucent, fluctuant swelling in the floor of the mouth, typically lateral to the lingual frenulum.

Key differentiating features:

• Ranula:

• Bluish, cystic swelling in the floor of the mouth
• Usually lateral to the midline
• Arises from the sublingual gland
• May enlarge into the neck (plunging/cervical ranula)

• Carcinoma of tongue:

• Ulceroproliferative or indurated lesion, often painful, associated with tobacco use

• Submandibular sialolithiasis:

• Painful swelling during meals with a palpable stone in Wharton’s duct

• Dermoid cyst:

• Midline doughy swelling in the floor of the mouth, classically described as “sac of marbles”

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.topic: General Pharmacology · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: Which of the following adverse effects is associated with long-term prophylactic use of nitrofurantoin?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Pulmonary fibrosis

Long-term prophylactic use of nitrofurantoin, especially for recurrent urinary tract infections, is classically associated with chronic pulmonary toxicity, leading to interstitial pneumonitis and pulmonary fibrosis. This occurs due to oxidative lung injury and immune-mediated mechanisms, typically after months to years of continuous therapy. Elderly patients are particularly susceptible, and symptoms include progressive dyspnea and dry cough.

Why other options are incorrect:

A. Tendon rupture: Seen with fluoroquinolones, not nitrofurantoin.

C. QT prolongation: Associated with macrolides and fluoroquinolones.

D. Optic neuritis: Classically linked to ethambutol.
questions.learning: Pulmonary fibrosis Long-term prophylactic use of nitrofurantoin, especially for recurrent urinary tract infections, is classically associated with chronic pulmonary toxicity, leading to interstitial pneumonitis and pulmonary fibrosis.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: The correct statement regarding the physiological changes in the respiratory system in pregnancy?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. FRC decreases

Functional residual capacity (FRC) decreases by 20 to 30 percent (400 to 700 mL) during pregnancy.

FRC = Expiratory Reserve Volume (ERV) + Residual Volume (RV). ERV decreases by 15 to 20 percent (200 to 300 mL). RV decreases by 20 to 25 percent (200 to 400 mL).

FRC and RV decline due to diaphragm elevation. Significant reductions occur by the sixth month with a progressive decline across pregnancy.

The increased minute ventilation during pregnancy is influenced by various factors. These include the stimulatory action of progesterone, reduced expiratory reserve volume, and compensatory respiratory alkalosis. Total lung capacity (FRC + IC) decreases in pregnancy.

Anatomical changes such as the elevation of the diaphragm, an increase in the subcostal angle, and an expansion of the transverse diameter of the thoracic cage are seen.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text:
Assertion: RMP is dependent on proteins and phosphate ions.
Reason: Diffusion potential can be calculated using Nernst Equation.

RMP- Resting membrane potential
options: The assertion is independently a true statement, but the reasons is independently a false statement.
The assertion is independently a false statement, but the reasons is independently a true statement.
Both assertion and reason are independently true and the reason is not the correct explanation for the assertion
Both assertion and reason are independently true and the reason is the correct explanation for the assertion
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Both assertion and reason are independently true and the reason is not the correct explanation for the assertion

Both assertion and reason are independently true and the reason is not the correct explanation for the assertion.

Resting membrane potential (RMP) is the difference in the electrical potentials between the cytoplasm of the cell and the extracellular space. It represents an equilibrium situation where the concentration gradient of ions across the membrane is equal and opposite to the electrical gradients.

Resting membrane potential is primarily influenced by sodium (Na+) and potassium (K+) ions, along with negatively charged intracellular proteins and organic phosphates. In neurons, the concentration of potassium is higher inside the cell, while sodium ions exhibit the opposite distribution. The establishment of this concentration difference is facilitated by the Na, K ATPase pump. Potassium ions passively move out of the cell, while sodium ions move into the cell.

The Goldman-Hodgkin-Katz equation is utilized to calculate the resting membrane potential since multiple ions are involved. Among these ions, potassium, which has the greatest conductance across the membrane at rest, becomes the primary contributor to the resting membrane potential.

Goldman-Hodgkin-Katz equation

The Nernst equation establishes a connection between the diffusion potential and the ion concentration difference across a membrane. The magnitude of the Nernst potential is determined by the ratio of the ion concentrations on the two sides of the membrane.

Nernst equation :

EMF(millivolts) = [61/z] X log [Co / Ci]

• EMF = electromotive force (Nernst potential)
• z = charge of ion
• Co = concentration outside
• Ci = concentration inside

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: In relation to which wall of the orbit is the canaliculi that opens into the lacrimal sac present?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Medial wall

The canaliculi that open into the lacrimal sac are present in relation to the medial wall of the orbit.

Anatomy

The lacrimal drainage system consists of the following structures:

* The puncta are openings on the lid margin.

* Each canaliculus (superior and inferior) has two parts:

* Vertical (2 mm)

* Horizontal (8 mm)

* The superior and inferior canaliculi usually unite to form the common canaliculus, which opens into the lateral wall of the lacrimal sac.

* A small flap of mucosa (Rosenmüller valve) overhangs the junction of the common canaliculus and the lacrimal sac and prevents the reflux of tears into the canaliculi.

* The lacrimal sac is 10–12 mm long and lies in the lacrimal fossa. The lacrimal bone and the frontal process of the maxilla separate the lacrimal sac from the middle meatus of the nasal cavity.

* The nasolacrimal duct is 12–18 mm long and is directed downwards, backward, and laterally.

Image: Lacrimal apparatus

Pearl PF1078: Structures opening into meatuses of nose

* Inferior meatus: Nasolacrimal duct, guarded by the valve of Hasner

* Middle meatus: Frontal sinus, maxillary sinus, anterior ethmoidal sinus. All these together form the osteo-meatal complex or Picadle’s circle.

* Superior meatus: Posterior ethmoidal sinus

* Sphenoethmoidal recess: Sphenoid sinus

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: With respect to long-term patency and durability of grafts used in coronary artery bypass graft (CABG) surgery, which graft material is known to provide the most long-lasting outcomes?
questions.explanation: In coronary artery bypass grafting (CABG), the durability of the graft is measured by its long-term patency rate. The Internal Mammary Artery (IMA), specifically the Left Internal Mammary Artery (LIMA), is the gold-standard graft material known for providing the most durable outcomes. IMA grafts have an exceptional 10-year patency rate of over 90% because their arterial wall is resistant to atherosclerosis. The long saphenous vein (Option A) is commonly used for multiple bypasses but has a significant risk of late occlusion, with only about 50% remaining patent after 10 years. PTFE (Option C) is a synthetic material used in peripheral grafts but is unsuitable and prone to failure in small-caliber coronary bypasses. The gastroepiploic artery (Option D) is an alternative arterial graft but is technically difficult and less durable than the IMA. Therefore, the internal mammary artery is the definitive superior choice for longevity

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Which of the following is NOT typically used for antenatal screening?
questions.explanation: In the context of antenatal screening and diagnosis, we categorize tests by the source of fetal genetic material. While (A), (B), and (C) are standard sources of fetal cells, peripheral lymphocytes from the mother are not used because they belong to the mother, not the fetus. Why (D) is the Correct Answer: Antenatal screening for genetic disorders (like Down Syndrome) requires fetal DNA. While modern Non-Invasive Prenatal Testing (NIPT) uses maternal blood, it analyzes cell-free fetal DNA (cffDNA) floating in the plasma, not the mother's own peripheral lymphocytes. Lymphocytes are part of the maternal immune system and do not carry the fetal genetic blueprint. Why the other options are used: (A) Cord blood: Obtained via cordocentesis (after 18 weeks), it provides rapid fetal karyotyping and is used to screen for fetal anemia or infections. (B) Amniotic fluid: Obtained via amniocentesis (15–20 weeks), it contains shed fetal cells (amniocytes) used for definitive chromosomal analysis. (C) Chorionic villi: Obtained via CVS (10–13 weeks), these placental tissues share the same genetic makeup as the fetus and are excellent for early screening of metabolic or genetic defects

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: The term “health worker” was first used by which committee?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Kartar Singh Committee

The Kartar Singh Committee (1973) introduced the concept and designation of the Multipurpose Health Worker (Health Worker) in India. It recommended integrating multiple vertical health programs at the peripheral level by creating:

• Male Health Worker (MPW-Male)
• Female Health Worker (MPW-Female)

It also recommended one Health Assistant (Male) and one Health Assistant (Female) to supervise health workers.

Why not the other options?

• A. Bhore Committee (1946): Proposed the comprehensive health service model and establishment of Primary Health Centres (PHCs), but did not introduce the term “health worker.”
• C. Mudaliar Committee (1962): Focused on strengthening existing PHCs and improving quality of health services.
• D. Jungalwalla Committee (1967): Recommended integration of health services, unified cadre, equal pay for equal work, and prohibition of private practice by government doctors.

questions.text: Which of the following conditions will shift the Oxygen-Hb dissociation curve to the left?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Alkalosis

An increase in the pH (alkalosis), shifts the O2-hemoglobin dissociation curve, to the left.

Oxygen-Hb dissociation curve (OHDC)

* This is a plot of the partial pressure of O2 and the % saturation of Hb with O2.

* It is normally sigmoid in shape.

* If OHDC is shifted to the right, it means that the affinity of Hb for O2 has become less (which favors O2 delivery) i.e. Higher the P50. (R - Right shift Releases oxygen)

Shift to the right is caused by: (Conditions with an increased requirement of O2 - metabolically active tissues)

* Hypoxia and Hypercarbia - Metabolically active tissues utilize O2 and tissues produce CO2

* ↓ pH - Secondary to increased CO2 production

* ↑ in temperature, heat

* ↑ in 2,3-DPG - increased anaerobic glycolysis

* Growth hormone, thyroid hormone, androgen - by increasing 2,3 DPG

* Sickle cell anemia - reduced affinity for O2

Shift to the left is caused by:

* ↑ pH (alkalosis)

* ↓ PCO2

* ↓ 2,3-DPG

* ↓ Temperature

* HbF

* Carboxyhemoglobin

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: What is the most likely diagnosis in a 35-year- old man who presents with scant, foul-smelling blood-stained discharge, associated hearing loss, and a persistent fever that does not subside?
questions.explanation: The symptoms of chronic ear discharge (likely due to cholesteatoma in an atticoantral type of CSOM) followed by a high, swinging "picket-fence" fever are characteristic of lateral sinus thrombophlebitis. This is a serious intracranial complication of ear infection where the infection spreads to the sigmoid or transverse dural sinuses. Hearing loss is common in CSOM. Meningitis (Option A) would present with severe neck stiffness and photophobia. A brain abscess (Option C) typically presents with signs of raised intracranial pressure and focal neurological deficits. An extradural abscess (Option D) is often asymptomatic or presents with a persistent deep-seated headache. The "foul-smelling blood-mixed discharge" indicates local tissue destruction. The characteristic "swinging" nature of the fever, caused by the periodic release of bacteria into the bloodstream from the thrombus, is the hallmark of lateral sinus involvement. Urgent surgical intervention and IV antibiotics are necessary

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.text: All of the following can be used for the identification of a dead body, except?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Nail

Among the options, nail is the least preferred in the identification of a dead body.

Nails have been used in the identification of dead bodies, however, their use has been deemed uncommon. Skeletal muscles are resistant to degradation and are therefore more likely to persist during decomposition, thus making them useful for the identification of corpses. It is also important to note that few studies show the amount of identical loci decreases with time.

Suitable samples for DNA analysis encompass several types of nucleated biological material, including but not limited to white blood cells, hair root bulb cells, and spermatozoa. In the past, a substantial quantity of samples was necessary for doing this analysis. However, the advent of the polymerase chain reaction (PCR), a technique capable of amplifying minute quantities of DNA, has enabled the identification of DNA from even the most limited samples.

When obtaining samples, whether from a deceased individual, a living victim, or the accused, the size of the sample that can be collected is typically not a significant concern. The collection of samples from various locations of staining inside the scene, the deceased, the surviving victim, or the accused can provide distinct challenges. These areas may consist of minute traces of blood, semen staining, and similar substances, necessitating meticulous collection procedures to mitigate the risk of contamination.

Blood and hair with intact follicles are utilized in both live and deceased individuals, while samples of the spleen can be obtained during post-mortem examinations. Additionally, buccal smears can be collected from living individuals. In situations where sexual assault is a potential occurrence, or in instances of suspicious deaths, it is advisable to collect vaginal, anal, and penile swabs. In the event of a potential delay in transporting samples to the laboratory, it is recommended that the samples be subjected to freezing conditions at a temperature of -20°C or as specifically directed by the laboratory.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text:
A child presents with a dog bite from a street dog. On examination, an abrasion of 1.5 cm is present, with slight oozing. Which of the following statements are correct?

1. Category 3 wound
2. Wash the wound with normal tap water for 15-20 minutes
3. Clean the wound with spirit
4. Loose suturing of the wound with a proper dressing
5. Equine immunoglobin is given at a dose of 40 IU/kg of body weight, twice
6. Intra-dermal vaccine is administered on days 0, 3, 7, 28
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. 1, 2, 3, 6

A child presenting with abrasion with slight oozing after a dog bite comes under category III. The correct statements are 1, 2, 3, and 6.

The following measures should be taken immediately to stop the contraction of rabies:

• Cleansing: The most important step in the prevention of rabies is washing the affected area with plenty of soap and water under a running tap for 15 minutes. This is a standard procedure that minimizes the contraction of rabies.
• Chemical treatment: After washing and drying the wound, disinfectants like povidone-iodine and spirit can be applied.
• Suturing: Bite wounds are not sutured generally. If suturing is unavoidable, rabies immunoglobulin should be infiltrated in the depth and around the wound, and suturing should be delayed by a few hours.
• In unavoidable situations, minimal loose sutures may be applied to arrest bleeding.
• Other measures: Local antibiotics and tetanus toxoids should be given.

Different wound categories for post-exposure prophylaxis:

Categories of wound
Post-exposure prophylaxis

Category I - touching or feeding animals, licks on intact skin
None

Category II - nibbling of uncovered skin, minor scratches, or abrasions
without bleeding
Immediate vaccination and
local treatment of the wound

Category III- single or multiple transdermal bites or scratches, licks on broken skin contacts with bats
Immediate vaccination and
administration of rabies
immunoglobulin; local
treatment of the wound

Post-exposure prophylaxis regimen for rabies:

Intramuscular regimen: In this regimen, 1 ml or 0.5 ml of vaccine is injected into the deltoid in patients with category II and III wounds.

• Essen regimen: A 5-dose regimen in which 1 dose of vaccine is given on days 0, 3, 7, 14, and 28.
• Zagreb regimen: A 4-dose multisite regimen in which 2 doses of vaccine are given on day 0, followed by 1 dose on days 7 and 21.

Intradermal regimen: In this regimen, 0.1 ml of injection is given at 2 sites on days 0, 3, 7, and 28.

Equine Rabies Immunoglobulin at a dose of 40 IU/kg (a maximum of 3000 IU) body weight is given once. It is given to all Category III bites and also Category II bites in the case of immune-compromised persons.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: A woman from Delhi travels to Ladakh, a high- altitude area, and soon after arrival develops breathlessness, headache, and lightheadedness. What is the primary underlying mechanism responsible for these symptoms?
questions.explanation: At high altitudes, the partial pressure of oxygen is lower, which stimulates peripheral chemoreceptors to increase the rate of pulmonary ventilation (hyperventilation). This compensatory mechanism results in an excessive removal of carbon dioxide (CO2) from the blood. The loss of CO2, which acts as an acid in the body, causes the blood pH to rise, leading to respiratory alkalosis. Respiratory acidosis (Option A) occurs with hypoventilation, where CO2 is retained, not at high altitudes. Metabolic alkalosis (Option B) is typically caused by loss of stomach acid from vomiting or diuretic use. Metabolic acidosis (Option D) is associated with conditions like renal failure, diarrhea, or diabetic ketoacidosis. Therefore, the acute hyperventilation in response to hypoxia specifically drives a respiratory alkalotic state until the kidneys compensate by excreting excess bicarbonate over several days
questions.learning: At high altitudes, the partial pressure of oxygen is lower, which stimulates peripheral chemoreceptors to increase the rate of pulmonary ventilation (hyperventilation).

questions.text: Which alternative method can be used for the procedure shown in the image below?

Correct answer: B. Arm span

The procedure shown in the image is the measurement of the height of a child using a stadiometer. The alternative method that can be used for the procedure is arm span. The proportion of arm span changes with age but is close to height.

For children older than 2 years of age, a stadiometer is used to measure their height. It is measured with the head in the Frankfurt plane, and the back of the head, thorax, buttocks, and heels all on the same axis as that of the stadiometer.

Arm span provides an assessment of proportionality. It is measured by asking the child to stand, the back against the wall with arms outstretched, and the distance between the tip of the middle fingers are measured.

The body proportion in a child is assessed by the ratio of the upper segment (US) and lower segment (LS) and by comparing the arm span with height.

A higher US:LS ratio is associated with bone disorders and conditions involving short-limb dwarfism, such as Turner syndrome, whereas a lower ratio is associated with hypogonadism and Marfan syndrome.

Other options:

Option-A: Head circumference is measured as the maximal circumference along the supraorbital ridge in the front and the occipital prominence at the back of the head. It is measured using a flexible tape. It reflects the brain growth in a child.

Option-C: Crown-rump length is used for the assessment of fetal growth as early as 6–8 weeks of gestation. This length is used to determine the gestational age in the first trimester.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A patient with symptoms of fatigue, pallor, and microcytic anemia undergoes stool microscopy examination as shown below. Which among the following statements is correct regarding the parasite?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Penetration of skin

The stool microscopy image shows the thin-shelled, oval egg of hookworm (Ancylostoma duodenale/Necator americanus). Hookworm infection commonly presents with iron deficiency (microcytic, hypochromic) anemia due to chronic intestinal blood loss.

• Infective filariform (L3) larvae of hookworms penetrate intact skin (typically bare feet), migrate through the lungs, are swallowed, and mature into adults in the small intestine.

Why not the other options?

• B. Consumption of contaminated water: Not the mode of transmission for hookworm (more typical of parasites such as Giardia).
• C. Fertilized egg of Ascaris: Ascaris lumbricoides is acquired by ingestion of embryonated eggs, not by skin penetration.
• D. Unfertilized egg of Enterobius vermicularis: Enterobius is transmitted by ingestion of infective eggs; diagnosis is by the Scotch tape test, not stool microscopy.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Which of the following is a rate-limiting enzyme of HMP pathway?
questions.explanation: The Hexose Monophosphate (HMP) shunt, or pentose phosphate pathway, is essential for generating NADPH and ribose-5-phosphate. The rate-limiting and primary regulated enzyme of this pathway is Glucose-6-Phosphate Dehydrogenase (G6PD). It catalyzes the irreversible oxidation of glucose-6-phosphate to 6-phosphogluconolactone, while reducing to . Glucose-6-phosphatase (Option A) is the terminal enzyme of gluconeogenesis and glycogenolysis in the liver. Phosphofructokinase-1 (Option C) is the rate-limiting enzyme of glycolysis. Glycogen phosphorylase (Option D) is the rate-limiting enzyme of glycogenolysis. G6PD deficiency is the most common enzyme-related genetic disorder worldwide. In red blood cells, NADPH is critical for maintaining glutathione in its reduced state, which protects the cells from oxidative damage. Patients with G6PD deficiency are prone to hemolytic anemia when exposed to oxidative stress from infections, certain fava beans, or drugs like primaquine and sulfonamides. This clinical correlation makes G6PD a high-priority topic in biochemistry

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: A 13-year old boy with presents to you with limitation of abduction and internal rotation of the left hip. The X-ray appearance of his left hip joint is shown in the below image. What is the diagnosis of this patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Slipped capital femoral epiphysis

The given clinical scenario and trethowan's sign seen in the x-ray are suggestive of slipped capital femoral epiphysis (SCFE).

The Klein line is a line along the superior aspect of the femoral neck which normally intersects the epiphysis. In SCFE, Klein's line does not intersect the epiphysis and passes superior to it. This is known as Trethowan's sign.

Slipped femoral capital epiphysis:

SCFE occurs during the period of rapid growth with the average age of presentation around 12 years.

Risk factors: Obesity, hypothyroidism, growth hormone excess, and chronic renal failure are all-important associations of SCFE.

Clinical features:

* Patients with SCFE typically present in the rapid growth phase of adolescence with pain in the thigh, groin, or knee.

* On examination, the affected limb is shortened and externally rotated.

* There is a limitation in abduction, flexion, and internal rotation on the affected side.

* Flexion of the hip might lead to obligate external rotation and abduction - positive Drehmann’s sign.

* Patients may have an antalgic or Trendelenburg gait.

Other radiological findings include:

* Wide or irregular physis with loss of the anterior head-neck concavity

* Sharp metaphyseal border of the head

* Loss of total epiphyseal height

* Steel sign (Metaphyseal blanch sign) - The posteriorly displaced femoral epiphysis overlaps over the metaphysis causing a crescent-shaped area of increased density on the AP radiograph.

* Capener’s sign –the metaphysis displaces laterally, worsening the slip and causes a reduction in the double-density crescent created by the overlap of the posterior acetabulum and proximal metaphysis on the AP radiograph.

* Southwick angle – The angle between the line drawn perpendicular to the physis and a line parallel to the femoral shaft. As slip worsens, the Southwick angle will increase. It is measured on the frog lateral X-ray view.

Other options:

Perthes disease:

It is characterized by idiopathic avascular necrosis of the proximal femoral epiphysis. This condition commonly affects children of 4-8 years of age. The child has pain in the hip while performing passive movements. The radiograph shows features of bone necrosis followed by remodeling.

Developmental Dysplasia of the hip: It is characterized by spontaneous dislocation of the hip joint before, during, or shortly after birth. This condition is more common in females. Children with this condition have a waddling gait and on examination abduction and lateral rotation of the hip are decreased. X-ray shows a broken Shenton's line and the femoral head lies in the upper and outer quadrants formed by Hilgenreiner’s line and Perkin’s line.

The image given below shows the vertical Perkin's line and the horizontal Hilgenreiner's line. Normally the femoral head lies in the inner and lower quadrant formed by these lines. But in DDH the femoral head is in the upper and outer quadrant.

Ankylosing spondylitis: It is a chronic progressive inflammatory condition affecting the sacroiliac joints and the axial skeleton. It is commonly seen in young male adults and they typically present with an insidious onset back pain that improves with exercise. The earliest radiological finding is erosion and fuzziness of the sacroiliac joints and the characteristic late sign is the bamboo-spine appearance.

X-ray showing bamboo-spine appearance-

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Based on the image, what condition has developed three days after catheterization?
questions.explanation: The image displays extensive necrotic sloughing of the scrotal skin, which is the hallmark of Fournier's gangrene. This is a rapidly progressive necrotizing fasciitis of the perineum and genitalia. While it can be idiopathic, it often follows local trauma or instrumentation, such as catheterization in a high-risk patient (e.g., diabetic). Gas gangrene (Option B) involves muscle necrosis and crepitus, usually in the limbs. Wet gangrene (Option C) is a more general term for infected necrotic tissue. Scrotal hematoma (Option D) would appear as a tense, purple swelling but not as open necrotic sloughing. Fournier's gangrene is a surgical emergency with a high mortality rate. It requires immediate, aggressive surgical debridement of all non-viable tissue, broad-spectrum intravenous antibiotics, and intensive supportive care. The goal of surgery is to stop the spread of the polymicrobial infection along the fascial planes. Early recognition of the "dirty" dishwater-fluid and necrotic skin is vital for saving the patient's life

• Hypersomnia (sleeping up to 18–20 hours a day),

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: What is the most common cause of breech presentation in pregnancy? (NEET PG 2016)
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Prematurity

Breech presentation is more common in preterm pregnancies because the fetus is smaller and has greater mobility within the uterine cavity.

As pregnancy advances:

• Most fetuses spontaneously rotate to a cephalic presentation by term
• Premature fetuses may not yet have undergone this rotation

Thus, prematurity is the most common cause of breech presentation.

Other causes/risk factors for breech presentation:

• Uterine anomalies
• Placenta previa
• Polyhydramnios or oligohydramnios
• Multiple gestation
• Fetal anomalies (eg, hydrocephalus)
questions.learning: Prematurity Breech presentation is more common in preterm pregnancies because the fetus is smaller and has greater mobility within the uterine cavity.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: An elderly lady presents with abdominal pain and distension. She has a history of scoliosis. Given below is the erect X-ray abdomen radiograph of the lady. What is the most likely diagnosis?
options: Large bowel obstruction due to sigmoid volvulus
Large bowel obstruction due to fecolith
Small bowel obstruction due to bowel perforation
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Large bowel obstruction due to sigmoid volvulus

The given clinical scenario with an old woman and the radiograph showing characteristic coffee bean appearance are highly suggestive of sigmoid volvulus causing a large bowel obstruction.

Sigmoid volvulus is a cause of large bowel obstruction and occurs when the sigmoid colon twists on the sigmoid mesocolon. Symptoms include constipation, abdominal bloating, nausea, and/or vomiting. The onset may be acute or chronic. It occurs more commonly in patients with a history of mental illness and chronic constipation.

X-ray abdomen shows a large, dilated loop of the colon, often with a few air-fluid levels. Specific signs include the coffee bean sign, Frimann-Dahl sign (three dense lines converge towards the site of obstruction), and the absence of rectal gas. CT may reveal a large gas-filled loop without haustral markings, forming a closed-loop obstruction.

Here are some pointers that help in differentiating the two volulus:

Sigmoid volvulus
Cecal volvulus

More common incidence
Less common incidence

Coffee bean sign is typical.
Coffee bean sign is occassionally seen

Seen in old age, psychiatric patients
Usually seen in those aged 30-60 years old

The top of the sigmoid volvulus usually lies very high in the abdomen with its apex on the left side.

• In half the patients, the caecum twists and inverts so that the pole of the caecum and the appendix occupy the left upper quadrant.
•

In other patients, the twist occurs in an axial plane without inversion and the caecum still occupies the right half of the abdomen.

Haustra aren't usually seen
Haustra usually seen

Multiple air-fluid level seen
One air-fluid level seen

Attached air-filled appendix can be seen

Other options:

Option B: In large bowel obstruction due to fecolith, the presence of haustrations is a feature. Haustral folds are irregular and do not cross the entire diameter of the bowel. These are absent in the cecum. The given image shows haustrations in large bowel obstruction.

The following image shows an x-ray radiograph of large bowel obstruction:

Option C: Cecal volvulus shows characteristic radiological findings like cecal dilatation, single air-fluid level that may extend into the left upper quadrant, and absence of gas in the distal colon. The colonic haustrations are well maintained.

The following image shows an x-ray radiograph of cecal volvulus:

Option D: In small bowel obstructions, the obstructed bowel loops are central in location and lie transversely. The jejunal obstruction shows valvulae conniventes (mucosal folds that cross the entire diameter of the bowel) giving it a ladder effect. The distended cecum may show the presence of gas shadow in the right iliac fossa.

Common causes of small bowel obstruction are adhesions (~60%), neoplasms (~20%), hernias (~10%), Crohn's disease (~5%) and other miscellaneous conditions (~5%).

The following image shows an x-ray radiograph of small bowel obstruction:

Cases of bowel perforation have an erect abdominal radiograph showing free gas under the diaphragm. A supine radiograph may show dilated gas-filled loops of the bowel, suggestive of paralytic ileus.

The below radiograph image shows a hollow viscus perforation:
questions.learning: Large bowel obstruction due to sigmoid volvulus — The given clinical scenario with an old woman and the radiograph showing characteristic coffee bean appearance are highly suggestive of sigmoid volvulus causing a large bowel obstruction.

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text:
Arrange the following in the correct sequence for the Thomas test:

1. Squaring of pelvis
2. Flexion of the hip
3. Look for exaggerated lumbar lordosis
4. Measure actual flexion deformity
5. Ensure that ischial tuberosity touches the ground
6. Monitor for overcorrection of the normal side
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. 3,2,6,5,4

Among the given options, the correct sequence for the Thomas test is given by option C i.e. 3,2,6,5,4.

Thomas test is used to detect flexion deformity of the hip. Flexion deformity is a common hip deformity, often caused by stronger flexor muscles overpowering the extensor muscles. When there is a spasm of the muscles, the stronger flexors pull the hip in flexion. Soft tissue contractures can convert this into a fixed flexion deformity, making locomotion impossible.

Steps of Thomas test:

• Positioning: The patient is instructed to lie supine on a hard surface with their legs fully extended.
• Observing lumbar lordosis: As the patient assumes the supine position, the curvature of the lower back is visually assessed for any exaggerated lumbar lordosis. It is noted that excessive lumbar lordosis may be a compensatory response to a flexion deformity.
• Gradual flexion of the normal hip: The normal hip is gradually flexed, with care taken not to exceed its normal range of motion.
• Monitoring for overcorrection: During the flexion of the normal hip, signs of overcorrection on the normal side are observed, such as the pelvis starting to lift off the ground. To prevent this, both ischial tuberosities are ensured to remain in contact with the surface.
• Automatic positioning of the affected hip: As a result of the flexion of the normal hip, the affected hip automatically assumes the deformed position characterized by flexion.
• Measuring the degree of flexion: Once the affected hip is in the flexed position, the angle formed between the affected thigh and the bed is measured. This angle represents the actual degree of flexion deformity.
questions.learning: 3,2,6,5,4 Among the given options, the correct sequence for the Thomas test is given by option C i.e. Thomas test is used to detect flexion deformity of the hip.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Which of the following is a true association with HRT?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Decreases risk of Colon cancer

HRT decreases the risk of colon cancer.

Indications of HRT:

• Therapeutic

• Symptomatic women who suffer from estrogen deficiency
• Gonadal dysgenesis in adolescents

• Prophylactic

• High-risk cases for menopausal complications such as cardiovascular disease, osteoporosis(Option D), stroke, Alzheimer’s disease, and colonic cancer
• Premature menopause, spontaneous or following surgery
• Menopause caused by radiotherapy and chemotherapy for cancer, especially alkylating agents
• Women demanding HRT as prophylaxis

Contraindications of HRT:

• Undiagnosed abnormal genital bleeding
• Known, suspected, or history of breast cancer
• Known or suspected estrogen-dependent neoplasia
• Active or prior venous thromboembolism
• Active or recent (e.g., within the past year) arterial thromboembolic disease
• Liver dysfunction or gallbladder disease
• Known hypersensitivity to the ingredients of the estrogen preparation
• Known or suspected pregnancy
• Uterine fibroids as the fibroids may enlarge in size.

Uses of HRT:

• Short term-hot flushes, vasomotor symptoms
• Dyspareunia, libido
• Urethral syndrome
• Long term-osteoporosis
• Cardiovascular disease
• Alzheimer’s disease

Risks of HRT:

• Endometrial cancer(Option C)
• Breast cancer(Option B)
• Ovarian cancer
• Thromboembolism
• Lipid profile dysfunction
• Gall stones, liver dysfunction

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: During the procedure shown below, which substance is taken up by the cancer cells?
questions.explanation: The image depicts a Positron Emission Tomography (PET) scan, which is a functional imaging technique used to visualize metabolic processes in the body. The most common tracer used is Fluorodeoxyglucose (FDG), a radioactive analog of glucose. Cancer cells characteristically exhibit a high rate of glycolysis to support their rapid proliferation (the Warburg effect), and therefore avidly uptake glucose at much higher levels than normal tissues. This "hot spot" uptake allows PET scans to identify primary tumors, assess for metastatic spread, and monitor the response to treatment. Alanine (Option A), Sodium (Option C), and Calcium (Option D) are not the standard metabolic tracers used for general oncological PET imaging. Clinicians must be aware that normal tissues with high glucose demand, like the brain and heart, will also show significant uptake. Therefore, PET results must be carefully correlated with anatomical imaging like CT or MRI
questions.learning: The image depicts a Positron Emission Tomography (PET) scan, which is a functional imaging technique used to visualize metabolic processes in the body.

questions.subject: Anaesthesia
questions.text: A patient planned for elective hip surgery is currently on aspirin, enalapril, a multivitamin, and metoprolol. The procedure is scheduled to take place in five days. What is the most appropriate perioperative management of these medications?
options: Stop aspirin to minimize perioperative bleeding risk
Stop metoprolol to increase cardiac output
Increase aspirin dosage for additional analgesic benefit
questions.explanation: ACE inhibitors like enalapril should typically be discontinued 24 hours prior to elective surgery to prevent clinically significant intraoperative hypotension. Orthopedic procedures, such as the hip surgery mentioned, generally allow the continuation of aspirin (Option B) because the cardiovascular risks of stopping it often outweigh the modest bleeding risk. Beta-blockers like metoprolol (Option C) must always be continued perioperatively; abrupt withdrawal can lead to dangerous sympathetic hyperactivity, tachycardia, hypertension, myocardial ischemia, or mortality. Increasing the aspirin dosage (Option D) has no proven analgesic benefit in this context and only serves to increase the surgical bleeding risk unnecessarily. Standard preoperative management usually involves continuing most chronic medications, such as antiepileptics, antidepressants, and calcium channel blockers, while specifically stopping ACE inhibitors and certain hypoglycemics. Therefore, the most appropriate step for this patient is to discontinue the enalapril one day before the procedure to ensure hemodynamic stability during anesthesia
questions.learning: ACE inhibitors like enalapril should typically be discontinued 24 hours prior to elective surgery to prevent clinically significant intraoperative hypotension.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Carotenoderma, due to ingestion of excessive amounts of carotene-containing fruits and vegetables, can be distinguished from jaundice by sparing of which of the following?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Sclerae

Carotenoderma results from excessive intake of β-carotene-rich foods (e.g., carrots, pumpkin, sweet potatoes). It causes yellow-orange discoloration of the skin, especially over the palms, soles, and nasolabial folds, but spares the sclerae, distinguishing it from jaundice, in which scleral icterus is the earliest clinical sign.

Why not the other options?

• A. Palms: Commonly affected in carotenoderma.
• B. Soles: Commonly affected in carotenoderma.
• C. Nasolabial folds: May also show yellow discoloration.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A patient with papillary carcinoma thyroid underwent thyroidectomy. She developed hoarseness of voice after surgery. Which of the following steps in surgery could not have resulted in this complication?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Division of strap muscles

The patient presenting with hoarseness of voice post thyroidectomy can be due to injury to external laryngeal nerve or unilateral recurrent laryngeal nerve. The step in thyroidectomy where it is least to happen is during division of strap muscles.

Recurrent laryngeal nerve is related to the posterior branch of the inferior thyroid artery near the lobes of the thyroid gland. Therefore, during surgery, Inferior thyroid artery is ligated close to the gland to avoid injury to the recurrent laryngeal nerve.

Thyroid surgery may cause injury to both external and recurrent laryngeal nerves (RLN). During thyroidectomy surgeries, there might be unilateral or bilateral recurrent laryngeal nerve injury. Unilateral RLN injury may be asymptomatic but in a few may cause hoarseness of voice.
Bilateral recurrent laryngeal nerve palsy can also occur postoperatively. It causes dyspnea and stridor but the voice is good. These cases required emergency tracheostomy. External laryngeal nerve injury is more common and could result in hoarseness of voice.

Other options

Option B: The RLN frequently passes immediately medial to the tubercle of Zuckerkandl. In order to find and protect RLN during thyroid surgery, a careful, bloodless, and meticulous dissection should be carried out around the tubercle.

Option C: Beahrs’ triangle is bounded by common carotid artery as base, inferior thyroid artery superiorly and RLN as the lower arm of triangle. Recognizing the boundaries of the triangle posterior to thyroid after retracting the ipsilateral thyroid lobe medially, helps in avoiding RLN injury.

Option D: The external branch of the superior laryngeal nerve courses along the cricothyroid muscle just medial to the superior pole vessels. To avoid injury to this nerve, the superior pole vessels are divided individually as close as possible to the point where they enter the thyroid gland
questions.learning: Division of strap muscles — The patient presenting with hoarseness of voice post thyroidectomy can be due to injury to external laryngeal nerve or unilateral recurrent laryngeal nerve.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: A newborn baby is brought to the OPD with complaints of noisy breathing. On performing Direct laryngoscopy, you notice the following findings. Which of the following stridor is seen in this patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Inspiratory stridor

The above clinical scenario along with the laryngoscopy image showing omega-shaped epiglottis is suggestive of laryngomalacia. Inspiratory stridor is seen in laryngomalacia.

Laryngomalacia is the most common congenital cause of stridor. It is characterized by excessive flaccidity of the supraglottic larynx which is sucked in during inspiration. This results in inspiratory stridor, a feature typical of laryngomalacia.

It presents just after birth and subsides by 2 years of age. Stridor is increased on crying but improves (decreases) in the prone position, and worsens during feeding or crying. The cry is normal.

Direct laryngoscopy shows an elongated epiglottis that is curled upon itself, making it appear omega (Ω)-shaped. Other features include floppy aryepiglottic folds and prominent arytenoids.

Stridor is noisy respiration produced by turbulent airflow through narrowed air passages. Stridor may be heard during inspiration, expiration or both

* Inspiratory stridor is seen in supraglottic lesions. It is often produced in obstructive lesions of the supraglottis or pharynx, e.g. laryngomalacia or retropharyngeal abscess.

* Expiratory stridor is produced in lesions of thoracic trachea, primary and secondary bronchi, e.g. bronchial foreign body, and tracheal stenosis.

* Biphasic stridor is seen in lesions of the glottis, subglottis, and cervical trachea, e.g. laryngeal papillomas, vocal cord paralysis, and subglottic stenosis.

Treatment of Laryngomalacia:

* Mostly, it self corrects by 2 years of age.

* Tracheostomy may be required for some cases of severe respiratory obstruction.

* Supraglottoplasty is required in cases of severe laryngomalacia.
questions.learning: Inspiratory stridor — The above clinical scenario along with the laryngoscopy image showing omega-shaped epiglottis is suggestive of laryngomalacia. Inspiratory stridor is seen in laryngomalacia.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following foods is not included in the DASH diet?
questions.explanation: The DASH diet (Dietary Approaches to Stop Hypertension) is a standardized nutritional plan designed to lower blood pressure. It is specifically characterized by being low in sodium (Option C is the correct "not included" choice). The diet emphasizes foods that are rich in potassium (Option A), calcium (Option B), and magnesium (Option D). These minerals help relax blood vessels and improve cardiac health. The DASH plan encourages the consumption of fruits, vegetables, whole grains, and low-fat dairy while strictly limiting salt (sodium), red meat, and added sugars. High sodium intake is a primary driver of fluid retention and elevated blood pressure. Therefore, because the fundamental goal of the diet is to reduce salt intake to either 2,300 mg or 1,500 mg per day, a "rich in sodium" diet is the definitive opposite of the DASH philosophy
questions.learning: The DASH diet (Dietary Approaches to Stop Hypertension) is a standardized nutritional plan designed to lower blood pressure. It is specifically characterized by being low in sodium (Option C is the correct "not included" choice).

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: An infant was brought to the OPD with complaints of poor feeding and irritability. On examination, neck rigidity was present. Her sister has been on antitubercular therapy for 2 months. What are the CSF analysis findings expected in this child?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Lymphocytosis, low sugar, high protein

The given clinical scenario, along with a neck stiffness and contact with patient of tuberculosis is suggestive of TB meningitis. The CSF picture is lymphocytosis, with low sugar and high protein

Tuberculous meningitis is the most severe form of tuberculosis.

Predisposing factors

* Young age

* Household contact

* Recent measles

* Protein-energy malnutrition

After the initial infection, the disease presents with vague symptoms accompanied by intermittent bacillemia. These feed the meninges forming Rich's foci. When the body's immunity is lowered during stress or coinfections, these ruptures cause widespread meningitis

Clinical Features

* Prodromal phase: irregular fever, anorexia, irritability and occasional vomiting. These could last 1 to 4 weeks

* The second stage has the nervous system involvement, with seizures, focal deficits and meningeal signs.

* The third stage is one of coma and sequelae like Hydrocephalus (communicating or obstructive), decerebrate posturing, cranial nerve palsies, optic atrophy, extrapyramidal signs, and focal deficits.

Diagnosis:

* CSP typically shows raised pressure, lymphocytic predominance, high protein, and low sugar

* Imaging can show exudates and if present, features of the sequelae

* The diagnosis is confirmed detection of tubercular bacilli in CSF. This can be by culture or cartridge-based tests like Gene Xpert

Treatment includes antitubercular treatment with two months of four drug-intensive therapy(HRZE) and 10 months of two-drug (maintenance) therapy  Sometimes, intravenous is dexamethasone is followed by oral administered for 8-12 weeks. This is to prevent sequelae of TB.. Patients with severe hydrocephalus may require shunts or ventriculostomy

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Which of the following is an orexigenic hormone?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Ghrelin

Ghrelin is an orexigenic hormone that increases appetite.

Ghrelin is produced by the oxyntic gland area of the stomach and is primarily involved in the central control of food intake. It is also secreted by the pancreas and adrenal glands.

Functions

* Increases appetite/food intake (orexigenic)

* It stimulates growth hormone secretion by directly acting on the anterior pituitary

* It increases gastric acid secretion and gastrointestinal motility to prepare the body for food intake

* It regulates the distribution and rate of use of energy

* It suppresses the action of leptin and increases the production of neuropeptide Y. It also causes lipolysis

Ghrelin levels increase during fasting, peaking just before food intake begins or when the subject is expecting a meal. The levels fall within 1 hour of the start of feeding.

Melanocyte-stimulating hormone, cholecystokinin, and leptin are anorexigenic and they decrease the appetite.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: The strict anaerobe among the following is __________.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Prevotella

The strict anaerobe in the given options is Prevotella.

Prevotella species are gram-negative rods or coccobacilli. The most commonly isolated Prevotella species are P melaninogenica, Prevotella bivia, and Prevotella disiens. P melaninogenica is associated with upper respiratory tract infections. P bivia and P disiens occur in the female genital tract. Prevotella species are also found in brain and lung abscesses, empyema, pelvic inflammatory disease and tubo-ovarian abscesses.

Other options

Option A: Burkholderia cepacia belongs to the pseudomonad group and is gram-negative, aerobic rods.

Option B: Yersinia enterocolitica are gram-negative facultative anaerobes.

Option C: Stenotrophomonas maltophilia also belong to the pseudomonad group and are gram-negative, aerobic rods.
questions.learning: Prevotella — The strict anaerobe in the given options is Prevotella. Prevotella species are gram-negative rods or coccobacilli.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Which part of the placenta is shown in this picture?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Fetal side

Fetal side of the placenta is depicted in the picture.

Placenta has two components - basal plate (the one on the maternal side) and chorionic plate (the one towards the fetal side which gives rise to the chorionic villi).

Usually, in a normal placenta, both basal and chorionic plates end simultaneously at the margin of the placenta.

The fetal surface, known as the chorionic plate, creates the roof of the intervillous space and is covered by the amnion, a thin avascular membrane. This plate contains chorionic vessels that branch from the umbilical vessels and is composed of distinct layers including the amniotic epithelium, connective tissue layer, primary stem villi containing fetal vessels, and both cytotrophoblast and syncytiotrophoblast layers. This complex arrangement facilitates the crucial transfer of nutrients and gases between mother and fetus.

The placental structure, from the maternal aspect, begins with the basal plate which forms the maternal floor of the intervillous space (Option B). This critical interface contains multiple components arranged in layers, including the decidual layer (composed of decidual cells from the endometrium) (Option A), the fibrinoid or Nitabuch's layer (containing fibrin deposits marking the boundary between maternal and fetal tissues), and the cytotrophoblastic shell. The basal plate is characterized by grooves that create cotyledons and houses the spiral arteries and veins from maternal circulation, making it essential for maternal-fetal exchange  (Option D).
questions.learning: Fetal side Fetal side of the placenta is depicted in the picture. Placenta has two components - basal plate (the one on the maternal side) and chorionic plate (the one towards the fetal side which gives rise to the chorionic villi).

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Which of the following drug dosages is not correct for the treatment of leprosy in adults?
questions.explanation: In the standard World Health Organization (WHO) Multi-Drug Therapy (MDT) for adult leprosy, the correct dose of Rifampicin is 600 mg administered once a month under supervision. A dose of 450 mg (Option D) is incorrect for adults; this lower dose is specifically designated for children aged 9–14 years. Regarding the correct dosages, Dapsone 100 mg (Option A) is the daily self-administered dose for both paucibacillary and multibacillary adult patients. For multibacillary cases, Clofazimine is administered as a 300 mg monthly supervised dose (Option C) combined with a 50 mg daily self-administered dose (Option B). Because the adult regimen relies on the higher 600 mg Rifampicin dose to ensure bactericidal activity against Mycobacterium leprae, 450 mg is inadequate and therefore the incorrect adult dosage in this list
questions.learning: In the standard World Health Organization (WHO) Multi-Drug Therapy (MDT) for adult leprosy, the correct dose of Rifampicin is 600 mg administered once a month under supervision.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: For a child with myopia, presenting with symptoms such as holding books close and squinting while watching TV, which type of lenses is recommended to correct his vision?
questions.explanation: Myopia, or nearsightedness, is a refractive error where the eye is too powerful or too long, causing light rays to focus in front of the retina rather than directly on it. This results in clear near vision but blurred distance vision, explaining the child's behavior. To correct myopia, concave (minus) lenses (Option B) are required. These are "diverging" lenses that move the focal point backward, precisely positioning it onto the retinal surface. Convex (plus) lenses (Option A) are "converging" lenses used to correct hypermetropia (farsightedness). Cylindrical lenses (Option C) are used to correct astigmatism by compensating for an irregular corneal shape. A combination of concave and convex (Option D) refers to bifocal or complex multifocal lenses which are not the standard primary correction for simple childhood myopia. Therefore, the concave lens is the definitive pharmacological and physical corrective tool for a nearsighted child
questions.learning: Myopia, or nearsightedness, is a refractive error where the eye is too powerful or too long, causing light rays to focus in front of the retina rather than directly on it.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: The cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) specimen of a patient is shown below along with the microscopy. The report shows mononuclear cytosis, elevated proteins, and low sugars. Which of the following is the likely etiology?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Tuberculous meningitis

The given clinical scenario along with the cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) sample with cobweb-like clot and slide showing lymphocytic predominance points to a diagnosis of tubercular meningitis.

Tuberculous meningitis caused by Mycobacterium tuberculosis is caused by the formation of tubercles in the brain parenchyma. This happens during the hematogenous spread of the bacilli during primary infection. It can also be due to the rupture of a subependymal tubercle into the subarachnoid space.

Tuberculous meningitis presents as a subacute infection and has a longer course than bacterial meningitis. Ocular nerve palsy is a common association as there is marked meningeal involvement at the base of the brain. The patient can also develop hydrocephalus.

The CSF sample shows a pellicle or cobweb-like clots. Acid-fast bacilli can be best isolated from these. There is usually lymphocytic leukocytosis, low glucose concentration, and elevated proteins. CSF culture remains the gold standard for diagnosis.

The clinical triad of fever, headache, and nuchal rigidity is common to all types of meningitis. Nuchal rigidity is the resistance of the neck to passive flexion and is pathognomonic of meningeal irritation. Kernig's and Brudzinski's signs are other features of meningeal irritation. Raised intracranial pressure (ICP) is a complication that presents as papilledema, disorientation, or dilated poorly reactive pupils.

Other options:

Option B - Aseptic meningitis is commonly caused by enteroviruses such as coxsackieviruses, and varicella-zoster virus. It is more benign and usually self-limiting compared to pyogenic meningitis. Gram's staining of the CSF sample shows lymphocytosis but not the organism.

Option C - Bacterial meningitis is most commonly caused by Streptococcus pneumoniae and Neisseria meningitidis. Blood culture can be used for diagnosis. CSF findings are described in the pearl below. Antibiotic prophylaxis is provided to the close contacts of persons with confirmed meningococcal disease.

Option D - Chemical meningitis is a common cause of chronic meningitis. It can arise due to the rupture of tumor contents from a cystic glioma, dermoid cyst, or craniopharyngioma into the CSF.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: A woman arrived at the hospital with edema, visual disturbances, and heart failure after consuming a food item purchased from a seller who has now been arrested for food adulteration. Which of the following is the most likely food adulterant used? Beta-oxalyl amino alanine (BOAA)
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Sanguinarine

The clinical presentation of edema, visual disturbances, and heart failure after consuming a food item purchased from a seller who has now been arrested for food adulteration is suggestive of epidemic dropsy. Sanguinarine is the toxic compound responsible for this.

Sanguinarine causes Epidemic Dropsy.

* Contamination of mustard oil with argemone oil.

* Toxic compound: Sanguinarine

Mechanism of action : Sanguinarine interfers with the oxidation of pyruvic acid which in turn accumulates in the blood and causes symptoms.

Clinical presentation: The patient presents with sudden onset, non-inflammatory swelling of bilateral legs which is often associated with diarrhoea. Some patients can develop glaucoma. Dyspnea, cardiac failure and death can occur in later stages.

Tests to detect argemone oil:

* Nitric acid test

* Paper chromatography: most sensitive(can detect very low concentration of argemone oil)

Other options:

Option A: Aflatoxins are produced by certain fungi, such as Aspergillus flavus and Aspergillus parasiticus, are the most potent hepatotoxins. These fungi can contaminate food grains such as groundnut, maize, parboiled rice, sorghum, wheat, and tapioca. It is mainly due to improper storage. It can be prevented by proper storage after drying. Moisture content should be kept below 10%. They do not cause the symptoms described in the question.

Option C: Lathyrism is a paralyzing disease of humans and animals and Beta-oxalyl amino alanine (BOAA) is the toxic compound causing this disease. Gradual spastic paralysis of lower limbs is associated with the consumption of Khesari dal/Lathyrus sativus leading to neurolathyrism.

Option D: Rapidly developing ascites and jaundice is associated with the consumption of millets contaminated with weed seeds of Crotalaria/Jhunjhunia which contain a toxic pyrrolizidine alkaloid and produce symptoms of endemic ascites, that manifest as rapidly developing ascites and jaundice.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: Pick the correct statement regarding the Sanchol cholera vaccine
options: Bivalent vaccine given in 2 liquid doses orally to children >=1 year of age
Bivalent given in single dose orally to children >1 years of age
Monovalent given in 2 liquid doses orally with a bicarbonate buffer
Monovalent given in a single dose orally with a bicarbonate buffer
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Bivalent vaccine given in 2 liquid doses orally to children >=1 year of age

The Sanchol cholera vaccine is a bivalent vaccine given in 2 liquid doses orally to children >=1 year of age.

The Sanchol cholera vaccine is a bivalent oral cholera vaccine (OCV) that targets both Vibrio cholerae O1 and Vibrio cholerae O139 serogroups, which are the primary causes of cholera outbreaks. It is designed to provide immunity by stimulating the production of antibodies in the intestines, the site of infection.

Key Features of the Sanchol Vaccine:
Bivalent Nature: The vaccine protects against two strains of the cholera bacterium: O1, which is responsible for most global cholera cases, and O139 which is seen in South Asia.

Dosing Schedule: The Sanchol vaccine is administered in two oral doses. The doses are given 14 days apart for children aged 1 year and above as well as adults. This two-dose regimen is essential for achieving effective immunity. The vaccine is provided in liquid form, making it easy to administer. It does not require any special preparation, such as mixing with a bicarbonate buffer, which is needed for some older cholera vaccines.

Age Recommendation: The vaccine is recommended for individuals aged 1 year and older. It is particularly useful in endemic regions or during outbreaks to prevent the spread of the disease.

Efficacy and Duration: Sanchol has been shown to provide significant protection against cholera for up to 3-5 years after vaccination, although booster doses may be required in areas with ongoing transmission.

The vaccine is widely used in mass vaccination campaigns, especially in areas prone to cholera outbreaks, such as refugee camps or regions with poor sanitation. It has been a critical tool in reducing the incidence of cholera in many endemic areas.
questions.learning: Bivalent vaccine given in 2 liquid doses orally to children >=1 year of age The Sanchol cholera vaccine is a bivalent vaccine given in 2 liquid doses orally to children >=1 year of age.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 7-year-old boy is brought with complaints of headache, vomiting and neck stiffness for a few days. He had undergone a ventriculoperitoneal (VP) shunt placement for hydrocephalus a year back. Which of the following is the most common cause of shunt malfunction?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Shunt obstruction

Obstruction of the shunt is the most common cause of shunt malfunction.

A ventriculoperitoneal (VP) shunt is used to drain excess cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) due to an obstruction in the normal outflow or there is a decreased absorption of the fluid.

Complications of the shunting procedure include the following -

* Shunt obstruction - most common cause for shunt malfunction

* Shunt infection due to skin flora entering the shunt, most commonly from Staphylococcus epidermidis.

* Intracerebral or intraventricular haemorrhage

* Tip migration or malposition

* Shunt overdrainage (slit ventricle syndrome) - usually occurs after many years

* Shunt nephritis

* Shunt disconnection or breakage or kinking

* Inguinal hernia

* Seizures

Shunt obstruction -

* It is the most common cause of shunt malfunction.

* The most common site is the ventricular catheter.

* Obstruction occurs due to clogging of the shunt by blood, proteinaceous material, choroid plexus, glial adhesions or secondary to infection.

* The patient comes with features of raised intracranial pressure like headache, vomiting and eye examination showing papilloedema.

* Diagnosis is done by CT Brain imaging which shows ventriculomegaly. On performing a lumbar puncture, the CSF flow is found to be slow despite the raised CSF pressure.

* Treatment is by revision of the shunt.

The image below shows the location of the shunt in the brain

The image below shows a CT scan of the brain with some proteinaceous material deposited in the ventricles and shunt insitu.

questions.text: Which of the following is normally seen in lumbar spine?
questions.explanation:

Lordosis is normally seen in lumbar spine.

In adults,

• The cervical curve is a lordosis (convex forwards),

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: False statement regarding nephroblastoma?
options: Treatment is chemotherapy followed by surgery
Most common intra abdominal malignancy in children
questions.explanation: Nephroblastoma (Wilms tumor) is the most common intra-abdominal malignancy in children and usually presents as a localized renal mass. It primarily spreads via the hematogenous route, most commonly to the lungs, and less commonly to the liver and bones. Hence, option (C) is correct. However, early lung metastasis is NOT typical. In most cases, Wilms tumor is confined to the kidney at diagnosis, and metastasis occurs later in advanced stages (Stage IV). Therefore, stating that early lung metastases are common is false, making option (B) the correct answer. Option (A) is considered correct in many exam settings following the SIOP protocol, where neoadjuvant chemotherapy is given before surgery to shrink the tumor and reduce surgical complications. Option (D) is also correct as Wilms tumor is the most common intra-abdominal malignancy in children

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A 15-day-old infant had conjunctivitis, which later developed into respiratory distress and pneumonia. Chest Xray examination revealed bilateral lung infiltrates. Peripheral smear count showed 14,300/µL (N 43, L 54, E3). Which of the following is the most likely pathogenic organism?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Chlamydia trachomatis

The organism most likely to cause conjunctivitis, progressing to respiratory distress, and then pneumonia is Chlamydia trachomatis.

It is not possible to differentiate between chlamydial pneumonia and other causes of atypical pneumonia, like Mycoplasma (option D) based solely on the clinical presentation. Here, the history of conjunctivitis makes it more likely to be a chlamydial infection.

Pneumonia caused by C. trachomatis can develop in infants born to women with an untreated chlamydial infection in 10-20% of cases. It has a very characteristic presentation in infancy, disease onset usually occurs around 1 and 3 months of age and is insidious, with a persistent cough, tachypnea, and absence of fever (atypical pneumonia). Auscultation reveals rales; wheezing is uncommon.

The absence of fever and wheezing helps to distinguish C. trachomatis pneumonia from respiratory syncytial virus pneumonia.

A distinctive laboratory finding is the presence of peripheral eosinophilia (>400 cells/µL). The most consistent finding on chest radiographs is hyperinflation accompanied by minimal interstitial or alveolar infiltrates.

Other options:

Option B: Pneumococcal pneumonia generally presents with features of lobar pneumonia. Fever, dyspnea, and productive cough are the primary symptoms.

Option C: Although Neisseria gonorrhoeae is an important cause of ophthalmia neonatorum, it does not cause pneumonia-like features.

Chlamydiae are obligate intracellular organisms that produce basophilic inclusion bodies. They are called energy parasites as they lack enzymes for ATP synthesis. They cannot grow on artificial media but can grow on cell lines (McCoy, HeLa, or the yolk sac of the chick embryo)

Chlamydiae occur in two forms, the elementary body (extracellular, infective form)  and the reticulate body (intracellular, non-infective, and replicative form) which are found inside inclusion bodies.

Chlamydia trachomatis is the most common cause of ophthalmia neonatorum in developed countries. Neonatal inclusion conjunctivitis is caused by serotypes D to K. Chlamydia trachomatis inclusion conjunctivitis manifests relatively late, usually over 1 week after birth.

It is usually a venereal infection derived from the cervix or urethra of the mother during delivery. On examination, the conjunctiva is swollen and edematous. The discharge is initially watery, but later becomes mucopurulent or bloody.

Newborns with suspected chlamydia infection should have samples drawn from both the conjunctivae and oropharynx. Since it is an obligate intracellular organism, swabs should also include conjunctival epithelial cells if possible. Giemsa staining shows characteristic intracellular inclusion bodies. Diagnosis is usually established by PCR.

The treatment includes oral erythromycin for two weeks. Topical erythromycin to tetracycline ointment may also be used.

If left untreated, associated systemic diseases such as chlamydial otitis and pneumonia may develop later. In all cases, both parents must receive appropriate treatment for genital infection.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: A peripheral blood smear of a 22-year-old man is shown below. The blast count is 65%. Immunophenotyping demonstrates positivity for CD13, CD33, and CD117, while CD19 and CD20 are negative. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. AML

Acute Myeloid Leukemia (AML) by the presence of ≥20% myeloblasts in the bone marrow or peripheral blood and expression of myeloid lineage markers such as CD13, CD33, and CD117. Negative B-cell markers (CD19, CD20) help exclude B-cell acute lymphoblastic leukemia (B-ALL). Morphologically, myeloblasts may contain Auer rods, which are pathognomonic of myeloid differentiation.

Why not the other options?

• A. ALL: Blasts express TdT and lymphoid markers (B-ALL: CD10, CD19, CD20, CD22; T-ALL: CD3, CD7); myeloid markers are absent.
• C. CML: Characterized by marked granulocytosis with all stages of myeloid maturation and BCR-ABL1 (Philadelphia chromosome); blast count is <20% unless in blast crisis.
• D. CLL: Mature small lymphocytes with smudge cells; immunophenotype CD5+, CD19+, CD23+; does not present with myeloblasts.
questions.learning: AML Acute Myeloid Leukemia (AML) by the presence of ≥20% myeloblasts in the bone marrow or peripheral blood and expression of myeloid lineage markers such as CD13, CD33, and CD117.

Condensor needs to be kept very close to the eye

An indirect ophthalmoscope produces an inverted real image of 3 to 5 times magnification.

Advantages of the binocular indirect ophthalmoscope are:

* Visualization through hazy media is possible due to strong in built illumination system.

* Field of view is much larger than direct ophthalmoscopy.

* Examination of peripheral retina up to ora serrata is possible.

* Depth perception of the lesion is possible due to stereopsis with binocular indirect ophthalmoscope.

* Visualization of fundus in very high refractive error is also possible, where it may not be possible to focus the lesion with direct ophthalmoscope.

* A real, Inverted image is formed (Option A).

* There is an arms distance between the condensing lens and the patient's eye (Option C).

Other options:

Option D: 15 times magnification is seen with a direct ophthalmoscope.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Which of the following mechanisms is seen in the baroreceptor reflex?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Negative feedback

The baroreceptor reflex maintains arterial pressure through negative feedback. A rise in BP increases baroreceptor firing, which reduces sympathetic outflow and lowers heart rate and vascular tone. A fall in BP produces the opposite response. The system continuously counteracts deviations from normal pressure.

↑ Blood pressure

↓

↑ Stretch of baroreceptors

↓

↑ Firing via CN IX (carotid) & CN X (aortic)

↓

Medulla (CV center)

↓

↓ Sympathetic + ↑ Parasympathetic

↓

↓ Heart rate + ↓ contractility + vasodilation

↓

↓ Blood pressure (returns to normal)

| Option | Mechanism | Correct/Incorrect | Explanation

| ------ | --------- | ----------------- | -----------

| A. Feedforward | Anticipatory response | ❌ Incorrect | Baroreflex responds AFTER change

| B. Positive feedback | Amplifies change | ❌ Incorrect | Would worsen BP instability

| C. Negative feedback | Opposes change | ✅ CORRECT |

| D. Adaptive control | Long-term adjustment | ❌ Incorrect | Baroreflex is short-term regulation

questions.text: Match the following intracranial bleed:
options: A -i B-ii C- iii D- iv

Correct answer: B. A -ii B-iv C-i D-iii

Epidural hematoma:

Noncontrasted axial computed tomography scan showing a lenticular area of increased density in left parietal region.

• Typically occur in the groove of the middle meningeal artery associated with temporal bone fractures that have resulted in a tear of middle meningeal artery.
• They tend to not to cross suture lines of the skull.

Subdural hematoma:

A non contrasted computed tomography scan of acute subdural hematoma shows a cresentric area of increased density in the right posterior parietal region between brain and the skull. An area of intraparenchymal haemorrhage also seen. In addition, mass effect causes a midline shift to left.

• They can cross suture lines but they do not cross the tentorium or falx.
• Can be acute or chronic

Subarachnoid haemorrhage:

A non contrasted axial computed tomography scan shows the blood as areas of increased density near the base of the brain shows blood in Texaco star pattern formed blood radiating from suprasellar cistern into the sylvian fissures and anterior interhemispheric fissure.

• Most often accompanied by severe sudden onset headache.
• Can really be visualised in acute stage, when blood is radiographically dense (whiter) than the CSF.

Intracereberal haemorrhage:

Non contrast computed tomography shows a large area of fresh blood appearing white in the region of right thalamus. Blood is denser than CSF so settles dependently.

This settling is not seen with subarachnoid or interparenchymal blood.

questions.text: A 28-year-old man presents with involuntary, purposeless, dance-like movements involving both upper and lower limbs. He has also become aggressive and irritable over the past few months. MRI brain is shown. What is the most likely diagnosis?

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Testosterone helps in the development of various organs in the fetus. Which of the following stimulates its production?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. hCG from placenta

hCG (human chorionic gonadotropin) from placenta stimulates the production of testosterone in the male fetus.

hCG released from the placenta is the initial stimulus for testosterone production in the male fetus. Later by the eighth week of gestation, fetal pituitary LH (luteinizing hormone) stimulates the Leydig cells of the testes to produce testosterone.

Sex differentiation of the embryo depends on the Y chromosome, which contains the testis-determining gene called the SRY (sex-determining region on Y) gene. In a genetically male embryo (46, XY), the gonad is converted into testis under the influence of this gene. Female development occurs in the absence of this gene.

Testosterone released from the Leydig cells acts on the Wolffian duct to develop vas deferens, epididymis, and seminal vesicles. Testosterone is converted to dihydrotestosterone (DHT) with the help of 5-alpha-reductase which helps in the differentiation of male external genitalia.

The Sertoli cells of the seminiferous tubules of testes secrete antimüllerian hormone (AMH)/Müllerian-inhibiting substance (MIS) by 7 weeks of gestation. It causes regression of the Mullerian duct and prevents the development of the uterus, fallopian tube, and upper vagina.

Other options:

Option A: It is LH from the fetal pituitary, and not the maternal pituitary that stimulates testosterone production in the male fetus.

Option C: Inhibin A is produced by the corpus luteum and inhibin B is produced by the granulosa cells of the ovary. They inhibit FSH secretion.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Endocrine · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: A 32-year-old woman comes to the physician because of a 3-month history of irregular menses, milky discharge from her nipples, fatigue, and weight gain. Menses occur at irregular 25-40-day intervals and last 1-2 days with minimal flow. 5 months ago, she was started on clozapine for treatment of schizophrenia. She has hypothyroidism but has not been taking levothyroxine over the past 6 months. Visual field examination show no abnormalities. Her serum thyroid-stimulating hormone is 17.0 U/mL and serum prolactin is 85 ng/mL. Which of the following is the most likely explanation for the nipple discharge in this patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Hypothyroidism

Untreated primary hypothyroidism can cause hyperprolactinemia and galactorrhea due to increased thyrotropin-releasing hormone (TRH) from the hypothalamus.

• In primary hypothyroidism, decreased thyroid hormone leads to increased TRH secretion.
• TRH stimulates both TSH and prolactin release from the anterior pituitary.
• Elevated prolactin suppresses GnRH, resulting in menstrual irregularities, oligomenorrhea, and galactorrhea.

Why other options are incorrect:

B. Prolactinoma: Usually causes very high prolactin (>200 ng/mL) and often visual field defects. This patient has moderate elevation (85 ng/mL) and normal visual fields.

C. Ectopic prolactin production: Extremely rare cause of hyperprolactinemia.

D. Adverse effect of medication: Antipsychotics can increase prolactin, but clozapine has minimal prolactin-elevating effect.
