questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text: During an anatomy teaching session, a spinal image is shown with a prominent blue line marked across the vertebral column. Based on the anatomical landmarks visible in the image, which vertebral level does this blue line correspond to?
questions.explanation: The "blue line" shown in the anatomical diagram represents Tuffier’s line (or the intercristal line). This is a horizontal line connecting the highest points of the iliac crests. In an adult, this clinically important landmark typically passes through the L4 vertebra or the L4-L5 intervertebral space. Options A (L2-L3), C (L5-S1), and D (L3-L4) are incorrect anatomical levels for this specific surface landmark. Tuffier's line is used as the primary guide for identifying the safe level for performing a lumbar puncture or administering spinal/epidural anesthesia. Since the spinal cord (conus medullaris) usually ends at the L1-L2 level in adults, inserting a needle into the spaces below Tuffier’s line (such as L4-L5 or L5-S1) minimizes the risk of direct spinal cord injury. Accuracy in identifying this landmark is essential for any clinician performing procedures involving the lumbar spinal canal
questions.learning: The "blue line" shown in the anatomical diagram represents Tuffier’s line (or the intercristal line). This is a horizontal line connecting the highest points of the iliac crests.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A baby was born at 34 weeks of pregnancy, the appearance of the baby is given below. What is the mother suffering from ?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Gestational diabetes

The image provided depicts a baby with macrosomia (large for gestational age), the most probable cause of which is gestational diabetes (GDM) in the mother.

GDM in a mother is defined as carbohydrate intolerance with onset/first recognition during the present pregnancy. Diabetes in Pregnancy Societies of India (DIPSI) criteria is used to diagnose GDM (Venous plasma >140mg % after 2h of ingestion of 75g of glucose).

Maternal Complications of GDM:

1. During pregnancy - Recurrent spontaneous abortion, preterm labor, urinary tract infection, polyhydramnios, and increased incidence of preeclampsia
2. During labor: Prolongation of labor (shoulder dystocia) and postpartum hemorrhage

Neonatal complications -

1. Electrolyte imbalances - hypoglycemia, hypocalcemia, hypokalemia, hypomagnesemia
2. Respiratory system - respiratory distress syndrome and delayed lung maturity
3. Hematological system - polycythemia and single umbilical artery
4. Renal system - hydronephrosis (renal agenesis) and polycystic kidneys
5. Cardiovascular system - VSD, ASD, Coarctation of the aorta, and TGA
6. Gastrointestinal system - duodenal atresia, tracheoesophageal fistula (TEF), and necrotizing enterocolitis
7. Central Nervous system - anencephaly, microcephaly, neural tube defects, caudal regression syndrome, and sacral agenesis

Other options:

Option B: Congenital rubella syndrome presents with the classical triad of deafness, cataract, and congenital heart disease (the most common being - patent ductus arteriosus). Eye findings also include salt and pepper retinopathy as shown below.

Option C: Congenital hypothyroidism is the most common preventable cause of mental retardation and presents as 6 P's - pot-bellied, pale, puffy-faced child with protruding umbilicus, protuberant tongue, and poor brain development

Option D: Gestational hypertension primarily occurs due to the failure of the invasion of extravillous trophoblasts into the spiral artery. It is defined as a rise in blood pressure >140/90 mmHg after 20 weeks of pregnancy (without proteinuria). It usually leads to intrauterine growth restriction (IUGR) and fetal death.
questions.learning: Gestational diabetes — The image provided depicts a baby with macrosomia (large for gestational age), the most probable cause of which is gestational diabetes (GDM) in the mother.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: The vestibulo-ocular reflex (VOR) is seen to stabilize the image on the retina while the head moves. What is the gain of VOR ( eye velocity/head velocity )?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. 1

The gain of the vestibulo-ocular reflex (VOR) is 1, which means there is a compensatory eye velocity equal to the head velocity and in the opposite direction.

VOR prevents the slipping of the retinal images when the head moves; it moves the eyes at the same speed but in the opposite direction as the head. If an object is being pursued with eye and head movement, vision cancels the vestibulo-ocular reflex to prevent the eyes from moving in the opposite direction as the head.

VOR is a physiological vestibular nystagmus that forms the basis of the caloric test. If cold water is poured into the right ear the patient develops left jerk nystagmus (rapid phase towards the left), while the reverse happens with warm water, i.e. patient develops right jerk nystagmus. It can be remembered by the mnemonic 'COWS' (Cold- Opposite, Warm-Same).
questions.learning: 1 The gain of the vestibulo-ocular reflex (VOR) is 1, which means there is a compensatory eye velocity equal to the head velocity and in the opposite direction.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Which substance functions as a second messenger in the pathway regulating gastric acid secretion?
questions.explanation: Gastric acid secretion by parietal cells is regulated by several neurohumoral pathways. When histamine binds to the H2 receptor on the parietal cell membrane, it activates the Gs protein, which stimulates adenylate cyclase to produce cyclic adenosine monophosphate (cAMP). In this specific pathway, cAMP acts as the critical secondary messenger that eventually activates protein kinase A, leading to the stimulation of the H+/K+ ATPase pump . cGMP (Option A) is a secondary messenger for other processes like vasodilation but not for primary gastric acid stimulation. The CCK-B receptor (Option C) is the primary binding site for gastrin, which utilizes the IP3-DAG/calcium pathway as its secondary messenger system rather than cAMP. Acetylcholine (Ach, Option D) is a neurotransmitter that acts as a first messenger by binding to muscarinic M3 receptors. Therefore, cAMP is the correct identification for the secondary messenger involved specifically in the histamine-regulated mechanism of acid secretion

questions.topic: Rheumatology · All Qbank Qs Excluding Pyqs
questions.text: 72-year-old woman comes to the OPD due to persistent headaches, fatigue, and muscle pain. She has a history of hypertension and osteoarthritis. Her father had a subarachnoid hemorrhage from a ruptured berry aneurysm. She is treated with prednisone, leading to marked and rapid improvement in her symptoms. Which of the following pathologic processes is most likely responsible for this patient's condition?
options: Homogenous acellular thickening of arteriolar walls
Onion-like concentric thickening of arteriolar walls
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Granulomatous inflammation of the media

An elderly patient with headache, fatigue, muscle pain (polymyalgia rheumatica symptoms) and rapid response to prednisone --> suggests Giant cell (temporal) arteritis.

Pathology of giant cell arteritis:

• Granulomatous inflammation of large and medium arteries
• Predominantly involves branches of carotid artery (temporal artery)
• Granulomatous inflammation of tunica media
• Multinucleated giant cells and fragmentation of internal elastic lamina
• Leads to luminal narrowing → ischemic symptoms (headache, jaw claudication, vision loss)

Key association:

• Strong association with polymyalgia rheumatica
• Elevated ESR/CRP
• Dramatic response to corticosteroids
questions.learning: Granulomatous inflammation of the media — An elderly patient with headache, fatigue, muscle pain (polymyalgia rheumatica symptoms) and rapid response to prednisone --> suggests Giant cell (temporal) arteritis.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A patient with a history of a road traffic accident 2 hours ago was brought to the emergency department with an altered sensorium. His GCS was 10 and the CT scan is given below. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Epidural hematoma

Axial CT shows a hyperdense lentiform (biconvex) opacity consistent with an epidural hematoma.

Extradural hematoma (EDH) is also known as an epidural hematoma. It is a collection of blood that forms between the inner surface of the skull and the outer layer of the dura, which is called the periosteal layer. It is commonly associated with a history of trauma and associated skull fracture.

The source of bleeding is usually a torn meningeal artery (most commonly the middle meningeal artery). It is associated with an underlying fracture of the squamous part of the temporal bone.

Investigations to be done include CT and MRI. It is seen as a biconvex lesion. It can cause a mass effect with herniation. They are usually limited by cranial sutures, but not by venous sinuses.

Swirl sign refers to the non-contrast CT appearance of acute extravasation of blood into a hematoma, for example, an extradural hematoma or subdural hematoma. It represents unclotted fresh blood which is of lower attenuation than clotted blood that surrounds it.

The following image shows a CT scan depicting swirl sign:

Pearl PF0338: Intracranial haemorrhage
questions.learning: Epidural hematoma Axial CT shows a hyperdense lentiform (biconvex) opacity consistent with an epidural hematoma. Extradural hematoma (EDH) is also known as an epidural hematoma.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: Giving class in a village for wound care after a dog bite by enacting it is which mode of health communication?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Demonstration

The best method of giving a class in a village for wound care after a dog bite is by demonstration.

A demonstration is a group approach to health communication where the audience is educated on how to follow the advice by enacting it. Here the procedure is carried out step by step before an audience or the target group. It can bring about behavioural change in practices by arousing interest.

Other options:

Option A: A lecture is an oral presentation of facts, thoughts and ideas with help of chalk and board. Its effectiveness depends to a large extent on the speaker's ability and the comprehension of listeners. It would not be an effective tool in teaching a procedure like wound care.

Option B: Group discussion involves members interacting in a face-to-face situation. A group leader initiates the subject, encourages everyone to participate, takes discussion in the proper manner, and sums up the discussion in the end.

Option C: Flash card is a card that has words, numbers, or pictures on it that helps to learn. They are a form of visual aids in communication.
questions.learning: Demonstration — The best method of giving a class in a village for wound care after a dog bite is by demonstration. A demonstration is a group approach to health communication where the audience is educated on how to follow the advice by enacting it.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 23-year-old male patient presents with midline swelling in the neck. The swelling moves with deglutition and protrusion of the tongue. What is the likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Thyroglossal cyst

The given clinical scenario is suggestive of a thyroglossal cyst. It moves with deglutition, protrusion of the tongue, and side-to-side movement is also possible.

A thyroglossal duct cyst is a congenital midline neck swelling that typically presents during childhood often noticed after an upper respiratory infection.

A thyroglossal cyst represents the persistence of the track of the thyroid gland and can be found adjacent to the midline. The thyroid gland descends early in fetal life from the base of the tongue towards its position in the lower neck. At the time of descent, the hyoid bone has not been formed and the track of the thyroid gland is variable, passing in front, through, or behind the eventual position of the hyoid body.

It can occur anywhere along the migratory course of the duct:

• Infrahyoid (most common site)
• Region of thyroid cartilage
• Suprahyoid
• Floor of mouth
• Beneath foramen cecum

Clinical features of thyroglossal cyst:

• Classically the cyst moves upwards on swallowing and on tongue protrusion. This indicates attachment to the hyoid bone.
• Swelling is smooth, soft, fluctuant (cystic), nontender, mobile, and shows transillumination.
• Thyroid fossa is empty, if there is no thyroid in the normal location.

Complications of thyroglossal cyst:

• The most common complication is infection.
• Thyroglossal fistula is an acquired condition that either follows infection of the cyst which bursts open or due to inadequate removal of the cyst.
• 1% of thyroglossal duct cysts are found to be malignant of which the most common type of cancer is papillary (85%).

However, only the thyroglossal cyst moves with tongue protrusion. This is because the duct extends from the foramen cecum of the tongue to the isthmus of the gland.

Sistrunk’s operation is performed to excise the cyst and prevent a recurrence. It involves excision of the whole thyroglossal tract, involving removal of the body of the hyoid bone, and suprahyoid tract through the tongue base to the vallecula at the site of the primitive foramen cecum along with the core of tissue on either side.

Features of hoarseness of voice, cough, neck swelling that increases in size on coughing/Valsalva maneuver, and a gurgling sound heard on pressing the swelling are suggestive of laryngocele.
questions.learning: Thyroglossal cyst — The given clinical scenario is suggestive of a thyroglossal cyst. It moves with deglutition, protrusion of the tongue, and side-to-side movement is also possible.

questions.text: Diagnose the image seen in a 10-year-old child.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Herbert pits

Herbert pits are depressed scars at the limbus resulting from healed follicles in trachoma.

• Seen in chronic trachoma (Chlamydia trachomatis infection)
• Represent healed limbal follicles
• Typically located at the superior limbus
• Associated with other sequelae:

• Pannus formation (superior corneal vascularization)
• Trichiasis
• Entropion

Why not others:

• Horner-Trantas spots: White limbal dots in vernal keratoconjunctivitis
• Pannus: Superficial vascularization, not pits
• Corneal dystrophy: Bilateral, hereditary, non-inflammatory

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: A young female patient presents with ptosis which reportedly worsens in the evening and improves in the morning. A diagnosis of Myasthenia gravis is made. What is the preferred treatment for this patient at this stage?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Pyridostigmine

Intermittent ptosis is considered one of the earliest signs of Myasthenia gravis. Pyridostigmine is the preferred treatment for symptomatic patients at this stage of the disease.

Myasthenia gravis is an autoimmune neuromuscular junction disorder that is characterized by weakness and fatigability of skeletal muscles. It is due to the autoantibody-mediated destruction of the acetylcholine receptors (AChRs) at the post-synaptic membrane. This consequentially leads to a decreased transmission at the neuromuscular junction. Failure of transmission results in muscle weakness. Hence the goal is to increase the duration of action of acetylcholine by inhibiting acetylcholinesterase. The most commonly used anticholinesterase drug is pyridostigmine.

Females are more commonly affected than males and the disease tends to occur in middle age.

Clinical features of myasthenia gravis:

* Muscle weakness and fatiguability increase with repeated use or late in the day and may improve following rest or sleep. Limb weakness is proximal and asymmetrical

* Cranial muscles particularly the lids and extraocular muscles are involved early in the course - diplopia, ptosis

* Facial weakness - snarling expression on smiling

* Weakness in chewing

* Speech with nasal timbre due to the weakness of the palate and tongue

* Difficulty in swallowing

* Deep tendon reflexes are intact

* Myasthenic crisis - acute exacerbation of muscle weakness especially intercostal and diaphragmatic muscles resulting in ventilatory failure. It is most commonly due to infection and anticholinesterase medication overuse.

Myasthenia gravis is associated with thymoma and other autoimmune diseases such as Hashimoto's thyroiditis, Grave's disease, Neuromyelitis optics, Systemic lupus erythematosus, etc.

Diagnosis:

* Ice-pack test - application of ice pack over the eyes improves ptosis (decreases the activity of acetylcholinesterase, this increases the amount of acetylcholine in the synaptic cleft and increases transmission).

* Antibodies associated with myasthenia gravis: Anti-AChR antibodies, Anti-MuSK antibodies, Anti-LRP4 antibodies

* Repetitive nerve stimulation test shows a decremental response.

* Edrophonium chloride or Tensilon test - improvement of symptoms occurs on injecting edrophonium. Edrophonium is an acetylcholinesterase inhibitor. This increases the amount of acetylcholine in the synaptic cleft and improves transmission.

Treatment:

* Symptomatic treatment: Anticholinesterase agents – Pyridostigmine is the initial therapy of choice.

* Chronic immunomodulating therapy: Glucocorticoids (prednisone) and immunosuppressive drugs (azathioprine, mycophenolate mofetil, cyclosporine) implemented in patients significantly symptomatic on pyridostigmine.

* Rapid immunomodulating treatment: IVIG and therapeutic plasma exchange—Used to tide over severe illness (myasthenic crisis) and as 'bridge' therapy before surgery, or starting chronic immunomodulating treatment.

* Surgical approach: Thymectomy
questions.learning: Pyridostigmine Intermittent ptosis is considered one of the earliest signs of Myasthenia gravis. Pyridostigmine is the preferred treatment for symptomatic patients at this stage of the disease.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Which CD markers are typically positive in Chronic Lymphocytic Leukaemia (CLL)?
questions.explanation: The hallmark immunophenotype of Chronic Lymphocytic Leukaemia (CLL) involves the expression of mature B-cell markers alongside a specific aberrant T-cell marker. CLL cells typically express CD19, CD20, and CD23. The most distinctive diagnostic feature is the aberrant co-expression of CD5, which is normally found on T-cells. This unique "B-cell plus CD5" profile helps clinicians distinguish CLL from other mature B-cell malignancies. Option A is incorrect as it contains pure T-cell markers like CD3 and CD8. Option B (CD10, CD19, CD22) is characteristic of precursor B-cell Acute Lymphoblastic Leukaemia (ALL), where CD10 represents the common ALL antigen (CALLA). Option D consists of myeloid lineage markers such as CD13, CD33, and CD117, which are used to diagnose Acute Myeloid Leukaemia (AML) rather than lymphoid neoplasms. Thus, the presence of CD19, CD20, CD23, and CD5 is definitive for CLL
questions.learning: The hallmark immunophenotype of Chronic Lymphocytic Leukaemia (CLL) involves the expression of mature B-cell markers alongside a specific aberrant T-cell marker.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Which of the following muscles is not involved in the formation of the perineal body?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Internal anal sphincter muscle

The perineal body (central tendon of the perineum) is a fibromuscular node located between the urogenital triangle and anal triangle, anterior to the anus. It serves as an important point of attachment for several perineal muscles that support the pelvic floor and maintain pelvic organ stability.

Muscles attached to the perineal body include:

• Bulbospongiosus muscle
• Superficial transverse perineal muscle
• Deep transverse perineal muscle
• External anal sphincter
• Fibers of levator ani (especially pubococcygeus)

The internal anal sphincter is not attached to the perineal body because it is a smooth muscle continuation of the circular layer of the rectum and functions involuntarily.
questions.learning: Internal anal sphincter muscle — The perineal body (central tendon of the perineum) is a fibromuscular node located between the urogenital triangle and anal triangle, anterior to the anus.

questions.subject: Anaesthesia
questions.text: Dale's vasomotor reversal can be best described as
options: Repeated administration of ephedrine decreases its effect on blood pressure
A patient pretreated with phentolamine develops severe hypotension on the administration of adrenaline
An increase in pulse pressure is produced by the intravenous administration of isoprenaline
questions.explanation: Dale’s vasomotor reversal is a classic pharmacological phenomenon involving the dual action of adrenaline on and receptors. Adrenaline normally causes a rise in blood pressure due to its dominant -1 mediated vasoconstriction. However, if a patient is pretreated with an -blocker like phentolamine, the effects are blocked. Subsequent administration of adrenaline then acts only on the unblocked -2 receptors in skeletal muscle blood vessels, causing profound vasodilation and a paradoxical severe drop in blood pressure (hypotension). Option A describes tachyphylaxis. Option D refers to the typical chronotropic/inotropic effects of isoprenaline. Option C is an incomplete description of "Dale’s reversal" for acetylcholine (which involves atropine pretreatment) but is not the standard "vasomotor reversal" linked to adrenaline. Therefore, the reversal of adrenaline’s pressor effect to a depressor effect by -blockade is the definitive description of this phenomenon
questions.learning: Dale’s vasomotor reversal is a classic pharmacological phenomenon involving the dual action of adrenaline on and receptors. Adrenaline normally causes a rise in blood pressure due to its dominant -1 mediated vasoconstriction.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Identify the type of pelvis in the given image below
questions.explanation: The pelvis in the given image shows a heart-shaped (triangular) pelvic inlet, which is the hallmark feature of an android pelvis. The anterior segment is narrow, and the side walls appear convergent, giving the inlet a more constricted appearance. Additionally, the subpubic angle is relatively narrow, and the sacrum is more prominent and directed forward, all of which are characteristic of the android type. The android pelvis resembles the typical male pelvis and is considered less favorable for childbirth due to its reduced space and narrower outlet. These features match the structure shown in the image, confirming option (C). Why Other Options Are Wrong (A) Platypelloid pelvis: Shows a flat, wide inlet (transverse > AP), not heart-shaped. (B) Anthropoid pelvis: Has an elongated oval inlet (AP > transverse), not triangular. (D) Gynecoid pelvis: Has a rounded, spacious inlet, which is not seen here

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: What is the first step in conducting an immunization survey?
options: Completing the cluster and summary forms
Calculating the total fertility rate of the area
questions.explanation: The standard methodology for assessing immunization coverage in a community is the "30-cluster sampling" technique recommended by the WHO. The first and most critical step in this process is cluster identification. This involves dividing the total population of the study area into smaller geographical units (clusters), such as villages or wards, and selecting 30 of them using a systematic random sampling method based on probability proportional to size (PPS). Option B (Conducting the survey) and Option C (Completing forms) are subsequent operational steps that can only occur after the specific clusters and households have been identified. Option D is unrelated to the specific methodology of an immunization coverage survey. Proper cluster identification ensures that the survey sample is statistically representative of the entire population, allowing for an accurate estimation of the percentage of children who have received their scheduled vaccines. This data is vital for identifying gaps in the health system
questions.learning: The standard methodology for assessing immunization coverage in a community is the "30-cluster sampling" technique recommended by the WHO. The first and most critical step in this process is cluster identification.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: What is the term for the number of maternal deaths occurring per 100,000 live births?
questions.explanation: The term used to define the number of maternal deaths per 100,000 live births is technically the Maternal Mortality Ratio (MMR). By definition: Maternal Mortality Ratio (MMR): Number of maternal deaths during pregnancy, childbirth, or within 42 days of termination of pregnancy per 100,000 live births However, there is a nomenclature issue in the options provided. Since “Maternal Mortality Ratio” is not listed, the intended and closest correct option is “Maternal mortality rate” (Option A). In many medical entrance and board examinations, the terms rate and ratio are often (though incorrectly) used interchangeably. Why other options are incorrect: 1. Under-5 Mortality Rate (B): Deaths of children under 5 years per 1,000 live births 2. Infant Mortality Rate (C): Deaths under 1 year of age per 1,000 live births 3. Perinatal Mortality Rate (D): Late fetal deaths + early neonatal deaths per 1,000 total births

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Which of the following is not a part of damage control surgery?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Vascular anastomosis

Vascular anastomosis is undertaken as a part of definitive surgery, not damage control surgery (DCS).

DCS is minimal intervention done in order to stabilize the patient and followed by definite surgery later. It aims to coordinate staged operative interventions with periods of aggressive resuscitation to salvage trauma patients sustaining major injuries.

The initial focus is hemorrhage control, resuscitation, followed by control and limitation of contamination. It includes an abbreviated laparotomy, temporary packing, and closure of the abdomen in an eﬀort to blunt the physiologic response to prolonged shock and massive hemorrhage.

After the initial steps of DCS, definitive surgery involving vascular anastomosis may be done. This is individualized to the patient and preferred to be completed in the first 24–72 hours.

Note: Vascular anastomosis is the option least likely to be part of the initial stages of DCS. Hence, it is the best option out of the four for this testing point.
questions.learning: Vascular anastomosis Vascular anastomosis is undertaken as a part of definitive surgery, not damage control surgery (DCS). DCS is minimal intervention done in order to stabilize the patient and followed by definite surgery later.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: What is the most common cause of Condyloma Acuminata?
questions.explanation: Condyloma Acuminata, also known as anogenital warts, are benign epithelial tumors of the skin and mucosa. The absolute most common cause, responsible for over 90% of all genital warts, is infection with the Human Papillomavirus (HPV) serotypes 6 and 11 (Option B) . These are classified as "low-risk" HPV types because they have a minimal association with the development of invasive cancer. In contrast, HPV 16 and 18 (Option C) are "high-risk" types most strongly linked to cervical, anal, and oropharyngeal carcinomas. HPV 31 and 33 (Option A) are also high-risk types but are less common than 16 and 18. Recognizing the difference between these serotypes is vital for understanding the rationale behind HPV vaccines (like the quadrivalent or nonavalent versions) which target both the high-risk types for cancer prevention and the low-risk types for wart prevention. Therefore, HPV 6 and 11 are the definitive causative agents

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: Drug causing adverse effects on the renal tubules?
questions.explanation: Cisplatin is a potent platinum-based chemotherapeutic agent used to treat various malignancies. Its most common dose-limiting toxicity is nephrotoxicity, specifically targeting the renal tubules. Cisplatin causes acute tubular necrosis (ATN) by inducing oxidative stress and direct cellular damage, often manifesting as electrolyte wasting (magnesium/calcium) and rising creatinine. Streptozocin (Option B) also has renal toxicities but is more specifically associated with islet cell damage. Methysergide (Option C) is linked to retroperitoneal fibrosis rather than direct tubular injury. Cyclophosphamide (Option D) is classically associated with hemorrhagic cystitis (bladder toxicity) caused by its metabolite acrolein, rather than primary tubular injury. To minimize cisplatin-induced renal damage, patients are typically pre-hydrated aggressively with saline and sometimes given mannitol or amifostine. Therefore, cisplatin is the definitive drug in this list known for damaging the renal tubules
questions.learning: Cisplatin is a potent platinum-based chemotherapeutic agent used to treat various malignancies. Its most common dose-limiting toxicity is nephrotoxicity, specifically targeting the renal tubules.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: What remnant is derived from the structure marked in the image?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Nucleus pulposus

The nucleus pulposus is derived from the notochord (marked by the arrow).

The nucleus pulposus is a mucoid, gel-like substance that lies between the centre of the intervertebral disc and its posterior surface. At birth, it is almost completely gelatinous and liquid, but as the individual ages, it becomes less differentiated from the remainder of the intervertebral disc, becoming less hydrated and increasingly fibrous.

The notochord is derived from the epiblast cells. Epiblast cells from the primitive knot region of the primitive streak multiply and pass cranially in the midline between the ectoderm and endoderm. They undergo several stages of rearrangement to form the notochord. During the initial stages of neurulation, the notochord induces overlying ectoderm to thicken and form the neural plate.

During vertebral column development, the notochord gradually regresses, with its cells persisting as the nucleus pulposus of the intervertebral discs.

Rarely, these notochordal remnants may give rise to slow-growing tumors known as chordomas. These malignant bone tumors arise from residual embryonic notochordal tissue and are usually located along the axial midline. It is the most common primary malignancy of the sacrum.

Pearl PF0426: Derivatives of Mesoderm

Mesoderm derivatives

Paraxial mesoderm

• Skeletal muscles of the trunk, limbs, head, and neck
• Extraocular muscles
• Intrinsic muscles of the tongue
• Bones: Vertebrae, ribs
• Dermis of Skin
• Duramater

Intermediate mesoderm

• Urinary system: Kidneys, ureters, trigone of the urinary bladder
• Dorsal part of prostatic urethra (males)
• Gonads: Testes and ovaries
• Genital ducts
• Adrenal cortex

Lateral plate mesoderm

• Bones: Sternum, limb bones
• Serous membranes of body cavities: Pleura, pericardium, peritoneum
• GIT layers: Lamina propria, muscularis mucosae, submucosa, muscularis externa, adventitia
• Blood cells: Microglia, Kupffer cells
• Cardiovascular system
• Lymphatic system
• Laryngeal cartilages

Pearl PF0425: Neural crest derivatives

Neural

Mesenchymal

All ganglions

Connective tissue and bones of the face and skull

All enteric plexus

Dermis of the head and face

Schwann cells and Satellite glial cells

Odontoblasts (Dentine)

Adrenal Medulla

Arachnoid and Piamater

Parafolliular C cells of Thyroid

Conotruncal septum in the heart

Melanoblast/Melanocytes (except Retinal Pigment Epithelium)
questions.learning: Nucleus pulposus — The nucleus pulposus is derived from the notochord (marked by the arrow). The nucleus pulposus is a mucoid, gel-like substance that lies between the centre of the intervertebral disc and its posterior surface.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A patient presents with left-sided facial paralysis and left-sided limb weakness for the past 1 hour. Her blood pressure is 160/100 mm Hg and her CT appears normal. What would be the next step of management?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Intravenous thrombolysis

Sudden onset hemiparesis with apparently normal CT indicates ischemic stroke in this patient. Intravenous thrombolysis(alteplase 0.9 mg/kg ) should be immediately administered to patients with ischemic stroke who arrive in the window period i.e., within 3-4.5 hours of symptom onset.

Aspirin + clopidogrel(Option B) is used in secondary prevention of stroke and also to prevent stroke following TIA.

Transient ischemic attacks (TIAs) refer to episodes of stroke symptoms that have a brief duration, the standard definition of duration is <24 h, but most TIAs last <1 hr. TIAs may arise from emboli to the brain or from in situ thrombosis of an intracranial vessel. With a TIA, the occluded blood vessel reopens and neurologic function is restored. If a relevant brain infarction is identified on brain imaging, the clinical entity is now classified as stroke regardless of the duration of symptoms.

The risk of stroke following a transient ischemic attack (TIA) is approximately 10-15% in the first three months, majorly in the first two days. A reliable estimation of this risk can be obtained using the ABCD2 score.
Other options:

Option A: If CT is normal it only rules out hemorrhagic stroke and changes of ischemic stroke usually take time to appear on NCCT.

Option D: BP control is done when BP exceeds 220/120 mmHg, if there is malignant hypertension or concomitant myocardial ischemia, or if blood pressure is >185/110 mmHg and thrombolytic therapy is anticipated.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: A young woman presents to the ENT OPD with sudden-onset unilateral hearing loss, tinnitus, and vertigo following an acute otitis media episode two weeks ago. Initially, the Rinne and fistula tests were positive, but she had declined treatment. She now reports worsened hearing in the affected ear, and the fistula test is negative. What is the most likely result of the Rinne test in this scenario?
questions.explanation: The patient’s initial symptoms (vertigo, tinnitus, and hearing loss) following ASOM, combined with a positive fistula test, indicated a labyrinthine fistula. However, the subsequent "worsened hearing loss" and the "negative fistula test" suggest that the inner ear has now completely failed, resulting in total sensorineural hearing loss (dead ear). In a dead ear, the Rinne test on the affected side will yield a false negative result. This occurs because when the tuning fork is placed on the mastoid bone (bone conduction), the sound is transmitted through the skull and heard by the healthy contralateral ear. Since the patient "hears" the sound by bone but cannot hear it by air conduction in the dead ear, it appears as if . Option A (True positive) occurs in normal hearing. Option B (True negative) occurs in conductive hearing loss ( with a functioning cochlea). Option C is not a standard clinical interpretation of the Rinne test. Therefore, the "crossover" of sound to the good ear is the defining mechanism of a false negative Rinne
questions.learning: The patient’s initial symptoms (vertigo, tinnitus, and hearing loss) following ASOM, combined with a positive fistula test, indicated a labyrinthine fistula.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Which of the following statements are correct regarding inguinal hernias in children? I. It is more common in full-term boys. II. It should be repaired promptly. III. It is always indirect. IV. It may frequently be transilluminant. Select the answer using the code given below:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. II, III and IV

Inguinal hernias in children are congenital and occur due to failure of obliteration of the processus vaginalis. This creates a persistent communication between the peritoneal cavity and the inguinal canal, allowing abdominal contents to herniate. Because of the risk of incarceration and strangulation, all diagnosed pediatric inguinal hernias should be repaired promptly.

The following statements are true:

• II. It should be repaired promptly: Pediatric inguinal hernias do not resolve spontaneously and have a high risk of incarceration, especially during infancy. Early herniotomy is the treatment of choice.
• III. It is always indirect: Almost all inguinal hernias in children are indirect, occurring through a patent processus vaginalis. Direct inguinal hernias are extremely rare in children.
• IV. It may frequently be transilluminant: Because a patent processus vaginalis is often associated with a communicating hydrocele, the swelling may transilluminate when fluid predominates. Clinically, differentiating a communicating hydrocele from an inguinal hernia can sometimes be difficult.

Why is I incorrect?

• I. It is more common in full-term boys: Although inguinal hernias are more common in boys, they are more common in premature infants than in full-term infants, making this statement incorrect.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: A 30-year-old woman presents with persistent bone pain, abdominal cramps, and episodes of abnormal behavior noted by her family. To confirm the suspected diagnosis and guide appropriate management, which diagnostic test should be performed first?
questions.explanation: The patient's triad of "bone pain" (skeletal involvement), "abdominal cramps" (renal stones or peptic ulcers), and "unusual behavior" (psychiatric moans) is the classic description of Hyperparathyroidism ("Bones, Stones, Abdominal Groans, and Psychic Moans"). This condition is caused by an overactive parathyroid gland, usually a solitary parathyroid adenoma. Once biochemical hyperparathyroidism is confirmed (high PTH and high Calcium), the most effective diagnostic imaging test prioritized for localizing the overactive gland is the Tc-99m Sestamibi scan. This nuclear medicine study is highly sensitive for identifying ectopic or orthotopic parathyroid adenomas, as they characteristically retain the tracer longer than thyroid tissue. While USG (Option B) is a useful adjunct, Sestamibi provides better functional localization. MRI (Option A) and CT (Option D) are generally reserved for complex, recurrent, or poorly localized cases. Thus, the Sestamibi scan is the standard priority imaging for pre-operative planning
questions.learning: The patient's triad of "bone pain" (skeletal involvement), "abdominal cramps" (renal stones or peptic ulcers), and "unusual behavior" (psychiatric moans) is the classic description of Hyperparathyroidism ("Bones, Stones, Abdominal Groans, and Psychic Moans").

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: While examining a patient’s jugular venous pulse, a physician observes a prominent V wave in the waveform. Which clinical condition is most commonly associated with this finding?
questions.explanation: The 'v' wave in the jugular venous pulse (JVP) waveform corresponds to atrial filling while the tricuspid valve is closed during ventricular systole. A prominent (large) 'v' wave is a classic physical sign of tricuspid regurgitation. In this condition, blood leaks backward from the right ventricle into the right atrium during systole, significantly increasing the pressure and volume in the atrium and producing an exaggerated 'v' wave. Aortic regurgitation (Option B) affects the left side of the heart and does not directly produce JVP changes. Tricuspid stenosis (Option C) would result in a prominent 'a' wave due to forceful atrial contraction against a narrowed valve. Atrial fibrillation (Option D) is characterized by the absence of the 'a' wave. Bedside assessment of the JVP waveform is a vital diagnostic skill in cardiology, allowing the clinician to differentiate between various right-sided heart pathologies. Thus, a giant 'v' wave is pathognomonic for severe tricuspid regurgitation
questions.learning: The 'v' wave in the jugular venous pulse (JVP) waveform corresponds to atrial filling while the tricuspid valve is closed during ventricular systole. A prominent (large) 'v' wave is a classic physical sign of tricuspid regurgitation.

options: Visual inspection after application of freshly prepared solution 5% acetic acid solution

Correct answer: A. Visual inspection after application of freshly prepared solution 5% acetic acid solution

The present day strategy of initial screening of women for cervical cancer is by visual inspection after application of freshly prepared solution 5% acetic acid solution.

Visual inspection with acetic acid is naked-eye examination of the uterine cervix, after application of 5% acetic acid and interpreting the result after one minute. This is a simple and inexpensive test for the detection of cervical precancerous lesions and early invasive cancer.

* Detection of well defined circum- orificial acetowhite areas or ulceroproliferative growth on the cervix will provide VIA or VIAM positive.

* In the district hospital treatment should be based on single visit colposcopy approach.

* Biopsy and Colposcopy are done to ensure that there are cytological and histological backup for the interventions.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 35-year-old female patient presents to you with fever, breathlessness, and cough with expectoration. A CT scan was done which is shown below. What is the most likely diagnosis?

Fever, breathlessness, and productive cough suggest an acute infective process.

CT showing a homogeneous area of increased attenuation with air bronchograms is classic for alveolar consolidation, where alveoli are filled with inflammatory exudate.

Mass lesions lack air bronchograms, pleural effusion shows fluid layering, and diaphragmatic hernia shows bowel shadows.

Key CT features:

• Homogeneous opacity
• Air bronchograms (air-filled bronchi in white lung)
• Segmental/lobar involvement

- Pus

- Inflammatory cells

| Location | Lung parenchyma | Pleural space | Focal lesion

| Air bronchogram | ✔ Present | ❌ Absent | Rare

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: In the peripheral tissue, which enzyme is accountable for converting T4 to T3?
questions.explanation: Thyroxine (T4) is a prohormone that is converted into the biologically active hormone triiodothyronine (T3) in peripheral tissues. This conversion occurs by deiodination, specifically removal of an iodine atom from the outer ring of T4. The enzyme responsible for this process in peripheral tissues such as liver, kidney, and thyroid is Iodothyronine deiodinase type I (D1). It plays a major role in maintaining circulating levels of T3. Another enzyme, type II deiodinase (D2), also converts T4 to T3 but mainly functions in specific tissues like the brain, pituitary, and brown adipose tissue for local (intracellular) T3 production rather than circulating levels. Why other options are incorrect: (B) Deiodinase III (D3) → Converts T4 to reverse T3 (inactive) (C) Deiodinase II (D2) → Local conversion, not main peripheral source (D) Iodotyrosine deiodinase → Involved in iodine recycling, not T3 formation
questions.learning: Thyroxine (T4) is a prohormone that is converted into the biologically active hormone triiodothyronine (T3) in peripheral tissues. This conversion occurs by deiodination, specifically removal of an iodine atom from the outer ring of T4.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: A 66-year-old man with chronic kidney disease has poorly controlled diabetes mellitus. While planning to optimize his antidiabetic therapy, which of the following drugs does not require dose adjustment in this patient?
questions.explanation: In patients with chronic kidney disease (CKD), many antidiabetic drugs accumulate and increase the risk of toxicity or severe hypoglycemia. Among the DPP-4 inhibitors (gliptins), Linagliptin is unique because it is primarily excreted through the biliary system (feces) rather than the kidneys. Consequently, it requires no dose modification regardless of the stage of renal impairment. Saxagliptin (Option D) is primarily renal-cleared and requires dose reduction in CKD. Glyburide (Option C), a sulfonylurea, has active metabolites that are renal-cleared; it is generally avoided in CKD due to the high risk of prolonged, fatal hypoglycemia. Repaglinide (Option A) is mostly hepatically cleared but usually requires cautious titration in advanced CKD, whereas linagliptin's pharmacological profile is the most robust for renal safety. This makes linagliptin the preferred gliptin for diabetic patients with failing renal function

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Identify the following image:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Ranula

The given scenario and the image of a cystic swelling on the floor of the mouth are suggestive of a ranula.

Ranula is a mucus extravasation cyst arising from the sublingual gland. It produces a characteristic translucent swelling that gives the appearance of a frog’s belly. A ranula usually resolves spontaneously.

A plunging ranula is a mucus retention cyst. It has mucus collecting below the gland and perforating through the mylohyoid muscle.

Treatment should include removal of the sublingual gland as this gland has multiple ducts and ranulas can recur if the gland is left behind. Incision, drainage and marsupialisation have low success rates.

Other options:

Options A: Hemangioma is the most common vascular tumor and is characterized by increased abnormal proliferation of endothelium. Hemangiomas develop in infancy and are usually not visible at birth. They appear red or maroon if superficial, and bluish if deep.

Option B: Cystic hygroma is usually seen in neonates and early childhood. They are cystic swellings filled with lymph fluid and are characteristically brilliantly translucent. They occur in the neck and can involve the parotid, submandibular, tongue, etc. The swelling is soft and partially compressible. Definitive treatment is the excision of the swelling.

Option C: The branchial cyst develops from the vestigial remnants of the second branchial cleft. Swelling in the neck beneath the anterior border of the upper third of the sternomastoid muscle. It is smooth, soft, fluctuant, and often transilluminate. The below image shows a large right-sided branchial cyst.
questions.learning: Ranula — The given scenario and the image of a cystic swelling on the floor of the mouth are suggestive of a ranula. Ranula is a mucus extravasation cyst arising from the sublingual gland.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Which of the following are correct for herniation via foramen of Morgagni? 1. It occurs posteriorly in chest. 2. Transverse colon is the commonest content. 3. Defect is between sternal and costal attachments. 4. It is a type of congenital hernia. Select the answer using the code given below.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. 2, 3 and 4

Foramen of Morgagni hernia is a rare congenital diaphragmatic hernia caused by a defect in the anterior diaphragm, located between the sternal and costal fibers of the diaphragm. It usually occurs on the right side and commonly contains the transverse colon or omentum.

Why is D correct?

• 1. It occurs posteriorly in chest. ✗

• Morgagni hernia is an anterior diaphragmatic hernia.
• The posterior diaphragmatic defect is the foramen of Bochdalek.

• 2. Transverse colon is the commonest content. ✓

• The transverse colon is the most common herniated viscus, followed by the omentum and occasionally the stomach or liver.

• 3. Defect is between sternal and costal attachments. ✓

• The foramen of Morgagni lies between the sternal and costal attachments of the diaphragm (sternocostal triangle).

• 4. It is a type of congenital hernia. ✓

• Morgagni hernia is a congenital diaphragmatic hernia, although it may remain asymptomatic until adulthood.
questions.learning: 2, 3 and 4 Foramen of Morgagni hernia is a rare congenital diaphragmatic hernia caused by a defect in the anterior diaphragm, located between the sternal and costal fibers of the diaphragm.

questions.text: A 64-year-old man comes to the OPD due to worsening dyspnea on exertion for the past 3 months. The patient has had a nonproductive cough but no chest pain, fever, or chills. He was diagnosed with hypertension several years ago but takes no medications. Physical examination shows bilateral inspiratory crackles as well as dullness to percussion and decreased breath sounds at the right lung base. Chest x-ray reveals a right-sided pleural effusion. Which of the following pleuropulmonary changes are most likely present in this patient?
options: Vascular hydrostatic pressure increased, Oncotic pressure increased, lymphatic flow normal
Vascular hydrostatic pressure normal, Oncotic pressure normal, lymphatic flow decreased
Vascular hydrostatic pressure increased, Oncotic pressure normal, lymphatic flow increased
Vascular hydrostatic pressure normal, Oncotic pressure decreased, lymphatic flow increased
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Vascular hydrostatic pressure increased, Oncotic pressure normal, lymphatic flow increased

Pleural effusion due to congestive heart failure occurs from increased pulmonary capillary hydrostatic pressure.

• Elevated hydrostatic pressure in pulmonary capillaries → transudation of fluid into the pleural space
• Oncotic pressure remains normal
• Lymphatic drainage increases initially to compensate but may eventually be overwhelmed.

Characteristics:

• Produces a transudative pleural effusion
• Commonly seen in heart failure

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.text: A woman gave birth to twins. The father who believed that they did not belong to him requested DNA testing. After testing, it was found that one child did not belong to him. This case would be best described as?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Superfecundation

The given clinical scenario where one twin is found to not belong to the father of the other twin is suggestive of heteroparental superfecundation.

Superfecundation is the fertilization of 2 different ova in the same menstrual cycle (as suggested by the same gestational age) by separate acts of coitus. It can occur even after artificial reproductive therapy. Hence, after embryo transfer, intercourse must be avoided. Heteropaternal superfecundation is used to refer to instances of two different males fathering fraternal twins. This leads to the possibility of twins also being half-siblings. This may give rise to the doubt of adultery and infidelity.

Option A: Superfetation is the fertilization of 2 different ova released in different menstrual cycles (i.e ovulation and fertilization during pregnancy). This can occur within 12 weeks of pregnancy after which the decidual space is obliterated and a detailed evaluation will reveal disparities in gestational ages.

Option C: Supposititious child is also known as a fictitious child. In such cases, a woman pretends to be pregnant and generally substitutes a male child for a female child born of her, or after an abortion. This is done for the purpose of claiming property.

Option D: Atavism is the reappearance of a characteristic in an individual after several generations of absence. For example, the child may not resemble his parents but resemble his ancestors. This is attributed to the recombination of genes.
questions.learning: Superfecundation — The given clinical scenario where one twin is found to not belong to the father of the other twin is suggestive of heteroparental superfecundation.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Which artery is the most common source of Cirsoid Aneurysms of the scalp? (NEET PG 2016)
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Superficial temporal artery

Cirsoid aneurysm is an arteriovenous malformation that most commonly affects the superficial temporal vessels on the forehead and scalp. These lesions present as pulsatile masses and represent abnormal communications between arteries and veins without an intervening capillary network. The superficial temporal artery is the primary arterial feeder in these malformations, making it the most common source of cirsoid aneurysms of the scalp.

questions.subject: Psychiatry
questions.text: A 39-year-old man reported that he washes his hands 15-20 times a day, to the point of it taking a toll on his workplace performance. He says this is due to repetitive thoughts that his hands are contaminated with dirt. What is the most probable diagnosis in this case?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Obsessive compulsive disorder

The man is suffering from obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD), as evidenced by the obsession (doubt that his hands are contaminated), followed by a compulsion (washing his hands way too many times). An obsession with contamination is a common symptom of adult OCD.

Obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD) comprises symptoms that include intrusive thoughts, rituals, preoccupations, and compulsions. These recurrent obsessions or compulsions cause severe distress to the patient. The patient might have an obsession, a compulsion, or both.

The recurrent and intrusive thoughts, feelings, ideas, and sensations are referred to as obsessions. A compulsion is a conscious, standardized, recurrent behavior, eg: counting, and checking, and is done in order to reduce the anxiety associated with the obsession.

Treatment of OCD includes:

* Pharmacotherapy: SSRIs or clomipramine

* Behavioral therapy: Approaches include:

* exposure and response prevention

* desensitization

* thought stopping

* flooding

* implosion therapy

* aversive conditioning

A combination of behavioural and pharmacotherapy is most effective.

Other Options:

Option A: Bipolar disorder is characterized by alternating episodes of mania and depression, with periods of normal mood in between. The patient's presentation shows no evidence of mood cycling, elevated mood, grandiosity, decreased need for sleep, or other manic symptoms.

Option C: Schizophrenia is a psychotic disorder characterized by delusions, hallucinations, disorganized speech, disorganized behavior, and negative symptoms like flat affect and avolition. The patient's concern about hand contamination might superficially resemble a delusion, but it differs significantly. In OCD, patients typically recognize their thoughts are excessive or irrational (though they still feel compelled to act on them), whereas in schizophrenia, delusions are firmly held false beliefs that the person fully believes.

Option D: Mania is characterized by abnormally elevated mood, increased energy, decreased need for sleep, racing thoughts, pressured speech, grandiosity, increased goal-directed activity, and often poor judgment. The patient's repetitive hand washing isn't driven by elevated mood or energy but rather by anxiety and intrusive thoughts about contamination.
questions.learning: Obsessive compulsive disorder — The man is suffering from obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD), as evidenced by the obsession (doubt that his hands are contaminated), followed by a compulsion (washing his hands way too many times).

In an urban area in the state of Madhya Pradesh, a primigravida goes for institutional delivery after being motivated by an ASHA worker. What are the benefits they will receive (in terms of money in rupees) under the Janani Suraksha Yojana?

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: What is represented by each of the following growth curves?
options: 1- Brain, 2- Waldeyer's ring, 3- somatic growth, 4- Testicular growth
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. 1- Brain, 2- Waldeyer's ring, 3- somatic growth, 4- Testicular growth

The correct answer is 1- Brain, 2-  Waldeyer's ring, 3- somatic growth, 4- Testicular growth.

Curve 1: The neural growth(brain) attains 90% of the growth by the age of 2 years.

Curve 2: The tonsils are collections of lymphatic tissue located within the pharynx. They collectively form a ringed arrangement, known as Waldeyer’s ring. Tonsils/lymphatic growth in children occur between 4-8 years of age and then shrink down in adult age.

Curve 3: Somatic growth shows a sigmoid curve, rapid growth in the initial years, and then during puberty.

Curve 4: Testicular growth/Gonadal growth starts during puberty, before that the curve is flat.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: Which of the following organisms is acid-fast in nature?
questions.explanation: Acid-fast organisms are those that have a high concentration of mycolic acids in their cell walls, making them resistant to decolorization by acid-alcohol during staining procedures (like Ziehl-Neelsen staining). The genus Mycobacterium is the classic group of acid-fast bacteria. Mycobacterium avium complex (MAC) is an important opportunistic pathogen, especially in patients with advanced HIV/AIDS, and characteristically stains positive with acid-fast techniques. Streptococcus pneumoniae (Option A) and Escherichia coli (Option B) are standard gram-positive and gram-negative bacteria, respectively, and are not acid-fast. Actinomyces (Option D) are filamentous branching bacteria that are typically gram-positive but not acid-fast (differentiating them from Nocardia, which is weakly acid-fast). Recognizing the acid-fast property is essential for the rapid laboratory diagnosis of mycobacterial infections. Clinically, finding acid-fast bacilli (AFB) in sputum or tissue is a critical "red flag" that necessitates the initiation of targeted multi-drug therapy and, in many cases, respiratory isolation for the patient
questions.learning: Acid-fast organisms are those that have a high concentration of mycolic acids in their cell walls, making them resistant to decolorization by acid-alcohol during staining procedures (like Ziehl-Neelsen staining).

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: A 30-year-old man weighing 70 kg had a sodium level of 120 mEq/L. Calculate the sodium deficit.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. 840 mEq

The sodium deficit in the given scenario is 840 mEq.

Sodium deficit is calculated as 0.6 x body weight x (target plasma sodium concentration - starting plasma sodium concentration).

Substituting the given values in the formula :

Sodium deficit = 0.6 x 70 x (140 - 120) = 840 mEq.

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text: A 3-year-old child presented to your OPD with genu varum and softening of skull bones. There is bony depression over the chest. What is the most likely deficiency?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Vitamin D deficiency

The clinical scenario with genu varum, craniotabes and Harrison groove of the chest with the given lab parameters suggests rickets caused by vitamin D deficiency.

Rickets occurs due to a nutritional deficiency in vitamin D. Decrease in vitamin D levels leads to decreased calcium and phosphate due to reduced absorption. The decreased calcium stimulates increased parathyroid hormone(PTH) production. ALP level is increased as it is involved in bone mineralization.

Clinical features of rickets include:

* General features include malnourishment, abdominal distension, proximal muscle weakness, etc.

* Head: Softening of the skull bones, called craniotabes, delayed closure of fontanels.

* Chest: Rachitic rosary, i.e. widening of the costochondral junctions that give the feeling of rosary beads on palpation. Harrison's groove, a horizontal groove in the lower chest, may appear from the inward pull of the softened ribs by the diaphragm during respiration.

* Vertebral column abnormalities like scoliosis, kyphosis, and lordosis

* In the distal extremities widening of the wrists and ankles, varus/ valgus deformities, windswept deformity (valgus on the side and varus on the contralateral side), anterior tibial bowing.

The laboratory findings in rickets show normal/decreased serum calcium, decreased phosphorous, elevated PTH, and increased ALP levels

Metabolic bone disorders due to nutritional deficiencies include:

* Vitamin D deficiency leads to Rickets- in children

* Osteomalacia- in adults

* Secondary hyperparathyroidism

* Vitamin C deficiency leads to scurvy

Other options:

Option A: Vitamin A deficiency- can lead to night blindness and recurrent childhood infections- diarrhoea, and respiratory infections.

Option C: Vitamin C deficiency - can lead to scurvy which has manifestations due to poor collagen synthesis- dry skin, poor wound healing, swelling of the knee and ankle, and radiographic findings of a radiolucent band (Trümmerfeld zone) under a white line of Fränkel.

Option D: Vitamin K deficiency- can be seen in neonates due to non-colonised gut, and in adults with chronic antibiotics-lead to manifestations of clotting disorders- purpura, ecchymoses.

Pearl PF1660: Radiological features of rickets

Radiological features of rickets:

* Loss of provisional zone of calcification: earliest radiological finding of rickets.

* Delayed appearance of the epiphysis

* Widening of growth plate: normal width of growth is 2-4mm. It is increased in cases of rickets due to excessive accumulation of uncalcified osteoid at the growth plate.

* Cupping of metaphysis: normally metaphysis meets epiphysis as a smooth line of sclerosis. But in rickets the line is absent and the metaphyseal ends appear irregular and the cartilage accumulating in the growth plate creates a depression in the metaphysis causing cupping.

* Fraying: indistinct margins of the metaphysis

* Bowing of diaphysis, with thinning of cortices

* In healing rickets, zone of calcification becomes denser.

The above features are prominent at the growth plates where growth is greatest:

* Knee: distal femur, proximal tibia

* Wrist: especially the ulna

* Anterior rib ends: rachitic rosary

The below image shows bowing of legs in rickets.

Pearl PF0382: Important Clinical Features of Rickets

Pearl PF1801: Radiological features of scurvy

Radiological features of scurvy:

* Generalised osteopenia

* Pencil-point cortex: Cortical thinning

* Periosteal reaction due to subperiosteal hemorrhage

* Scorbutic rosary: Expansion of the costochondral junctions

* Hemarthrosis

* Wimberger ring: Circular, opaque radiological shadow surrounding epiphyseal centers of ossification, which may result from bleeding

* Frenkel line: Dense zone of provisional calcification

* Trummerfeld zone: Lucent metaphyseal band underlying Frankel line

* Pelken spur: Metaphyseal spurs which result in cupping of the metaphysis

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A 45-year-old man presents with a three-day history of persistent fever, malaise, and splinter hemorrhages. Echocardiography shows valvular vegetations suggestive of endocarditis. Blood cultures reveal alpha-hemolytic cocci in chains that are resistant to optochin and bile. Which bacterium is most likely causing his condition?
questions.explanation: The patient presents with subacute Infective Endocarditis, characterized by valvular vegetations and peripheral markers like splinter hemorrhages . The microbiology results are definitive: alpha-hemolytic cocci in chains that are resistant to optochin and bile identify the organism as a member of the Viridans group Streptococci, of which Streptococcus sanguis is a primary member. Streptococcus pneumoniae is also alpha-hemolytic but is sensitive to optochin and bile. Mycoplasma (Option A) lacks a cell wall and would not show these Gram-stain/culture features. Enterococcus (Option C) is usually gamma or alpha-hemolytic but is bile-esculin positive (meaning it grows in bile). Streptococcus agalactiae (Option D) is beta-hemolytic. Viridans group organisms like S. sanguis are part of the normal oral flora and are the most common cause of subacute endocarditis after dental procedures. Therefore, Option B is the correct pathogen

questions.text: A 24-year-old sexually active male presents to the outpatient department with complaints of painful urination and a thick yellow urethral discharge for the past 3 days. He denies any fever, chills, or flank pain. He reports multiple unprotected sexual encounters in the past month. A urethral swab is sent for Gram stain, which shows intracellular gram-negative diplococci within polymorphonuclear leukocytes. The organism is resistant to penicillins. Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment?

Correct answer: A. Ceftriaxone

Disseminated Gonococcal Infection (DGI): Triad:

• Dermatitis
• Tenosynovitis
• Migratory polyarthritis

Resistance Mechanisms for penicillin

1. β-lactamase production (penicillinase)
2. Altered PBPs (↓ binding affinity)
3. Efflux pumps

Penicillins (amoxicillin) become ineffective

Intracellular gram-negative diplococci in urethral discharge indicate Neisseria gonorrhoeae. Penicillin resistance is common due to β-lactamase production. A third-generation cephalosporin like ceftriaxone is the drug of choice for resistant gonorrhea. It provides reliable activity and high cure rates for uncomplicated infection.

Match the following poisons with their probable mechanism of action:
A. Zinc chloride
B. Chloral hydrate
C. Quinine
D. Potassium carbonate

questions.explanation:

For the above-given options, the correct match is given as

Poison
Mechanism

A.Zinc Chloride
2. Irritant

B.Chloral hydrate
4. Stupefying

C. Quinine
1. Abortifacient

D.Potassium
carbonate

Rationale for the classification

Zinc chloride also known as butter of zinc is highly irritant to the eyes on topical application. It can cause erosive esophagitis on ingestion. It has a fatal dose of 350mg. It could've also been classified as a corrosive, but since potassium carbonate is an alkali with stronger corrosive action, it is better classified as an irritant for this question

Chloral hydrate is a CNS depressant. It is also known as knockout drops because of its rapid action and used in robbery or rape to quickly render the victim helpless.

Quinine is a cardiotoxic drug with the additional action of being an abortifacient. It's overdose may lead to an echolic action (contract the pregnant uterus)

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Which ion is primarily responsible for the function of oxygen-sensitive channels in peripheral chemoreceptors?
questions.explanation: Potassium As detailed in Question 18, the detection of low arterial oxygen levels by peripheral chemoreceptors is fundamentally tied to Potassium (K+) ions. The closure of channels in response to hypoxia is the initiating event that leads to cellular excitation. Sodium (Na+) (Option B) is involved in the later stages of action potential generation but is not the primary ion for the "oxygen-sensitive" channel itself. Bicarbonate (HCO3 -) (Option C) and Chloride (Cl-) (Option D) are vital for acid-base balance and transport but do not serve as the primary triggers for oxygen sensing. The carotid bodies, located at the bifurcation of the common carotid arteries, are the most important peripheral chemoreceptors for the hypoxic drive. Their high rate of blood flow and sensitive channel mechanism allow them to continuously monitor arterial blood and send immediate signals to the respiratory centers in the medulla via the glossopharyngeal nerve whenever oxygen levels become critically low.
questions.learning: Potassium As detailed in Question 18, the detection of low arterial oxygen levels by peripheral chemoreceptors is fundamentally tied to Potassium (K+) ions.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: A 5-year-old child was brought to the OPD with a history of URTI and poor academic performance. He breathes through his mouth and has a high-arched palate. What type of hearing loss can be expected in this child? URTI- Upper respiratory tract infection
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Conductive hearing loss

The given clinical scenario of a child with mouth breathing and a high-arched palate points towards the diagnosis of serous otitis media secondary to adenoid hypertrophy, which is characterised by conductive hearing loss.

Adenoid hypertrophy causes typical facies characterised by an elongated face with a dull expression, an open mouth, a hitched-up upper lip, prominent upper teeth causing crowding (malocclusion of teeth), a high arched hard palate (due to loss of the tongue's molding action on the palate), and a pinched-in nose due to disuse atrophy of the alae nasi.

Enlarged adenoids in children can present as nasal obstruction, recurrent acute otitis media, and serous otitis media. Chronic nasal obstruction resulting in mouth breathing leads to this characteristic facial appearance in children. Patients can also present with a speech disorder, most probably rhinolalia clausa (hyponasality) due to adenoid hypertrophy.

Serous otitis media, also known as secretory otitis media, mucoid otitis media, or glue ear, is characterised by the accumulation of nonpurulent, serous effusion in the middle ear cleft. Glue ear can occur either due to eustachian tube dysfunction (adenoid hyperplasia, chronic sinusitis, tonsillitis or rhinitis, cleft palate, or tumours of nasopharynx) or due to increased secretory activity of the middle ear mucosa (allergy, unresolved otitis media, or viral infections).

Glue ear is commonly seen in children aged 5-8 years and is associated with insidious onset of hearing loss (not exceeding 40 dB), mild earaches, and a history of upper respiratory tract infections. Delayed or defective speech may also result from hearing loss.

Otoscopy shows:

* Dull and opaque tympanic membrane with loss of light reflex

* A thin leash of vessels along the handle of the malleus

* Fluid levels and air bubbles can be seen when the tympanic membrane is transparent.

The otoscopy image of serous otitis media is shown below:

Enlarged adenoids in children can present as nasal obstruction, rhinolalia clausa, recurrent acute otitis media, and serous otitis media. Adenoid facies, characterised by an elongated face, open mouth, teeth crowding, high-arched hard palate, and pinched-in nose, may also be present.

The tuning fork test reveals a conductive type of hearing loss, and audiometry reveals hearing loss in the range of 20–40 dB. The fluid accumulation in glue ear causes decreased mobility (compliance) of the tympanic membrane, leading to a flat or dome-shaped curve or type B curve on a tympanogram.

Treatment is mainly aimed at the removal of fluid and preventing recurrence.

* Medical management includes decongestants, antihistamines, and antibiotics.

* Surgical management is done if the condition cannot be controlled with medications. It includes myringotomy and aspiration of fluid with grommet insertion. Adenoidectomy and tonsillectomy may be required and are usually done at the time of myringotomy.

Other options:

Option A: Primary auditory canal cholesteatoma is characterised by normal hearing.

Option C: Waardenburg syndrome is a genetic condition characterised by sensorineural hearing loss, pigmentary abnormalities (such as two different coloured eyes or early graying of hair), and dystopia canthorum (widely spaced eyes).

Option D: A mixed type of hearing loss presents with defects in both conductive and sensorineural pathways. This type of hearing loss is seen in chronic suppurative otitis media and otosclerosis.

Pearl PF1978: Pure tone audiometry (PTA)

A pure tone is the sound of a single frequency. An audiometer is a device that generates pure tones and its frequency can be increased or decreased by 5Hz.

The threshold for air conduction (AC) of sound frequencies from 125-8000 Hz and the threshold for bone conduction (BC) of sound frequencies from 250-4000 Hz is measured and the result is plotted on an audiogram.

Normal thresholds:

* For AC: 15 dB

* For BC: 25 dB

Symbols used in pure tone audiometry:

Disease
Findings in PTA audiogram

Conductive hearing loss
AC abnormal, BC normal, air-bone gap present

Sensorineural hearing loss
Both AC and BC are abnormal and no air-Bone gap

Mixed hearing loss
Both AC and BC abnormal and air-bone gap present

Presbycusis, ototoxicity, noise-induced hearing loss (higher frequencies affected first)
Downsloping or descending audiogram

Early stages of Meniere's disease (lower frequencies affected first)
Upsloping or ascending audiogram

Congenital hearing loss and cochlear otosclerosis (mid-frequency hearing loss)
U-shaped or trough-shaped or cookie bite shaped audiogram

Early cases of noise-induced hearing loss

Acoustic dip - characteristic dip in both AC and BC at 4000 Hz

Otosclerosis
Carhart's notch- dip at 2000 Hz in BC curve

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Identify the correctly matched pair of substances with their renal clearance from the graph given below?
options: A - Glucose, B - PAH, C - Bicarbonate and D - Inulin
A - Glucose, B - Bicarbonate, C - Inulin and D - PAH
A - PAH, B - Inulin, C - Glucose and D - Bicarbonate
A - Inulin, B - Glucose, C - Bicarbonate and D – PAH
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. A - Glucose, B - Bicarbonate, C - Inulin and D - PAH

Glucose shows zero clearance as it is freely filtered and completely reabsorbed under normal plasma levels.

Bicarbonate has low but positive clearance due to near-complete reabsorption with regulated secretion.

Inulin clearance equals GFR as it is freely filtered with no reabsorption or secretion.

PAH has the highest clearance as it is filtered and actively secreted, approximating renal plasma flow.

| Substance | Handling | Clearance | Key Concept

| --------- | -------- | --------- | -----------

| Glucose | Fully reabsorbed | 0 | Tm limited

| Bicarbonate | Mostly reabsorbed | Low | pH regulation

| Inulin | Filtered only | = GFR | Gold standard

| PAH | Filtered + secreted | Highest | RPF marker
questions.learning: A - Glucose, B - Bicarbonate, C - Inulin and D - PAH Glucose shows zero clearance as it is freely filtered and completely reabsorbed under normal plasma levels.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A condition requires the surgery depicted in the image shown below. All the following are usually seen associated with this condition except?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Absent kidney

The given image shows a Roux-en-Y loop of the small intestine (jejunum) attached to an area of the liver capsule (Roux-en-Y hepaticojejunostomy), which is suggestive of Kasai hepatoportoenterostomy procedure done for biliary atresia in infants. An absent kidney is not associated with this condition.

Extrahepatic biliary atresia (EHBA) is defined as a partial or total absence of permeable bile duct between porta hepatis and the duodenum. It is due to inflammatory fibrosis of the biliary tree. It leads to obstruction to bile flow thereby causing leaking of conjugated bilirubin into the circulation.

Associated anomalies include cardiac lesions, polysplenia, situs inversus, absent vena cava, and a preduodenal portal vein.

Management of extrahepatic biliary atresia

Type I

Atresia restricted to the common bile duct

Roux-en-Y hepaticojejunostomy

Type II

Atresia of the common hepatic duct

Kasai procedure (Roux-en-Y hepatoportoenterostomy)

Type III

Atresia of the right and left hepatic duct

In the Kasai procedure, the extrahepatic biliary tree is dissected proximally till the liver capsule, the porta hepatis is transected and a jejunal loop is anastomosed in order to provide a drainage pathway for bile.

Infants with biliary atresia, who do not achieve successful drainage after Kasai's procedure, require liver transplantation within the first year of life. This is the most common reason for liver transplantation in children.

questions.text: Identify function of the instrument given below:
questions.explanation: The instrument shown in the image is a Rubin’s cannula or a similar uterine insufflation cannula, which is primarily used for Hysterosalpingography (HSG) (Option B). This procedure involves injecting a contrast medium or gas through the cannula into the uterine cavity and fallopian tubes to check for patency and uterine anomalies. Myomectomy (Option A) is the surgical removal of fibroids, which requires scalpels or laparoscopic tools rather than a simple contrast cannula. Endometrial biopsy (Option C) utilizes a Pipelle or curette to sample the lining of the uterus.
