questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Fluorescence in-situ hybridization(FISH) is required in which of the following IHC interpretations of Her2/neu?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. 2+

Fluorescence in situ hybridization (FISH) for gene amplification should be performed in all cases of breast tumors with an immunohistochemistry (IHC) score of 2+.

HER2/neu is a protein promoting rapid growth of breast cancer cells. All invasive breast cancers show undergo HER2/neu testing on biopsy or post-surgical removal. HER2 status is crucial for guiding breast cancer treatment. Two tests, immunohistochemistry (IHC) and fluorescence in situ hybridization (FISH), determine the presence of high HER2 protein levels. As FISH is costlier and more time-consuming, IHC is often performed as the initial test.

Her-2/neu IHC interpretation:

• 0 to 1+: Negative for HER2. These cancers do not respond to drugs targetting HER2 receptors.
• 2+: Equivocal. Hence, further testing with FISH is required to clarify the HER2 status.
• 3+: Positive for HER2. These cancers respond to drugs targetting HER2 receptors.

Transtuzumab and pertuzumab are monoclonal antibodies specifically used for HER2/neu-positive tumors.
questions.learning: 2+ Fluorescence in situ hybridization (FISH) for gene amplification should be performed in all cases of breast tumors with an immunohistochemistry (IHC) score of 2+.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: Identify the lesion of vocal cord in the image given below :
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Laryngeal papilloma

The image showing grape-like projections, involving the anterior part of the vocal cords depicts a laryngeal papilloma.

Laryngeal papilloma is a benign tumor of the larynx caused by the human papillomavirus (HPV type 6 and 11). They can occur in children, most commonly around 3 -5 years of age (juvenile papillomatosis), as well as in adults. They involve the supraglottic and glottic regions of the larynx. Seeding of the lesions can occur during invasive laryngeal procedures, such as intubation. They have a high recurrence rate and very low potential for malignancy.

Adult-onset laryngeal papillomatosis is less common and usually seen in males aged 30-50 years. It is less aggressive and involves the anterior part of the vocal cords. The treatment is the same as juvenile papillomatosis.

Patients present with hoarseness, aphonia, dyspnea, or stridor. Laryngoscopy shows pinkish to white grape-like projections that can be sessile or pedunculate with a visible central vascular core. The diagnosis is confirmed by direct laryngoscopy and biopsy. Treatment consists of micro-laryngoscopy and CO2 laser excision.

The image below depicts laryngeal papillomatosis on laryngoscopy:

Reinke's edema (Option A) is a collection of fluid in the subepithelial space of Reinke. It generally occurs in patients with vocal abuse or smoking. The vocal cords will show diffuse, symmetrical swelling.

The laryngoscopic image below shows Reinke's edema:
questions.learning: Laryngeal papilloma — The image showing grape-like projections, involving the anterior part of the vocal cords depicts a laryngeal papilloma. Laryngeal papilloma is a benign tumor of the larynx caused by the human papillomavirus (HPV type 6 and 11).

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: A 10-year-old boy presented with seizures. His past history is significant for an episode of fever with rash at 1 year of age which resolved spontaneously. What is the most helpful investigation to diagnose his condition?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. IgG measles in CSF

The clinical scenario of a child with a previous history of fever with rash at 1 year, now presenting with seizures, is highly indicative of subacute sclerosing panencephalitis (SSPE), a rare chronic complication of measles. Anti-measles antibodies are elevated in cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) (IgG >IgM); hence, it is the most helpful investigation to diagnose this condition.

SSPE is a fatal progressive demyelinating disease caused by chronic CNS infection with the genetically altered variant of the measles virus. It occurs several years after primary measles infection and is more common in males.

Clinical manifestations progress through four stages:

• Stage I: involves mild symptoms like irritability and poor school performance.
• Stage II: is characterized by myoclonic seizures.
• Stage III:choreoathetosis, immobility, dystonia, lead-pipe rigidity, and cognitive decline are seen.
• Stage IV: leads to coma and death.

Diagnosis of SSPE is established by documentation of a compatible clinical course along with one of the following supporting findings: elevated measles antibody (IgG >IgM) in CSF analysis or characteristic electroencephalographic (EEG) patterns, suppression-burst episodes (high voltage sharp slow waves) or typical histological findings or isolation of virus from brain tissue.

CT and MRI show evidence of multifocal white matter lesions, cortical atrophy, and ventricular enlargement. Increased T2 signaling in the white matter of the brain is seen as the disease progresses (shown below):

Treatment is mainly supportive. Isoprinosine along with interferons is said to have additional effects. Carbamazepine is found to be useful in controlling myoclonic jerks in the early stages of the illness.

In measles, after an incubation period of 8-12 days, the prodromal phase starts with mild fever and is followed by conjunctivitis, photophobia, coryza, cough, and increasing fever. Koplik spots, appearing 1-4 days prior to the rash, are a characteristic sign of measles. The rash (shown below) appears on the 4th day of fever and typically begins on the forehead (around the hairline), and behind the ears, as a red maculopapular eruption.

The most common complication of measles is acute otitis media. The most common cause of death in measles is pneumonia. Low serum retinol levels in children with measles are associated with higher morbidity and mortality and hence Vitamin A therapy is indicated for all patients with measles.

Other options:

Option B: A common cause of temporal lobe epilepsy is mesial (medial) temporal sclerosis. It is the most common cause of surgically remediable partial epilepsy in adolescents and adults. It is often preceded by febrile seizures. Pathologically, these patients have atrophy and gliosis of the hippocampus. MRI shows hippocampal sclerosis (shown below).

Option D: C1Q4 antibodies in the CSF are seen in neuromyelitis optica. Neuromyelitis optica, also known as Devic’s disease, is an aggressive inflammatory demyelinating disorder characterized by recurrent attacks of optic neuritis and myelitis.
questions.learning: IgG measles in CSF — The clinical scenario of a child with a previous history of fever with rash at 1 year, now presenting with seizures, is highly indicative of subacute sclerosing panencephalitis (SSPE), a rare chronic complication of measles.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: Which government program is designed to provide health checkups and services for children aged 0–18 years, with special attention to out-of-school children?
questions.explanation: The Rashtriya Bal Swasthya Karyakram (RBSK) is the specific national initiative designed for the early screening and management of children from birth up to 18 years. Crucially, it targets children enrolled in government and government-aided schools as well as out-of-school children through Anganwadi centers. The program screens for the "4 Ds": Defects at birth, Diseases, Deficiencies, and Developmental delays. Janani Suraksha Yojana (Option B) is a maternal health scheme promoting institutional birth. Navjaat Shishu Suraksha Karyakram (Option C) focuses exclusively on basic newborn care and resuscitation. The Mid day meal program (Option D) provides nutritional support but only to children attending school. RBSK ensures a continuum of care by referring identified cases to District Early Intervention Centres (DEICs) for free treatment. This universal screening is a major public health effort to reduce the burden of childhood morbidity and disability, particularly among marginalized populations who may not have regular access to healthcare or education
questions.learning: The Rashtriya Bal Swasthya Karyakram (RBSK) is the specific national initiative designed for the early screening and management of children from birth up to 18 years.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: The patient came to the ER with pain on the left side of the chest radiating to the left arm and shoulder following exercise. The pain subsided after some time. What is the next step in management? ECG-Electro cardio graphy
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. ECG

The given clinical scenario of a patient coming to the ER with pain on the left side of the chest radiating to the left arm and shoulder can be suggestive of ACS (Acute Coronary Syndrome), and the next best step in management is doing an ECG.

Acute coronary syndromes (ACS) includes:

* Unstable angina(UA)

* Non-ST elevation myocardial infarction(NSTEMI)

* ST-elevation myocardial infarction (STEMI)

The diagnosis of ACS can be based on the ECG findings-:

STEMI-  Features of MI on ECG:

* ST-segment elevation: Zone of injury

* T wave inversions

* Deep Q waves: late sign to develop

* New left bundle branch block (LBBB)

NSTEMI- Features of NSTEMI on ECG (Troponins are elevated)

*  ST-segment depression

* Deep T-wave inversions

Unstable Angina - Features of Unstable Angina on ECG (Troponins are not elevated)

* Hyperacute T-wave

* T-wave flattening

* Inverted T-waves

* ST depression

The following protocol must be followed in the management of patients with acute coronary syndrome:

* Stabilization of airway, breathing, and circulation

* Administration of O2

* Treatment of sustained ventricular arrhythmia rapidly according to ACLS protocols

* Give aspirin 325 mg

* History and examination, assess cardiac biomarkers

* Give three sublingual nitroglycerin tablets each 5 min apart. Add IV nitroglycerin for the persistence of symptoms.

* Treat left heart failure if present with an after-load reducing agent or loop diuretic

* Give beta-blockers

* Give morphine for the persistence of anxiety and discomfort related to MI

* In patients with STEMI - Reperfusion with PCI or fibrinolysis (if PCI is unavailable within 120 min) followed by antiplatelet and anticoagulant therapy. In patients with NSTEMI - antiplatelet and anticoagulant therapy are indicated.

Pearl PF1415: Localisation of MI based on ST elevations in different leads

Extensive anterior - I, aVL, V1-V6

Lateral - I, aVL

Inferior - II, III, aVF

Anteroseptal - V1-V4

Anterolateral - I, aVL, V3-V6

Posterior - ST depression and tall R in V1-V4
questions.learning: ECG — The given clinical scenario of a patient coming to the ER with pain on the left side of the chest radiating to the left arm and shoulder can be suggestive of ACS (Acute Coronary Syndrome), and the next best step in management is doing an ECG.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A patient presents with delayed wound healing, dermatitis, recurrent diarrhea, and alopecia. This combination of symptoms indicates a deficiency of an essential dietary mineral involved in skin maintenance, immune function, and gastrointestinal health. Which mineral deficiency is most likely responsible for these findings?
questions.explanation: The symptoms of alopecia, dermatitis (often perioral and acral), diarrhea, and impaired wound healing are the classic presentation of Zinc deficiency. Zinc is a critical trace mineral that serves as a cofactor for over 300 enzymes, including those involved in DNA synthesis, protein metabolism, and immune function. Severe congenital zinc deficiency is known as acrodermatitis enteropathica. Iron deficiency (Option A) primarily results in microcytic anemia, fatigue, and pica. Calcium deficiency (Option B) leads to muscle cramps, tetany, and osteoporosis. Magnesium deficiency (Option C) can cause neuromuscular irritability, tremors, and cardiac arrhythmias. Zinc's role in epithelial health and cell division explains why its lack so profoundly affects the skin and gastrointestinal tract. Supplementation typically leads to a rapid improvement in symptoms. Clinicians should consider zinc deficiency in patients with malabsorption syndromes, chronic alcoholism, or those on long-term parenteral nutrition without adequate mineral replacement
questions.learning: The symptoms of alopecia, dermatitis (often perioral and acral), diarrhea, and impaired wound healing are the classic presentation of Zinc deficiency.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: The instrument shown in the image is not used for which of the following?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Upper airway examination

The image shows a tracheostomy tube. It is not used for upper airway examination.

Tracheostomy involves making an opening and placing a stoma in the anterior wall of the trachea.

Functions:

1. Provides an alternative pathway for breathing by bypassing the obstruction.
2. Improves alveolar ventilation by reducing dead space by 30-50% and reducing airway resistance
3. Uses a cuff to protect the airways from secretions and blood
4. Allows suction of secretions in the setting of the impaired cough reflex.
5. Allows positive pressure respiration
6. Allows administration of anesthesia

Indications:

1. Respiratory obstruction due to

1. Infections (laryngo-tracheo-bronchitis, epiglottitis, diphtheria)
2. Trauma due to external injury, mandibular or maxillofacial fractures
3. Neoplasms
4. Foreign bodies or edema
5. Bilateral abductor paralysis
6. Congenital anomalies

2. Retained secretions

1. Inability to cough due to coma, spasm, or paralysis of respiratory muscles
2. Aspiration of pharyngeal secretions
3. Painful cough

3. Respiratory insufficiency due to emphysema, chronic bronchitis
questions.learning: Upper airway examination — The image shows a tracheostomy tube. It is not used for upper airway examination.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A woman presents with secondary amenorrhea for 9 months and infertility. She has a history of dilatation and curettage, with both the progesterone and estrogen-progesterone challenge tests negative and normal LH and FSH levels. What is the most likely diagnosis? PCOS - Polycystic ovarian syndrome
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Asherman syndrome

A history of dilatation and curettage followed by secondary amenorrhea and infertility, in the presence of normal LH and FSH levels and negative progesterone as well as estrogen-progesterone challenge tests, is highly indicative of Asherman’s syndrome.

Asherman syndrome refers to the presence of uterine synechiae, due to the destruction of the endometrium. It can occur as a result of trauma to the endometrium following vigorous curettages for elective abortion, tuberculous endometritis, and uterine surgeries. Depending on the degree of scarring, patients may have amenorrhea, hypomenorrhea, or recurrent pregnancy loss because of inadequate placentation.

Hysterosalpingography (HSG) is used to evaluate the uterine cavity and tubal patency, where intrauterine adhesions typically appear as irregular, angulated filling defects with a characteristic “moth-eaten” appearance. The gold standard for definitive diagnosis and treatment is hysteroscopy, with hysteroscopic adhesiolysis being the preferred surgical approach.

Hormonal assays also aid in the diagnosis of Asherman syndrome. All women with amenorrhea in the reproductive age group are considered pregnant unless proven otherwise by negative urinary or serum β-HCG levels. Once negative for pregnancy, further testing is done by a progesterone challenge test.

This test is done by administering medroxyprogesterone acetate as a 10-mg daily oral dose for 10 days. If the woman bleeds, then she is assumed to produce estrogen and to have a developed endometrium, and the presence of a patent outflow tract is confirmed. If she does not bleed, then she is given estrogen followed by progesterone treatment in the form of combined OCPs. If she fails to bleed after completing the 21 hormone-containing pills, then an anatomic abnormality is diagnosed such as Asherman syndrome.

Below is the HSG showing moth-eaten appearance in asherman syndrome.

Other options:

Option A: Sheehan's syndrome/ pituitary apoplexy is hemorrhagic infarction of large pituitary adenomas or pituitary infarction due to traumatic major blood loss. If this blood loss occurs during delivery, it's called Sheehan's syndrome. Affected women may present with panhypopituitarism and may have persistent hypotension, tachycardia, hypoglycemia, and lactation failure. The most prominent symptoms are lactation failure (due to the deficiency of prolactin) and postpartum amenorrhea (due to the deficiency of gonadotropins).

Option B: PCOS is a multisystem, metabolic, endocrine dysfunction that commonly occurs among women in the reproductive age group. LH level is raised over 10 IU/mL. FSH level remains normal to low, but FSH/LH ratio falls. Estrone(E1) levels are elevated but estradiol level in PCOS is low in comparison to Estrone (E1).

Option C: Premature Ovarian failure or premature menopause is the development of menopause before the age of 40 years. It is diagnosed when at least 2 serum FSH levels are elevated (>40 mIU/l) when measured at least 1 month apart in a woman <40 years. The other findings consistent with POF include low estradiol and an elevated FSH/LH ratio.

Condition

Lab markers

1. Sheehan's syndrome

C. Low LH, Low FSH, Low estradiol

2. Premature Ovarian failure

D. High LH, High FSH, Low estradiol

3. PCOS

B. High LH, Low FSH, Low estradiol

4. Asherman's syndrome

A. Normal FSH, Normal LH, Normal estradiol

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: A 35-year-old man wakes up after sleeping with his arm hanging over a chair and complains of pain and sensory symptoms. In this condition, which sequence correctly represents the order of susceptibility of different nerve fiber types to compression?
questions.explanation: The clinical scenario describes "Saturday night palsy," a compression injury of the radial nerve. Nerve fibers have different sensitivities to external stressors based on their size and myelination. When subjected to pressure or mechanical compression, large myelinated fibers are the most susceptible, following the order: A > B > C. Fiber type A (specifically Alpha) is the most sensitive to pressure, while Type C is the least. In contrast, if the stressor were local anesthesia, the order would be C > B > A, as small unmyelinated fibers are blocked most easily. If the stressor were hypoxia, Type B fibers would be the most susceptible. Because this patient experienced mechanical compression by draping his arm over a chair, the largest and most metabolically demanding fibers (Type A) are affected first, making Option B the correct hierarchy
questions.learning: The clinical scenario describes "Saturday night palsy," a compression injury of the radial nerve. Nerve fibers have different sensitivities to external stressors based on their size and myelination.

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following is incorrect about heat exhaustion?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Loss of thermoregulatory mechanism

Heat exhaustion is due to fluid and electrolyte depletion with intact thermoregulation, making option A (loss of thermoregulatory mechanism) incorrect.

• Core temperature: Usually < 40°C (104–105°F)
• Mechanism: Thermoregulatory system is still functioning (sweating present)
• Clinical features:

• Profuse sweating
• Orthostatic hypotension
• Weakness, dizziness
• May have mild confusion but no severe CNS dysfunction

Differentiation from heat stroke:

• Heat exhaustion:

• Thermoregulation intact
• Sweating present
• Mild/no altered consciousness

• Heat stroke:

• Failure of thermoregulation
• Core temp > 40°C
• Severe CNS symptoms (delirium, coma)
• Often dry skin

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: During which gestational period is it legally required to obtain the approval of two registered medical practitioners for performing a medical termination of pregnancy (MTP)?
questions.explanation: According to the Medical Termination of Pregnancy (Amendment) Act, 2021 in India, the legal requirements for abortion change based on gestational age. For pregnancies up to 12 weeks (Option C), the opinion of only one registered medical practitioner is required. For pregnancies between 20 and 24 weeks (Option B), the opinion and approval of two registered medical practitioners are mandatory. Option A is partially correct but includes the week period where rules differ. Option D (greater than 24 weeks) generally requires the approval of a State-level Medical Board for specific cases of substantial fetal abnormalities. Therefore, the 20-24 week window is the specific legal threshold where a "second opinion" is required for termination. This ensures additional oversight for later-term procedures
questions.learning: According to the Medical Termination of Pregnancy (Amendment) Act, 2021 in India, the legal requirements for abortion change based on gestational age.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: What is the recommended treatment for inguinal hernia in infants?
questions.explanation: In infants and children, nearly all inguinal hernias are of the indirect type and result from a patent processus vaginalis (a congenital developmental defect). Because the underlying abdominal wall muscles are typically strong and normal, the only surgical step required is the high ligation and excision of the patent hernia sac. This procedure is called a Herniotomy (Option A). Herniorrhaphy (Option B) involves suturing the abdominal wall to reinforce it, which is unnecessary in infants. Hernioplasty (Option D) involves using a synthetic mesh for reinforcement, which is standard in adults but strictly avoided in growing children. A Truss (Option C) is an outdated external belt that is ineffective and can lead to skin damage and incarceration. Inguinal hernias in infants never resolve spontaneously and carry a high risk of strangulation, so early surgical herniotomy is mandatory. Therefore, simple excision of the sac is the gold standard pediatric surgical intervention
questions.learning: In infants and children, nearly all inguinal hernias are of the indirect type and result from a patent processus vaginalis (a congenital developmental defect).

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: A primary health centre provides nutritional counselling and treatment to 100 diabetic patients. To assess the effectiveness, the medical officer compares patients’ weights before and after the intervention. Which statistical test is most appropriate for this analysis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Paired t-test

The same 100 diabetic patients are assessed before and after the intervention, producing paired (dependent) continuous data. Data in paired tests are continuous variables.

The paired t-test evaluates whether the mean difference between two related measurements is statistically significant. It tests whether the intervention caused a significant change.

The paired t-test is used to compare the means of two related samples, making it the most appropriate test here.
questions.learning: Paired t-test — The same 100 diabetic patients are assessed before and after the intervention, producing paired (dependent) continuous data. Data in paired tests are continuous variables.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: Which of the following statements is not an accurate description of the clinical condition discussed above?
options: Abnormal activity of p53 is seen in the pterygium tissue
Decreased activity of tissue inhibitors of metalloproteinases is seen
Destruction of Bowman's layer occurs when the pterygium invades the cornea
Elastotic degeneration and hyalinization of the connective tissue of the conjunctiva occur.
questions.explanation: The image shows pterygium — a fibrovascular conjunctival growth invading the cornea, labeled "am" (advancing margin) in image (a), with histology in image (b) showing "bm" (Bowman's membrane) and "am" (advancing margin). The question asks which statement is NOT accurate. Option C is incorrect because pterygium does NOT destroy Bowman's layer during invasion — rather it grows underneath Bowman's layer, lifting and displacing it rather than destroying it. Bowman's layer remains intact as pterygium advances beneath it. Why other options are wrong (i.e., they ARE accurate statements): (A) is accurate — abnormal p53 activity due to UV-induced mutations is indeed documented in pterygium tissue, contributing to its proliferative behavior. (B) is accurate — decreased tissue inhibitors of metalloproteinases (TIMPs) are seen in pterygium, allowing matrix metalloproteinases to facilitate tissue remodeling and invasion. (D) is accurate — elastotic degeneration and hyalinization of subconjunctival connective tissue is the classic histopathological hallmark of pterygium seen on microscopy
questions.learning: The image shows pterygium — a fibrovascular conjunctival growth invading the cornea, labeled "am" (advancing margin) in image (a), with histology in image (b) showing "bm" (Bowman's membrane) and "am" (advancing margin).

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A patient presents with acute-onset, severe abdominal pain. He is hemodynamically stable. A chest x-ray is shown below. What is the next step in management?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Emergency laparotomy

The given clinical scenario and the chest radiograph showing air under the diaphragm are suggestive of a hollow viscus perforation. The next best step in management among the given options is emergency laparotomy.

Perforation of a viscus is a life-threatening condition that occurs following the rupture of the alimentary tract. This leads to the leakage of the enteric contents, thereby leading to acute bacterial peritonitis. Peritonitis is the generalized or localized inflammation of the peritoneum either due to the free spillage of fluids into the peritoneal cavity or secondary bacterial infection.

Clinical features of hollow viscous perforation occur due to the developed peritonitis and the features include abdominal pain and distension, nausea, vomiting, tachycardia, tenderness, rebound tenderness, decreased or absent bowel sounds, and guarding on palpation. Fever may be present. Sometimes, features of septic shock can be seen at later stages.

Investigations include estimating the white blood cell count, urea, serum electrolytes, and an erect abdominal radiograph showing free gas under the diaphragm. A supine radiograph may show dilated gas-filled loops of the bowel, suggestive of paralytic ileus. The below image shows a hollow viscus perforation.

Management of a hollow viscous perforation is mainly resuscitation, analgesics, intravenous broad-spectrum antibiotics, and emergency laparotomy. Peritonitis is managed by nutritional support, pain relief, correction of fluid loss and circulating volume, urinary catheterization with or without gastrointestinal compression, antibiotics, analgesics, and specific surgical treatment of the cause.
questions.learning: Emergency laparotomy — The given clinical scenario and the chest radiograph showing air under the diaphragm are suggestive of a hollow viscus perforation.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 26-year-old pregnant woman, on examination was found to have infra-umbilical flattening. The fetal heart sounds were heard over the lateral side. What could be the fetal presentation/position?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Occipitoposterior

The presence of infra-umbilical flattening and fetal heart sounds on the lateral side indicates that the fetus is in the occipito-posterior position.

Occipito-posterior (OP) position of the fetus is when the occiput is situated posteriorly over the sacroiliac joint, or directly over the sacrum. The fetus is in vertex presentation.

Examination findings of OP position:

• On inspection, the abdomen appears flattened below the umbilicus (infra-umbilical flattening).
• Pelvic grips:

• The head is not engaged.
• The sinciput (cephalic prominence) is not prominently felt.

• Auscultation: Fetal heart sounds are heard maximally over the flanks. However, in the direct OP position, they are heard in the midline.

There are three variants of OP position:

• Left OP position (fourth position of the vertex) - When the occiput points towards the left sacroiliac joint.
• Right OP position (third position of the vertex) - When the occiput points towards the right sacroiliac joint. It is more common than the left OP position.
• Direct OP position - When the occiput points directly towards the sacrum.

All three positions may be primary (present before the onset of labor) or secondary (develops after the onset of labor).

Other options:

Option A: Brow presentation is a rare type of cephalic presentation where the position of the head is in between full flexion and full extension. The part of the head between the orbital ridge and the anterior fontanel presents at the pelvic inlet.

Option B: Knee presentation is a type of breech presentation. Here, the thighs are extended but the knees are flexed, presenting at the pelvic inlet. The head will be palpable as a hard globular mass at the fundus.

Option D: Right dorso-anterior position is when the fetal back is directed anteriorly. This occurs in a transverse lie. On examination, the abdomen appears wide, and a hard plane of resistance is felt. The fundus extends just above the umbilicus. The head is felt in one iliac fossa and the breech is felt in the other.
questions.learning: Occipitoposterior — The presence of infra-umbilical flattening and fetal heart sounds on the lateral side indicates that the fetus is in the occipito-posterior position.

questions.subject: Paediatrics
questions.text: Identify the chromosomal abnormality from the karyotyping shown below :
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Trisomy 18

The given karyotype is Trisomy 18- Edward's syndrome.

Edward's syndrome: Trisomy 18 results in Edward’s syndrome, in which a complete extra copy of chromosome 18 is inherited as a result of meiotic nondisjunction. The clinical features include micrognathia, low-set ears, prominent occiput, and rocker bottom feet Prenatal ultrasound reveals fetal growth restriction.

The craniofacial features include dolichocephaly, short palpebral fissures, micrognathia, external anomalies of the ears, and redundant skin at the back of the neck.

Other features include a clenched fist with overriding fingers, i.e. index finger overlapping the third and 5th finger overlapping the 4th, small fingernails, underdeveloped thumbs, short sternum, and club feet.

Heart defects are the most common structural malformations seen in Edwards syndrome. It includes defects of septum, patent ductus arteriosus, valvular defects. Other structural malformations associated with other systems(in decreasing order) are,

* Renal: Horseshoe kidney

* GIT: Omphalocele, esophageal atresia with tracheo-oesophageal fistula, pyloric stenosis.

* CNS: Spina bifida, cerebellar hypoplasia, corpus callosum agenesis

* Eye: Microphthalmia, cataract, corneal opacities

* Limb: Radial aplasia/hypoplasia

Other options :

Option A: Trisomy 13 - Patau Syndrome

* It is characterized by forebrain and midline facial abnormalities.

* Patients can develop holoprosencephaly, which is characterized by fused frontal lobes and a single ventricle. Olfactory bulbs are also absent.

* The midline facial abnormalities that are seen with trisomy 13 include cleft lip, cleft palate, nasal defects, and a single central eye (“cyclops”).

* Other defects associated with Patau’s syndrome include polydactyly, rocker-bottom feet, and congenital heart diseases.

The image below shows the facial abnormalities seen in Patau syndrome:

Option B: Trisomy 21: Down's Syndrome

* It is the most common chromosomal abnormality.

* Children with Down’s syndrome have severe mental retardation, which progressively declines with advancing age.

* Patients have characteristic facial features that include a flat facial profile, oblique palpebral fissures, and epicanthal folds.

* There is a horizontal palmar crease, and muscle tone at birth is decreased, which leads to a “floppy baby".

Option D: Trisomy 11 is extremely rare and often leads to miscarriage in early pregnancy.
questions.learning: Trisomy 18 — The given karyotype is Trisomy 18- Edward's syndrome. Edward's syndrome: Trisomy 18 results in Edward’s syndrome, in which a complete extra copy of chromosome 18 is inherited as a result of meiotic nondisjunction.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: A factory worker sustains burns covering 25% of his body surface area. Later, he develops infections and other complications. Under the Employees’ State Insurance (ESI) Act, he will be immediately eligible for which of the following benefits?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Extended sickness benefit (ESB)

Under the Employees’ State Insurance (ESI) Act, Extended Sickness Benefit (ESB) is provided for specified long-term or severe conditions requiring prolonged treatment.

| Feature | Details

| ------- | -------

| Purpose | Long-term diseases requiring prolonged treatment

| Wage compensation | About 80% of wages

| Duration | Up to 2 years

| Indication | Certain specified chronic diseases

Extensive burns (>20–25% body surface area) with complications like infections qualify for ESB, allowing extended cash benefits beyond the normal sickness benefit period.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: In a patient presenting with weight gain, fatigue, and cold intolerance suggestive of hypothyroidism, thyroid hormones primarily exert their effects through which type of receptor?
questions.explanation: The patient's symptoms of weight gain, fatigue, and cold intolerance are classic indicators of hypothyroidism. Thyroid hormones ( and ) exert their primary physiological effects by binding to Nuclear receptors. These receptors act as ligand-regulated transcription factors. Once enters the nucleus, it binds to the thyroid hormone receptor (TR), which is often pre-bound to thyroid response elements (TREs) on the DNA. This binding triggers the recruitment of coactivators and the initiation of gene transcription, leading to the synthesis of various proteins that regulate basal metabolic rate, thermogenesis, and heart rate. Cytoplasmic receptors (Option A) are used by steroid hormones but they eventually translocate to the nucleus. Tyrosine kinase receptors (Option C) are used by insulin and growth factors. G-protein coupled receptors (GPCR, Option D) are used by peptide hormones and TSH (the hormone that stimulates the thyroid). Understanding the nuclear mechanism is fundamental for explaining why thyroid hormone effects have a slow onset and long duration, as they require changes in protein synthesis
questions.learning: The patient's symptoms of weight gain, fatigue, and cold intolerance are classic indicators of hypothyroidism. Thyroid hormones ( and ) exert their primary physiological effects by binding to Nuclear receptors.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Klenow fragment lacks the activity of
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. 5'→3' Exonuclease

Klenow fragment lacks 5’ → 3’ exonuclease activity.

DNA polymerase I is an enzyme involved in DNA replication. It has polymerase activity along with both 3' → 5' and 5' → 3' exonuclease activity. When the 5' → 3' exonuclease domain is removed, the remaining fragment is called Klenow fragment. It retains the polymerization and proofreading activities of DNA polymerase I.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A 70-year-old man is admitted with a cardiac murmur, and blood cultures reveal Gram- positive cocci. Which organism is most commonly responsible for infective endocarditis involving a prosthetic heart valve?
questions.explanation: Staphylococcus epidermidis, a coagulase-negative Staphylococcus (CoNS), is the most common cause of prosthetic valve infective endocarditis (PVE). It is particularly notorious for producing biofilms that allow it to adhere to artificial surfaces, accounting for 68–85% of cases regardless of the onset time after surgery. Regarding the distractors, Streptococcus viridans (Option A) is the leading cause of native valve endocarditis, often following dental procedures, but is less common in PVE. Staphylococcus aureus (Option C) is a virulent pathogen that causes acute, rapidly progressive endocarditis in both native and prosthetic valves, but overall, CoNS are more frequent in the prosthetic context. Enterococci (Option D) are opportunistic pathogens that cause subacute endocarditis, often in elderly patients with genitourinary issues, but are not the primary PVE agents. Thus, the specific association with prosthetic materials makes S. epidermidis the most likely organism in this elderly patient

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: A 45-year-old woman comes to the emergency department with severe back pain, vomiting, and hypotension. CT findings are given below. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Renal angiomyolipoma

The given CT image shows well-circumscribed lesions with low attenuation (black in colour) that indicate fatty tissue. This is suggestive of renal angiomyolipomas.

Angiomyolipomas (AMLs) are benign tumours that occur sporadically or in association with tuberous sclerosis. It is commonly seen in adults between 30 and 50 years of age, with a female predilection. AMLs predominantly affect the kidneys, though they can occur in other sites such as the liver (a common extra-renal location) and less frequently in the ovary, fallopian tube, spermatic cord, palate, and colon.

Histologically, angiomyolipomas consist of perivascular epitheloid cells with varying proportions of vascular, immature smooth muscle cells, and fat cells. Patients with AMLs present with flank pain, a palpable mass, hematuria, recurrent urinary tract infections, hypertension, or renal failure. Larger tumours increase the risk of complications, such as spontaneous retroperitoneal hemorrhage, which can manifest as sudden-onset abdominal or flank pain, along with symptoms like nausea, vomiting, and hypotension.

Everolimus is used for the treatment of angiomyolipomas. Treatment should be considered for asymptomatic, growing AMLs measuring >3 cm in diameter. Angiomyolipomas do not normally require surgery unless life-threatening bleeding is present.

Other options:

Renal cyst is a broader term that includes the cystic lesions of the kidney. They can be simple cysts that are benign. Complex or complicated cystic lesions need evaluation and can be malignant. Bosniak classification is used for renal cysts. Cysts appear as hypodense lesions (greyish) with a thin wall, with or without septations.

CT image showing a simple renal cyst:

Renal cell carcinoma (RCC) is the most common malignant tumour of the kidney. It usually occurs in the age group 50-70 years and macroscopic hematuria is seen in about 60% of the cases. It is a differential for angiomyolipoma but it is important to note that macroscopic fat is almost always associated with ossification or calcification.
questions.learning: Renal angiomyolipoma — The given CT image shows well-circumscribed lesions with low attenuation (black in colour) that indicate fatty tissue. This is suggestive of renal angiomyolipomas.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: A patient presents with proptosis that increases when bending down. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Orbital varices are abnormal, dilated veins within the orbit that typically present with intermittent proptosis. A characteristic diagnostic feature is that the bulging of the eye increases during maneuvers that raise venous pressure, such as bending down, coughing, or performing the Valsalva maneuver. These lesions are usually unilateral and slowly progressive. Thyroid Eye Disease (Option B) is the most common cause of proptosis but is typically bilateral and does not fluctuate rapidly with head position. Cavernous Sinus Thrombosis (Option C) presents with painful proptosis, cranial nerve palsies, and systemic signs of infection rather than postural changes. Orbital Cellulitis (Option D) is an acute, painful infection of the orbit featuring redness, swelling, and fever. Diagnosis of orbital varices is aided by CT scans showing dense structures that enlarge during a Valsalva maneuver. Treatment is only needed for severe symptoms or optic nerve compression
questions.learning: Orbital varices are abnormal, dilated veins within the orbit that typically present with intermittent proptosis. A characteristic diagnostic feature is that the bulging of the eye increases during maneuvers that raise venous pressure, such as bending down,…

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 16-year-old boy presents with recurrent episodes of abdominal pain and a history of blood in the stools. Physical examination reveals darkly pigmented macules on the lips and oral mucosa, and endoscopy shows multiple hamartomatous polyps in the small intestine. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The classic triad of hamartomatous GI polyps, mucocutaneous pigmentation (dark spots on lips and oral mucosa), and symptoms of intestinal obstruction or bleeding is diagnostic of Peutz-Jeghers Syndrome (PJS). PJS is an autosomal dominant disorder caused by mutations in the STK11/LKB1 gene. Familial Adenomatous Polyposis (Option A) involves hundreds of adenomatous polyps in the colon but lacks the characteristic oral pigmentation. Juvenile Polyposis Syndrome (Option C) presents with hamartomas in younger children but also lacks perioral spotting. Cronkhite-Canada Syndrome (Option D) is a non-hereditary condition appearing in older adults, presenting with polyps alongside alopecia and nail atrophy, which are not present here. In adolescents with PJS, intussusception caused by large polyps is a frequent cause of the reported abdominal pain. Therefore, the specific pigmentation and polyp type confirm Peutz-Jeghers Syndrome
questions.learning: The classic triad of hamartomatous GI polyps, mucocutaneous pigmentation (dark spots on lips and oral mucosa), and symptoms of intestinal obstruction or bleeding is diagnostic of Peutz-Jeghers Syndrome (PJS).

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A female patient presents with severe restlessness, palpitations, and tremors to the emergency department. She is a known case of bronchial asthma. On examination, the neck looks swollen. Blood pressure is elevated, and tachycardia is noted. ECG shows atrial fibrillation. Which of the following drugs is used for immediate management in this patient?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Diltiazem

The given clinical scenario suggests the diagnosis of thyroid storm/thyroid crisis presenting with atrial fibrillation, and the immediate management in this patient is to rate control the arrhythmia with diltiazem (calcium channel blocker).

Thyroid storm/Thyrotoxic crisis is a rare but severe life-threatening complication of hyperthyroidism induced by the release of excessive thyroid hormones.

It is caused by abrupt cessation of antithyroid medications, infection, inadequately prepared hyperthyroid patient for thyroidectomy, amiodarone administration, exposure to iodinated contrast agents, and following radioactive iodine (RAI) therapy.

Features:

• Fever and severe dehydration
• Cardiovascular: Circulatory collapse, palpitations, tachycardia, cardiac arrhythmias, and cardiac failure
• GI symptoms: Vomiting, diarrhea, jaundice
• Neurological symptoms: Restlessness, irritability, delirium, tremor, convulsions, and coma

Treatment:

• If the patient presents with atrial fibrillation, the first step in the management is to do rate control using beta-blockers, calcium channel blockers, digoxin, or amiodarone. Since this patient is a known asthmatic, beta-blockers (propranolol and esmolol) are contraindicated. So, a calcium channel blocker (diltiazem) is the preferred drug for immediate management in this patient.
• Supportive measures – rehydration by proper fluid therapy, tepid sponging, and cooling blankets.
• Thionamides like propylthiouracil (PTU) or methimazole or carbimazole can be used. PTU (Option D) is the drug of choice in thyroid storm, but it is given only after controlling atrial fibrillation.
• Lugol’s iodide is given one hour after intake of thionamides. They inhibit thyroid hormone synthesis by Wolff- Chaikoff effect.
• Glucocorticoids – reduce the peripheral conversion of T4 to T3 and controls the shock.
• Digoxin and cardiac monitoring are crucial.

Other options:

Options B & C: Beta-blockers like propranolol and esmolol are contraindicated in bronchial asthma patients.
questions.learning: Diltiazem — The given clinical scenario suggests the diagnosis of thyroid storm/thyroid crisis presenting with atrial fibrillation, and the immediate management in this patient is to rate control the arrhythmia with diltiazem (calcium channel blocker).

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Which of the following is deficient in a patient with phenylketonuria with normal phenylalanine hydroxylase levels?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Dihydrobiopterin reductase

In a patient with hyperphenylalaninemia but normal phenylalanine hydroxylase (PAH), the defect lies in the cofactor tetrahydrobiopterin (BH₄) metabolism.

Key enzyme involved: Dihydrobiopterin reductase (DHPR) Deficiency → ↓ BH₄ availability

• Impaired phenylalanine → tyrosine conversion → ↑ phenylalanine
• Also affects neurotransmitter synthesis:

o    ↓ dopamine (tyrosine pathway)

o    ↓ serotonin (tryptophan pathway)

Clinical importance:

• More severe than classical PKU
• Presents with neurological deficits due to neurotransmitter deficiency

Why other options are incorrect:

• Tyrosine transaminase: Involved in tyrosine metabolism (tyrosinemia)
• Dopa decarboxylase: Involved in dopamine synthesis, not primary cause here
• Tyrosine hydroxylase: Requires BH₄ but is not the defective enzyme in this condition
questions.learning: Dihydrobiopterin reductase — In a patient with hyperphenylalaninemia but normal phenylalanine hydroxylase (PAH), the defect lies in the cofactor tetrahydrobiopterin (BH₄) metabolism.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.topic: Cardiovascular System · Acute Coronary Syndrome Mi
questions.text: A patient with triple-vessel coronary artery disease, including chronic total occlusions of two major vessels, presents with recurrent angina despite multiple PCIs. What is the most appropriate management?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Coronary artery bypass grafting (CABG)

Coronary artery bypass grafting (CABG) is the preferred method of revascularization in patients with complex multivessel coronary artery disease (CAD), especially those with triple-vessel disease, chronic total occlusions (CTOs), or recurrent angina despite previous PCI and optimal medical therapy. Compared with PCI, CABG provides more complete revascularization, reduces the need for repeat procedures, and improves long-term outcomes in appropriately selected patients.

Why not the other options?

• A. Repeat PCI: Less effective in patients with complex multivessel disease and chronic total occlusions, especially after multiple prior PCI procedures.
• B. Continue medical therapy: Inappropriate because the patient remains symptomatic despite prior revascularization and medical therapy.
• D. Thrombolytic therapy: Indicated for acute STEMI when timely PCI is unavailable, not for chronic stable multivessel CAD.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: What is the most useful test in vesicovaginal fistula?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Cystoscopy

Cystoscopy is the most useful test and also the investigation of choice for vesicovaginal fistula (VVF).

Cystoscopy or cystourethroscopy helps to visualize the size of the fistulas, the exact location of multiple fistulas and their proximity to the ureteral orifice. It can also assess the bladder mucosa for any injuries.

The 3-swab test (Option B) is done to identify the types of genitourinary fistula.

In this test, three sterile pieces of cotton swabs are serially placed in the vaginal cavity, while 50-100ml of methylene blue solution is instilled in the bladder using a catheter. The cotton swabs are placed one at the vault, one at the middle, and one just above the introitus.

Interpretation:

• Uppermost swab gets wet and not stained - the leak is from the ureter, as seen in ureterovaginal fistula
• Middle swab gets stained - the leak is from the bladder, as seen in vesicovaginal fistula
• Lowermost swab gets stained- the leak is from the urethra,as seen in urethrovaginal fistula

The below image shows the 3-swab test.

Option C: MRI is usually not needed for the diagnosis of VVF. They can be used to study vesicouterine fistulas.

Option D: Cystometry is done to measure the capacity of the bladder. It is used to investigate urge incontinence.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following is associated with a Graham-Steel murmur?
questions.explanation: The Graham-Steel murmur is a high-pitched, early diastolic decrescendo murmur caused by pulmonary regurgitation in the setting of severe pulmonary hypertension. It is heard best at the left upper sternal border. Ventricular septal defect (Option A) classically causes a harsh holosystolic murmur. Hypertrophic obstructive cardiomyopathy (Option B) presents with a crescendo-decrescendo systolic murmur that increases with the Valsalva maneuver. Aortic regurgitation (Option D) also causes a diastolic decrescendo murmur, but it is heard at the right upper or left mid-sternal border and may be associated with an "Austin Flint" murmur at the apex. Therefore, the Graham-Steel murmur specifically indicates pulmonary valve incompetence resulting from dilation of the pulmonary artery due to high pressure
questions.learning: The Graham-Steel murmur is a high-pitched, early diastolic decrescendo murmur caused by pulmonary regurgitation in the setting of severe pulmonary hypertension.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: A study was conducted in three states to measure the mean blood pressure in each community. Health workers visited every household in the three communities, and the mean blood pressures were then compared across communities. What type of study design does this represent?
questions.explanation: This study involves health workers visiting households and measuring blood pressure at a single point in time. The data is collected simultaneously from individuals in each community and then summarized (mean BP) for comparison. Since exposure/outcome (here BP levels) are measured at one time without follow-up, it fits the definition of a cross-sectional study. Although results are later compared between communities, the primary data collection is at the individual level, which is key. Therefore, it is not an ecological study, where only group-level data is used. Why other options are incorrect: (A) Case-control: Involves selecting cases and controls and looking back for exposure—not done here. (C) Cohort: Requires follow-up over time to assess outcomes—absent here. (D) Ecological study: Uses only group-level data, but here individual measurements were collected first. Hence, this is a cross-sectional study
questions.learning: This study involves health workers visiting households and measuring blood pressure at a single point in time. The data is collected simultaneously from individuals in each community and then summarized (mean BP) for comparison.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A 45-year-old woman arrives at the emergency department with the following arterial blood gas (ABG) results: pH 7.55, PaCO2 40 mmHg, HCO3- 32 mEq/L What is the most probable cause for these findings?
questions.explanation: The ABG interpretation begins with the pH; a value of 7.55 (normal 7.35–7.45) indicates alkalosis. Next, the is 40 mmHg (normal range), which indicates that the primary problem is not respiratory in nature. The (bicarbonate) is 32 mEq/L (normal 22–26 mEq/L), which is elevated. An elevated bicarbonate level leading to an alkaline pH is the hallmark of metabolic alkalosis. Metabolic acidosis (Option A) would show a low pH and low bicarbonate. Respiratory acidosis (Option C) would show a low pH and high . Respiratory alkalosis (Option D) would show a high pH and low . Common causes of metabolic alkalosis include severe vomiting (loss of acid), diuretic use, or excessive alkali ingestion. In this case, the lack of respiratory compensation (normal ) suggests either an acute presentation or a mixed disorder
questions.learning: The ABG interpretation begins with the pH; a value of 7.55 (normal 7.35–7.45) indicates alkalosis. Next, the is 40 mmHg (normal range), which indicates that the primary problem is not respiratory in nature.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: Which investigation is considered the most appropriate for diagnosing distal bowel tumors?
questions.explanation: Enteroclysis is the most appropriate investigation for diagnosing distal small bowel tumors because it provides excellent distension and detailed visualization of the small intestine mucosa. In this technique, contrast material is directly infused into the small bowel through a nasojejunal tube, allowing precise detection of subtle lesions, strictures, and tumors, especially in distal segments like the ileum. Its high sensitivity makes it superior to routine contrast studies. Other options are less suitable: (B) Barium meal primarily evaluates the esophagus, stomach, and proximal duodenum, so it cannot adequately visualize distal small bowel tumors. (C) Barium meal follow-through does examine the small intestine, but it is less sensitive and less detailed because contrast passes naturally, leading to poor distension and missed lesions. (D) Barium enema is used to study the large intestine (colon and rectum) and has no role in assessing small bowel tumors. Thus, due to its superior imaging quality and diagnostic accuracy for distal small bowel lesions, enteroclysis is the best choice
questions.learning: Enteroclysis is the most appropriate investigation for diagnosing distal small bowel tumors because it provides excellent distension and detailed visualization of the small intestine mucosa.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: A patient working in a factory presented with lung fibrosis and thickening of pleura. Biopsy was done. Diagnosis from the histopathology picture is:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Asbestosis

This clinical scenario and image showing typical asbestos bodies are suggestive of asbestosis.

Asbestosis is a type of pneumoconiosis associated with asbestos exposure. The disease-causing capabilities of the different forms of asbestos depend on concentration, size, shape, and solubility. This condition is marked by diffuse pulmonary interstitial fibrosis.

Asbestos bodies are a typical finding. They are golden brown, fusiform, or beaded rods with a translucent center. They consist of asbestos fibers coated with an iron-containing proteinaceous material and arise when these fibers are phagocytosed by macrophages.

Other inorganic particulates may become coated with similar iron-protein complexes and are called ferruginous bodies.
questions.learning: Asbestosis — This clinical scenario and image showing typical asbestos bodies are suggestive of asbestosis. Asbestosis is a type of pneumoconiosis associated with asbestos exposure.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: Under which category of bioterrorism is Anthrax classified?
questions.explanation: The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) classifies biological agents into three categories based on their potential to pose a threat to public health. Anthrax (Bacillus anthracis) is classified as a Category A (CAT A) agent. This highest-priority category includes organisms that are easily disseminated or transmitted from person to person, cause high mortality rates, and have the potential for major public health impact. Other CAT A agents include Plague, Botulism, and Smallpox. Category B (Option B) agents are moderately easy to disseminate and cause moderate morbidity (e.g., Vibrio cholerae). Category C (Option C) includes emerging pathogens that could be engineered for mass dissemination in the future (e.g., Hantavirus). Category D is not a standard CDC classification for bioterrorism. Anthrax is particularly dangerous because its spores are highly resilient and can be aerosolized. Recognizing these classifications is essential for national security, emergency preparedness, and the rapid deployment of medical countermeasures
questions.learning: The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) classifies biological agents into three categories based on their potential to pose a threat to public health.

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine
questions.text: Acute liver failure is a clinical feature of which of the following?
questions.explanation: Amanita phalloides, commonly known as the "death cap" mushroom, is a highly toxic fungus. Its primary toxins, amatoxins, are potent inhibitors of RNA polymerase II, which stops protein synthesis in cells. This leads to severe, irreversible tissue damage, with the liver being the primary target due to high metabolic activity and first-pass exposure. Acute liver failure (fulminant hepatitis) is the classic and often fatal clinical feature of this poisoning. Organophosphate (OP) poisoning (Option A) causes a cholinergic crisis but not primary liver failure. Belladonna (Option C) leads to an anticholinergic syndrome. Morphine (Option D) causes opioid toxicity (respiratory depression/coma). Mushroom poisoning often starts with a latent period, followed by severe gastrointestinal symptoms, and finally catastrophic hepatic and renal failure. There is no specific antidote for amatoxins, making early recognition and supportive care, including potential liver transplantation, the only management options
questions.learning: Amanita phalloides, commonly known as the "death cap" mushroom, is a highly toxic fungus. Its primary toxins, amatoxins, are potent inhibitors of RNA polymerase II, which stops protein synthesis in cells.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: A 35-year-old carpenter presents with sudden anterior shoulder pain after lifting a heavy object overhead. He reports hearing a “pop” at the time of injury, followed by immediate swelling and bruising. Examination reveals a bulge in the mid–upper arm, and he has marked weakness in elbow flexion and forearm supination. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The clinical presentation described is a classic case of a long head of the biceps tendon rupture. The patient’s sudden "pop" sound during heavy overhead lifting and the subsequent formation of a visible bulge in the mid-upper arm—commonly referred to as the "Popeye deformity"—are pathognomonic. This muscle bulge occurs because the detached muscle belly retracts distally toward the elbow. The long head of the biceps is essential for elbow flexion and forearm supination, which explains the significant weakness the patient experiences. Triceps muscle rupture (Option B) would present with a bulge on the posterior aspect of the arm and weakness in elbow extension. A humerus fracture (Option C) would cause severe localized bone pain, instability, and usually a different radiographic appearance rather than an isolated muscle bulge. Tennis elbow (Option D), or lateral epicondylitis, involves chronic overuse pain at the lateral epicondyle rather than acute muscle deformity or flexion weakness

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A patient presents with obstructed labor, and abdominal examination reveals a palpable groove or band across the uterus. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: A Bandl’s ring is a pathological retraction ring that develops during obstructed labor. It forms at the junction between the upper contractile segment of the uterus and the lower, pathologically thinned and stretched segment. On physical examination, it is felt as a palpable groove or band running transversely across the abdomen, and it is a grave warning sign of impending uterine rupture. Constriction rings (Option A) are localized muscle spasms that occur around the fetus rather than at the segment junction. Schroeder's ring (Option B) is a pathological ring often associated with oxytocin misuse and atony. A contraction ring (Option C) is the normal physiological boundary between segments that is not palpable in a healthy labor. Immediate cesarean section is required when a Bandl's ring is identified to prevent rupture
questions.learning: A Bandl’s ring is a pathological retraction ring that develops during obstructed labor. It forms at the junction between the upper contractile segment of the uterus and the lower, pathologically thinned and stretched segment.

questions.subject: Anaesthesia
questions.text: According to the American Society of Anaesthesiologists (ASA) classification, what grade is given to a normal healthy individual?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. ASA I

A normal healthy individual is given ASA I grade.

Pearl PF1220: American Society of Anesthesiologists’ Physical Status Classification of Patients

American Society of Anesthesiologists’(ASA) classification is used to define relative risk prior to conscious sedation and surgical anesthesia.

It is simple, reproducible and strongly correlates to perioperative risk.

ASA PS Classification & Definition
Examples, including, but not limited to:

ASA I: A normal healthy patient
Healthy, non-smoking, no or minimal alcohol use

ASA II: A patient with mild systemic disease
Without substantive functional limitations. Eg: current smoker, social alcohol drinker, pregnancy, obesity (30 < BMI < 40), well-controlled DM/HTN, mild lung disease

ASA III: A patient with severe systemic disease
Substantive functional limitations; One or more moderate to severe diseases. Eg: poorly controlled DM or HTN, COPD, morbid obesity (BMI ≥40), active hepatitis, alcohol dependence or abuse, implanted pacemaker, moderate reduction of ejection fraction, ESRD undergoing regularly scheduled dialysis, premature infant PCA < 60 weeks, history (>3 months) of MI, CVA, TIA, or CAD/stents.

ASA IV: A patient with severe systemic disease that is a constant threat to life
Eg: recent ( < 3 months) MI, CVA, TIA, or CAD/stents, ongoing cardiac ischemia or severe valve dysfunction, severe reduction of ejection fraction, sepsis, DIC, ARD or ESRD not undergoing regularly scheduled dialysis

ASA V: A moribund patient who is not expected to survive without the operation
Eg: ruptured abdominal/thoracic aneurysm, massive trauma, intracranial bleed with mass effect, ischemic bowel in the face of significant cardiac pathology or multiple organ/system dysfunction

ASA VI: A declared brain-dead patient whose organs are being removed for donor purposes

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: Most common site of ossifying fibroma is?
questions.explanation: An ossifying fibroma is a benign but locally aggressive fibro-osseous lesion. It is characterized by the replacement of normal bone with a combination of fibrous tissue and mineralized material. Statistically, the mandible is the most common site of occurrence, specifically in the premolar and molar regions. While it can occur in the maxilla (Option B) or paranasal sinuses like the frontal (Option A) or maxillary sinus (Option D), these locations are less frequent than the lower jaw. Ossifying fibromas typically present as a painless, slowly enlarging hard swelling that can cause facial asymmetry or tooth displacement. On imaging, they appear as a well-demarcated lesion with varying degrees of radiopacity depending on the amount of calcified tissue present. Therefore, Mandible is the correct anatomical site recognized as the most frequent location for this tumor
questions.learning: An ossifying fibroma is a benign but locally aggressive fibro-osseous lesion. It is characterized by the replacement of normal bone with a combination of fibrous tissue and mineralized material.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following conditions is cannabinoid oil not indicated in?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Rett syndrome

Cannabinoid oil is not indicated in Rett syndrome.

The FDA recently approved cannabidiol oral solution for the treatment of seizures associated with tuberous sclerosis complex in patients one year of age and older. It was previously approved for the treatment of seizures associated with Lennox-Gastaut syndrome and Dravet syndrome.

Cannabinoid oil is an oral derivative of the cannabis plant. The mechanism by which it improves seizure threshold is not understood yet and there are various studies ongoing to survey its use. The cannabinoid receptors are G protein-coupled receptors located predominantly in the presynaptic nerve terminals.

The CB1 receptor is located in the central nervous system. Activation of CB1 receptor results in euphoria and alleviation of pain (anti-nociceptive effect). The CB2 receptor is located mainly in the periphery and their activation does not have a euphoric effect.

The endogenous cannabinoid system is a potential target for use in the treatment of chronic pain. The most common adverse effects of CBD at doses used for treating epilepsy include somnolence, fatigue, decreased appetite, diarrhea, and elevated hepatic transaminases. The elevations in liver transaminases are dose-related.
questions.learning: Rett syndrome Cannabinoid oil is not indicated in Rett syndrome. The FDA recently approved cannabidiol oral solution for the treatment of seizures associated with tuberous sclerosis complex in patients one year of age and older.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 33-year-old man was referred to the surgery OPD from the infertility clinic. On inspection, the scrotum appeared as in the image. On palpation, a bag of worms sensation was felt. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Varicocele

The clinical scenario is suggestive of a varicocele.

Varicocele may present with a dull aching scrotal pain and enlargement. Additionally, patients may have infertility. A bag of worms, which gets prominent on Valsalva’s maneuver is palpated due to the engorged pampiniform plexus.

Often, patients may be asymptomatic and do not require treatment.

Grades of varicocele

Grade 1
Varicocele only palpable on Valsalva’s maneuver

Grade 2
Varicocele palpable without Valsalva’s maneuver

Grade 3
Varicocele is seen on inspection of the testis

Left-sided varicocele is more common. Isolated right-sided varicocele should always raise suspicion of renal cell carcinoma.

Treatment of young patients includes surgical ligation of the gonadal vein. It may be achieved through embolectomy or varicocelectomy. Approaches to varicocelectomy are:

* Inguinal ( Ivanisevic method )

* Retroperitoneal (Palomo procedure)

* Natural orifice transluminal endoscopic surgery through the transvesical route

In older patients, NSAIDs and scrotal support are adequate.
questions.learning: Varicocele — The clinical scenario is suggestive of a varicocele. Varicocele may present with a dull aching scrotal pain and enlargement.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: The histological section of a skin lesion is given below. What is the probable diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Squamous cell carcinoma

The image shows keratin pearls which are characteristic of Squamous cell carcinoma.

* Squamous cell carcinoma is characterized by the proliferation of atypical squamous cells with 'horn pearls', also called as keratin pearls.

* Macroscopic appearance of SCC may vary from smooth nodular, verrucous, papillomatous to ulcerating lesions.

* SCC stains positive for cytokeratins 1 and 10.

* SCC can be histologically graded according to Broders' histological grading.

Option A : Basal cell carcinoma histopathology shows basal cells arranged in a palisading pattern.

Option C : Adenocarcinoma shows a lepidic pattern of growth at the periphery of the tumor. The tumor cells appear to crawl along the normal-appearing alveolar septa, as shown in the image below.

Option D: Malignant melanoma histopathology shows dense intracytoplasmic brownish-black melanin pigment. Malignant melanoma primarily arises from melanocytes at the epidermal-dermal junction.
questions.learning: Squamous cell carcinoma — The image shows keratin pearls which are characteristic of Squamous cell carcinoma. * Squamous cell carcinoma is characterized by the proliferation of atypical squamous cells with 'horn pearls', also called as keratin pearls. *…

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: All of the following supply the marked structure except :
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Diagonal artery

The structure marked is the right ventricle. It is not supplied by the diagonal artery.

The diagonal artery is a branch of the anterior interventricular artery supplying the left ventricle. This is present in about 30-50% of the population.

The right ventricle is mostly supplied by the right coronary artery and its branches such as the marginal artery.

The anterior interventricular artery gives off 1-2 anterior right ventricular branches.
questions.learning: Diagonal artery — The structure marked is the right ventricle. It is not supplied by the diagonal artery.

questions.subject: Ophthalmology
questions.text: In the image provided, which refractive error is observed in the depicted condition?
questions.explanation: The image depicts "Keratoconus," characterized by progressive thinning and cone-shaped protrusion of the cornea. Because the cornea becomes both steeper (more powerful) and irregular in shape, it induces two specific refractive errors: Myopia and Astigmatism. The steepening causes light to focus in front of the retina (high axial myopia), while the irregular cone shape causes light to focus at multiple different points (irregular astigmatism). Option B, C, and D are incorrect because hypermetropia is caused by a flat cornea or short eyeball, which is the opposite of this pathology. Patients with keratoconus often present with a history of frequent prescription changes and "ghosting" of images. Advanced signs include Munson’s sign (V-shape of the lower lid on downgaze) and Vogt’s striae. Treatment ranges from rigid gas permeable (RGP) contact lenses to corneal cross-linking (CXL) or penetrating keratoplasty in severe cases
questions.learning: The image depicts "Keratoconus," characterized by progressive thinning and cone-shaped protrusion of the cornea. Because the cornea becomes both steeper (more powerful) and irregular in shape, it induces two specific refractive errors: Myopia and Astigmatism.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 39-year-old nulliparous female has presented to Gynaecology OPD with complaint of post coital bleeding for past six months. The first investigation to be offered to this female will be:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Pap smear

A woman with postcoital bleeding should first undergo cervical evaluation, and the initial screening investigation is a Pap smear (cervical cytology) to detect premalignant or malignant cervical lesions.

Why not the other options?

• A. Colposcopy: Performed after an abnormal Pap smear or when the cervix appears suspicious on examination.
• B. Dilatation and Curettage (D&C): Used for evaluation of endometrial pathology, not as the first test for postcoital bleeding.
• D. Cone biopsy of cervix: Reserved for confirmed high-grade CIN or suspected microinvasive carcinoma, not as the initial investigation.
questions.learning: Pap smear — A woman with postcoital bleeding should first undergo cervical evaluation, and the initial screening investigation is a Pap smear (cervical cytology) to detect premalignant or malignant cervical lesions.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: What is the most common site of gastrinoma in MEN 1 syndrome?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Duodenum

The most common site of gastrinoma in MEN 1 syndrome is the duodenum.

Gastrinoma is the most common pancreatic islet tumor in MEN 1 syndrome, arising from the G cells of the pancreas. Gastrinoma, associated with marked gastric acid production and recurrent peptic ulcers, is called Zollinger-Ellison syndrome. The majority of gastrinomas occur in the gastrinoma (Passaro's) triangle.

In MEN 1, they often occur in patients <30 years. Patients present with abdominal pain (the most common symptom), diarrhea and steatorrhea.

Management:

• Medical management for tumors <2 cm with proton-pump inhibitors.
• Surgery for tumors >2 cm.
• Proton-pump inhibitors with somatostatin analogues for advanced locoregional disease or metastasis.
questions.learning: Duodenum — The most common site of gastrinoma in MEN 1 syndrome is the duodenum. Gastrinoma is the most common pancreatic islet tumor in MEN 1 syndrome, arising from the G cells of the pancreas.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: According to the Medical Termination of Pregnancy (Amendment) Act, 2021, MTP for pregnancy between 20 to 24 weeks needs opinion of:
options: One registered medical practitioner and court order
Two registered medical practitioners and court order
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Two registered medical practitioners

Under the Medical Termination of Pregnancy (Amendment) Act, 2021, for pregnancies >20 weeks but ≤24 weeks in the specified categories of women, termination requires the opinion of not less than two registered medical practitioners, formed in good faith. A court order is not required.

Therefore, B. is correct.

To understand the MTP Act 2021 gestational-age-based requirements for termination of pregnancy and the number of registered medical practitioners required at different gestational ages.

≤20 weeks → 1 RMP

>20 to ≤24 weeks → 2 RMPs

Court order → Not routinely required
