questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: All of the following are major diagnostic criteria for allergic fungal sinusitis except?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Positive fungal culture

A positive fungal culture is a minor and not a major diagnostic criterion for allergic fungal rhinosinusitis (AFRS).

The Bent and Kuhn diagnostic criteria for allergic fungal rhinosinusitis include:

Major criteria:

1. Type I hypersensitivity
2. Nasal polyposis
3. Characteristic CT findings
4. Eosinophilic mucin without invasion
5. Positive fungal stain

Minor criteria:

1. Asthma
2. Unilateral disease
3. Bone erosion
4. Fungal cultures
5. Charcot-Leyden crystals
6. Serum eosinophilia

All the major criteria must be met by the patient while the minor criteria serve to support the diagnosis and describe individual patients.

Characteristic CT findings in AFRS include heterogeneous signal intensities within the paranasal sinuses filled with allergic mucin (double density sign), expansion of the paranasal sinuses/nasal cavity, unilateral or asymmetric disease load, and bony erosion.

The treatment of allergic fungal sinusitis includes avoidance of allergen exposure, antihistamines, corticosteroid nasal sprays, aggressive surgical intervention for mucin removal which improves sinus drainage, post-surgery oral corticosteroids, and immunotherapy against fungal and non-fungal allergens.
questions.learning: Positive fungal culture — A positive fungal culture is a minor and not a major diagnostic criterion for allergic fungal rhinosinusitis (AFRS). The Bent and Kuhn diagnostic criteria for allergic fungal rhinosinusitis include: Major criteria: 1.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: A 65-year-old patient with uncontrolled diabetes developed severe rhino-orbito-cerebral mucormycosis following a severe COVID-19 infection. Surgical debridement of the affected area has been done. Which of the following drugs is not used in this condition?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Voriconazole

Mucormycosis is a life-threatening opportunistic fungal infection caused by fungi of the order Mucorales (e.g., Rhizopus). Management requires urgent surgical debridement, correction of underlying risk factors (e.g., diabetes, ketoacidosis), and prompt initiation of active antifungal therapy.

• Voriconazole has no reliable activity against Mucorales and should not be used for the treatment of mucormycosis. It is active against Aspergillus, but not Rhizopus or other Mucor species.

Why not the other options?

• A. Liposomal Amphotericin B ✓: Drug of choice (first-line therapy) for mucormycosis.
• B. Posaconazole ✓: Used as step-down (oral) therapy or salvage therapy after initial control.
• D. Isavuconazole ✓: Effective against Mucorales; an alternative first-line agent or step-down therapy.
questions.learning: Voriconazole Mucormycosis is a life-threatening opportunistic fungal infection caused by fungi of the order Mucorales (e.g., Rhizopus). Management requires urgent surgical debridement, correction of underlying risk factors (e.g., diabetes, ketoacidosis),…

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: A child is presenting with palpable blanching purpura, abdominal pain, and pain in the knee joint resulting from arthritis. Urine examination showed hematuria and proteinuria. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Henoch-Schonlein purpura

The clinical presentation and the investigations are suggestive of Henoch-Schonlein purpura.

Henoch-Schönlein purpura is a systemic immune disorder characterized by a purpuric rash, abdominal pain, polyarthralgia, and renal abnormalities. It is most commonly seen in the age group of 3-8 years. The patient may present with the following clinical features:

• Skin lesions- characteristically involve the extensor surfaces of arms and legs, and also the buttocks
• Abdominal manifestations- include pain, vomiting, and intestinal bleeding.
• Renal manifestations- include gross or microscopic hematuria, nephritic syndrome, or nephrotic syndrome. Renal manifestations are more severe in adults. A rapidly progressive form of glomerulonephritis is seen in some cases.

This condition usually occurs following an upper respiratory tract infection and there is a history of atopy in one-third of the cases. IgA is deposited in the glomerular mesangium in a distribution similar to that of IgA nephropathy.

Microscopic findings:

• IgA deposition in the mesangial region. Sometimes there is the deposition of IgG and C3 along with IgA.
• Renal lesions show focal or diffuse mesangial proliferation, and/or endocapillary proliferation to crescentic glomerulonephritis.
• Skin lesions show subepidermal hemorrhages and necrotizing vasculitis of small vessels.

Other options:

Option A: Immune thrombocytopenic purpura(ITP): It occurs due to antibody-mediated destruction of platelets. It can be acute or chronic. Acute ITP is usually self-limiting in nature. Cutaneous bleeding can be in the form of petechiae and ecchymoses. The patient can also have hematuria, melena, or excessive menstrual flow.

Option B: Dengue: It is a viral illness caused by the dengue virus. The clinical manifestations include fever, headache, musculoskeletal pain, and rash. The rash which is maculopapular in nature begins on the trunk and then spreads centrifugally to the face and extremities.

Option C: Churg- Strauss syndrome (Eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis): It is characterized by eosinophilic vasculitis of multiple organs. The features of this condition include asthma, peripheral eosinophilia, pulmonary infiltrates, neuropathy, paranasal sinus abnormality, and the presence of eosinophilic vasculitis.
questions.learning: Henoch-Schonlein purpura — The clinical presentation and the investigations are suggestive of Henoch-Schonlein purpura. Henoch-Schönlein purpura is a systemic immune disorder characterized by a purpuric rash, abdominal pain, polyarthralgia, and renal…

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: A patient with a history of bronchospasm is found to have a tumor in the ileum along with elevated urinary 5-hydroxyindoleacetic acid (5- HIAA) levels. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Carcinoid syndrome is a paraneoplastic condition caused by neuroendocrine tumors (carcinoid tumors), most commonly found in the ileum. These tumors secrete excessive serotonin into the systemic circulation, bypassing liver metabolism when they metastasize. The elevated serotonin levels lead to clinical manifestations such as bronchospasms (wheezing), diarrhea, and cutaneous flushing. Serotonin is subsequently metabolized and excreted in the urine as 5-hydroxyindoleacetic acid (5-HIAA), making elevated 5-HIAA the hallmark diagnostic marker for this syndrome. Neuroblastoma (Option B) is a pediatric tumor that secretes catecholamines. Chromaffinoma (Option C), or pheochromocytoma, also secretes catecholamines and presents with hypertension. Leiomyoma (Option D) is a benign smooth muscle tumor that does not have neuroendocrine activity. Therefore, the combination of an ileal tumor, respiratory symptoms, and excessive urinary 5-HIAA confirms the diagnosis of carcinoid syndrome
questions.learning: Carcinoid syndrome is a paraneoplastic condition caused by neuroendocrine tumors (carcinoid tumors), most commonly found in the ileum. These tumors secrete excessive serotonin into the systemic circulation, bypassing liver metabolism when they metastasize.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: The factors that can cause a person to drink water due to stimulation of thirst mechanism is/are ___________.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. All of the above

Dehydration, hemorrhage, and prandial drinking: All three can cause increased thirst resulting in water drinking.
Increased osmolality acts via osmoreceptors in the anterior hypothalamus.

The decreased plasma volume, as in hemorrhage, acts via
1. Renin-angiotensin system
2. Baroreceptors in heart and blood vessels.
The intake of liquids during a meal is known as prandial drinking. The increase is known as learned or habit response but is not understood completely.

The following factors are thought to play a role
1. Increase in plasma osmolality due to food absorption
2. Action on hypothalamus by one or more gastrointestinal hormones
questions.learning: All of the above Dehydration, hemorrhage, and prandial drinking: All three can cause increased thirst resulting in water drinking. Increased osmolality acts via osmoreceptors in the anterior hypothalamus.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: The elimination rate constant of a drug is 0.05/hr. What is its half-life?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. 13.8 hours

The half-life of the given drug is 13.8 hours.

The half-life of a drug or t1/2 is the time taken for the plasma concentration to be reduced by 50%. The elimination rate constant or k value of a drug reflects the fraction of drug removed from the body compartment per unit of time.

The half-life of a drug and its elimination rate constant are inversely proportional to each other. They are represented by the equation:

k t1/2 =  0.693

Therefore, t1/2 = 0.693/ k

The given value for elimination rate constant 𝑘 is 0.05, therefore the half-life of the given drug would be:

0.693/ 0.05 = 13.8

Therefore, the half-life of the drug would be 13.8 hours.
questions.learning: 13.8 hours The half-life of the given drug is 13.8 hours. The half-life of a drug or t1/2 is the time taken for the plasma concentration to be reduced by 50%.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: For a population of 10,000, what is the minimum land area needed to implement the trench method of controlled waste tipping effectively?
questions.explanation: The trench method of controlled tipping (a type of sanitary landfill) is commonly used for solid waste disposal in small towns or rural areas. In this method, trenches are dug, waste is deposited, compacted, and then covered with soil daily. For planning purposes in community medicine/public health, standard guidelines suggest that for a population of 10,000, a minimum of about 5 acres of land is required to ensure proper functioning of the trench method over a reasonable period. This land requirement considers: 1. 1. Daily waste generation 2. 2. Space for trench digging and covering 3. 3. Future expansion and rotation of trenches 4. 4. Safe distance from habitation and water sources Why other options are incorrect: (A) 4 acres: Slightly inadequate for long-term use (C) 2 acres: Too small → leads to overcrowding and improper disposal (D) 1 acre: Grossly insufficient
questions.learning: The trench method of controlled tipping (a type of sanitary landfill) is commonly used for solid waste disposal in small towns or rural areas. In this method, trenches are dug, waste is deposited, compacted, and then covered with soil daily.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Which of the following is not a function of glucagon?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Glycolysis

Glycolysis is not a function of glucagon but is a function of insulin.

Role of insulin and glucagon:

When blood glucose falls during fasting, there is increased secretion of glucagon and decreased release of insulin.

Effects of increased glucagon: insulin ratio on enzymes of glycogenolysis and gluconeogenesis:

* It activates glycogen phosphorylase, the key enzyme of glycogenolysis, and deactivates glycogen synthase. This causes a rapid mobilization of liver glycogen stores to be utilized as fuel.

* It favors the synthesis of glucose-6-phosphatase which converts glucose-6-phosphate to glucose. The resulting glucose is used by red blood cells (lack mitochondria) and the brain as they are largely dependent on glucose in the fasting state.

* Phosphoenol pyruvate carboxykinase and fructose-1, 6-bisphosphatase are induced, leading to increased gluconeogenesis.

Metabolic process
Fasting state
Fed state

Glucagon: insulin
Increased
Decreased

Gluconeogenesis
Increased
Decreased

Glycogenolysis
Increased
Decreased

Ketogenesis
Increased
Decreased

Glycogen storage
Decreased
Increased
questions.learning: Glycolysis Glycolysis is not a function of glucagon but is a function of insulin. Role of insulin and glucagon: When blood glucose falls during fasting, there is increased secretion of glucagon and decreased release of insulin.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: A tall, obese patient with a known history of hypertension is newly diagnosed with metabolic syndrome during a routine health check-up. Which of the following clinical or biochemical findings is most likely to be present in this patient?
options: Increase in uric acid and insulin
Increase in triglycerides and total cholesterol
questions.explanation: Metabolic syndrome is defined by a cluster of abnormalities, but dyslipidemia is a core diagnostic component. The most characteristic lipid changes are elevated triglycerides and reduced HDL cholesterol, reflecting altered lipid metabolism due to insulin resistance. Among the given options, increase in triglycerides (and often total cholesterol) best represents this defining biochemical disturbance. In fact, raised triglycerides are one of the standard diagnostic criteria for metabolic syndrome (along with waist circumference, BP, glucose, HDL). Although insulin resistance with hyperinsulinemia and raised blood glucose is the underlying mechanism, these are pathophysiological features, not always the most specific “finding” highlighted in exam questions. Why other options are less appropriate: (A) Uric acid → not a diagnostic criterion (B) BP + insulin → incomplete picture (D) Glucose + insulin → mechanism, not defining profile
questions.learning: Metabolic syndrome is defined by a cluster of abnormalities, but dyslipidemia is a core diagnostic component. The most characteristic lipid changes are elevated triglycerides and reduced HDL cholesterol, reflecting altered lipid metabolism due to insulin…

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: A 30-year-old male presents with a history of fatigue over the past year. Upon examination, a significantly enlarged spleen is noted. The following blood test results are obtained: TLC count: 1,50,000/microL. Peripheral blood smear: Myeloblasts, myelocytes, and metamyelocytes. Myeloid to erythroid ratio: 18:1. What is the most likely diagnosis for this patient?
questions.explanation: The patient’s presentation of chronic fatigue and massive splenomegaly, combined with an extreme leukocytosis (TLC 150,000), is highly characteristic of Chronic Myeloid Leukemia (CML). The diagnostic hallmark on the peripheral smear is the presence of the full spectrum of myeloid cells in various stages of maturation, including myeloblasts, myelocytes, and metamyelocytes, alongside a markedly increased myeloid to erythroid (M:E) ratio (18:1, normal is ~3:1). ALL (Option A) and AML (Option B) are acute leukemias that would typically present with a high percentage of blasts (>20%) and a more rapid, severe clinical course. CLL (Option D) would show a predominance of mature lymphocytes rather than myeloid precursors. CML is classically associated with the Philadelphia chromosome (t(9;22)). Given the maturity spectrum of the cells and the massive splenic enlargement, CML is the definitive diagnosis
questions.learning: The patient’s presentation of chronic fatigue and massive splenomegaly, combined with an extreme leukocytosis (TLC 150,000), is highly characteristic of Chronic Myeloid Leukemia (CML).

questions.subject: Orthopaedics
questions.text: A 45-year-old man presents with progressively worsening pain and a palpable lump in the left foot. Histopathological examination reveals an aggressive tumor that produces bone. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The key deciding factor in this question is "aggressive tumor that PRODUCES BONE" on histopathology — this is the definitive hallmark of osteosarcoma. Osteosarcoma is derived from primitive osteoid-producing mesenchymal cells, commonly involving the proximal humerus metaphysis. Chondrosarcomas are typically found in older patients (40–75 years) — however they produce cartilaginous matrix, NOT bone. The question specifically states histopathology reveals bone production — this definitively points to Osteosarcoma, not Chondrosarcoma. Why other options are wrong: (B) Ewing's sarcoma is incorrect because it shows small round blue cells on histopathology — no bone or matrix production occurs. (C) Osteoclastoma is incorrect because it is a purely lytic, soap-bubble lesion with giant cells — no bone production. (D) Chondrosarcoma is incorrect because it produces cartilaginous/chondroid matrix — NOT bone as specifically stated in the question
questions.learning: The key deciding factor in this question is "aggressive tumor that PRODUCES BONE" on histopathology — this is the definitive hallmark of osteosarcoma.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: Vitamin K in its coenzyme form is regenerated by the enzyme ____
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. Epoxide reductase

The coenzyme form of Vitamin K is regenerated by the enzyme epoxide reductase.

Epoxide reductase reduces Vitamin K epoxide to its coenzyme form hydroquinone.

Note: In addition to vitamin K reductase, epoxide reductase can also catalyse the reduction of quinone to hydroquinone. Thus, it can regenerate hydroquinone by itself.
questions.learning: Epoxide reductase — The coenzyme form of Vitamin K is regenerated by the enzyme epoxide reductase. Epoxide reductase reduces Vitamin K epoxide to its coenzyme form hydroquinone.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: Which one of the following statements regarding Cantlie’s line is correct?
options: Runs between gall bladder fossa and right hepatic vein
Runs between gall bladder fossa and right branch of portal vein
Runs between gall bladder fossa and middle hepatic vein
Runs between gall bladder fossa and left branch of portal vein
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Runs between gall bladder fossa and middle hepatic vein

Cantlie’s line is an imaginary line extending from the gallbladder fossa anteriorly to the inferior vena cava posteriorly, following the course of the middle hepatic vein. It divides the liver into the functional right and left hemilivers based on vascular inflow and biliary drainage.

Why not the other options?

• A. Right hepatic vein: Right hepatic vein divides the right lobe into anterior and posterior sectors.
• B. Right branch of portal vein: Not the landmark for Cantlie’s line.
• D. Left branch of portal vein: Not the landmark for Cantlie’s line.
questions.learning: Runs between gall bladder fossa and middle hepatic vein Cantlie’s line is an imaginary line extending from the gallbladder fossa anteriorly to the inferior vena cava posteriorly, following the course of the middle hepatic vein.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: What is the correct order of the normal phases of wound healing?
options: Proliferative phase > Hemostatic phase > Inflammatory phase > Remodeling phase
Hemostatic phase > Inflammatory phase > Proliferative phase > Remodeling phase
Inflammatory phase > Hemostatic phase > Proliferative phase > Remodeling phase
Remodeling phase > Proliferative phase > Destructive phase > Inflammatory phase
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Hemostatic phase > Inflammatory phase > Proliferative phase > Remodeling phase

The correct order of the normal phases of wound healing is as follows: Hemostatic phase > Inflammatory phase > Proliferative phase > Remodeling phase.

Inflammatory phase: begins immediately after wounding and lasts 2-3 days. Bleeding is followed by vasoconstriction and thrombus formation to limit blood loss. Occasionally, the early part of inflammatory phase is called hemostatic phase.

Proliferative phase lasts from 3rd day to 3rd week consisting mainly of fibroblast activity with production of collagen and ground substance, growth of new blood vessels and re-epithelialization of the wound surface.

Remodeling phase is characterized by maturation of collagen- type 1 replacing type 3 until a ratio of 4:1 is achieved. The mature collagen leads to increased tensile strength and represents approximately 80% of the uninjured skin strength.
questions.learning: Hemostatic phase > Inflammatory phase > Proliferative phase > Remodeling phase The correct order of the normal phases of wound healing is as follows: Hemostatic phase > Inflammatory phase > Proliferative phase > Remodeling phase.

questions.subject: Dermatology
questions.text: A 23-year-old male came with complaints of orange hue over the body with hyperkeratotic perifollicular erythematous papules associated with scaling, which started near the face and slowly progressed to involve the entire body. Islands of sparing noted over the body. Palmoplantar keratoderma noted. Histology shows alternating orthokeratosis and parakeratosis. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. Pityriasis Rubra Pilaris

Pityriasis rubra pilaris (PRP) is characterized by orange-red scaling plaques with follicular hyperkeratosis and distinctive clinical-histological features.

• Key clinical features:

o    Orange/salmon-colored plaques

o    Follicular hyperkeratotic papules

o    “Islands of sparing” (normal skin within lesions)

o    Palmoplantar keratoderma
• Histopathology (hallmark):

o    Alternating orthokeratosis and parakeratosis (checkerboard pattern)

Differentiation:

• Psoriasis → silvery scales, Auspitz sign, uniform parakeratosis
• Mycosis fungoides → atypical lymphocytes, epidermotropism
• Keratosis follicularis (Darier disease) → greasy papules, acantholysis
questions.learning: Pityriasis Rubra Pilaris Pityriasis rubra pilaris (PRP) is characterized by orange-red scaling plaques with follicular hyperkeratosis and distinctive clinical-histological features. • Key clinical features: o Orange/salmon-colored plaques o Follicular…

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.text: True statements about the HMP shunt: 1. Non-oxidative phase is reversible 2. End products are ribose-5-P, O₂ and NADH 3. No ATP produced in oxidative phase 4. Transketolase requires thiamine
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. 1, 3 and 4

The HMP shunt (Pentose Phosphate Pathway) is an alternative pathway of glucose metabolism that occurs in the cytosol and primarily functions to produce NADPH and ribose-5-phosphate.

1. Non-oxidative phase is reversible – TRUE

The non-oxidative phase interconverts pentose phosphates with glycolytic intermediates (fructose-6-phosphate and glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate), allowing flexibility depending on cellular needs.

3. No ATP is produced in the oxidative phase – TRUE

The oxidative phase generates NADPH, not ATP. NADPH is used for:

• Fatty acid synthesis
• Cholesterol synthesis
• Maintenance of reduced glutathione in RBCs

4. Transketolase requires thiamine – TRUE

The enzyme transketolase in the non-oxidative phase requires thiamine pyrophosphate (TPP) as a cofactor. Reduced transketolase activity is seen in thiamine deficiency.

Why statement 2 is incorrect: The end products of the oxidative phase are ribulose-5-phosphate, CO₂, and NADPH, not O₂ or NADH.
questions.learning: 1, 3 and 4 The HMP shunt (Pentose Phosphate Pathway) is an alternative pathway of glucose metabolism that occurs in the cytosol and primarily functions to produce NADPH and ribose-5-phosphate.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: In a patient, the hypothalamic thermostat was reset from point A to point C as shown below. Which of the following happens in stage A compared to stage B?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Shivering

In the above scenario, the patient's hypothalamic thermostat has been reset from point A to a higher temperature (point C). The body responds to this change by using certain measures in stage A such as shivering.

In stage A the body activates various heat gain mechanisms to match the hypothalamic temperature setpoint. These include:

• Shivering- the shivering center is located in the posterior hypothalamus. It is normally inhibited by signals from the heat center in the anterior hypothalamic-preoptic area but is excited by cold signals from the skin and spinal cord. A sudden increase in heat setpoint results in the activation of this center. It then transmits non-rhythmic signals through bilateral tracts through the lateral columns of the spinal cord, and finally to the anterior motor neurons. They increase the tone of the skeletal muscles throughout the body. As the tone rises above a certain critical level, shivering begins. During maximum shivering, body heat production can rise to four to five times normal.
• Vasoconstriction (decreased blood flow to skin) is mediated by increased sympathetic drive by the activation of the posterior hypothalamic sympathetic center.
• An increase in chemical thermogenesis in which heat production takes place in the brown fat by the mechanism of uncoupling of oxidative phosphorylation. This is the predominant mechanism seen in neonates.

In stage B, the hypothalamic temperature setpoint is lower than the normal body temperature. Hence body activates various heat loss mechanisms to match the hypothalamic temperature setpoint. It includes vasodilatation of the skin blood vessel, sweating, and decreased thermogenesis.

The temperature of the body is regulated majorly by a nervous feedback mechanism that operates through temperature-regulating centers located in the hypothalamus. Minor regulation is done by the thermal receptors in the skin and the deep thermal receptors present in the spinal cord and abdominal viscera.
questions.learning: Shivering — In the above scenario, the patient's hypothalamic thermostat has been reset from point A to a higher temperature (point C). The body responds to this change by using certain measures in stage A such as shivering.

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: A total of 60 patients were diagnosed with COVID-19, out of which 12 cases of deaths were reported. Calculate the case fatality rate.
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. 20%

In this scenario, among 60 diagnosed COVID-19 patients, 12 deaths were recorded, resulting in a case fatality rate of 20%.

The case fatality rate is determined using the formula: (Number of deaths from a specific disease / Total number of cases of the same disease) × 100. Applying this formula: (12 deaths / 60 cases) × 100 = 20%.

Case Fatality Rate (CFR) is a key epidemiological measure used to assess the severity of a disease by indicating the proportion of deaths among diagnosed cases. It is calculated using the formula: (Number of deaths due to a specific disease / Total number of confirmed cases) × 100.

CFR helps in understanding the lethality of an infection and is crucial in public health planning and response strategies. A higher CFR suggests a more severe disease or inadequate healthcare interventions, while a lower CFR indicates better treatment outcomes and disease management. However, CFR may vary based on factors such as healthcare access, population demographics, and disease reporting accuracy.

Pearl PF0955: Case Fatality Rate

* Case fatality rate =  (Total number of deaths due to a particular disease)/(Total number of cases due to the same disease)x 100

* It is a good indicator of severity or killing power of a disease.

* It is used mostly in acute and infectious diseases.

* No time interval is used.

* Case fatality rate is closely related to virulence.

* Limitation of CFR is that its usefulness for chronic diseases is limited because the period from onset to death is variable.

* It is expressed in percentage.

* CFR is an incidence proportion and not a true rate.

* CFR may vary for the same disease in different epidemics.

*

Case fatality of a few diseases:

* Rabies - 100% especially after symptoms manifest

* Ebola - 25 to 90%, average - 50%

* Yellow fever - 15 to 50%

* Chicken pox - 0.001%

* Diseases with a high case fatality rate: Tetanus, Rabies, Botulism, Ebola.

* Diseases with a low case fatality rate: Leprosy, Trachoma, Lymphatic filariasis.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.text: Match the following cytokines with their function: 1. IL-5 2. IL-6 3. IL-7 4. IL-8
questions.explanation: 1-D, 2-A, 3-B, 4-C. Interleukins (IL) are essential signaling molecules in the immune system. 1. IL-5 (1-D) is the primary cytokine responsible for the growth, differentiation, and activation of eosinophils, playing a key role in allergic diseases and helminth infections. 2. IL-6 (2-A) is a major pro-inflammatory cytokine that stimulates the liver to produce acute phase reactants like CRP and fibrinogen. 3. IL-7 (3-B) is critical for lymphopoiesis, specifically the survival and maturation of B and T cell precursors. 4. IL-8 (4-C) is a potent chemokine specifically responsible for neutrophil recruitment and chemotaxis to sites of infection. Options A, C, and D are incorrect mathematical pairings. Knowledge of these specific cytokine functions is fundamental to understanding the pathophysiology of inflammation and the targets of modern biologic therapies.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A 40-year-old patient presents with mucus and blood in the stool. Sigmoidoscopy shows inflammation mainly in the rectum, and biopsy reveals crypt abscesses. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The clinical presentation of blood and mucus in the stool combined with rectal inflammation (proctitis) and the pathognomonic histological finding of crypt abscesses is highly diagnostic of Ulcerative Colitis (UC) . UC is an inflammatory bowel disease that uniquely begins in the rectum and spreads proximally in a continuous fashion. Crohn’s disease (Option C) typically involves "skip lesions" anywhere in the GI tract (most often the terminal ileum) and is characterized by transmural inflammation and non-caseating granulomas rather than primary rectal crypt abscesses. Irritable bowel syndrome (Option B) is a functional disorder and would show a normal sigmoidoscopy and biopsy. Pseudomembranous colitis (Option D) is caused by C. difficile and shows characteristic yellowish plaques on endoscopy. Therefore, the specific combination of localized rectal disease and microscopic crypt abscesses confirms Ulcerative Colitis as the definitive diagnosis. Treatment involves aminosalicylates, corticosteroids, or immunosuppressants
questions.learning: The clinical presentation of blood and mucus in the stool combined with rectal inflammation (proctitis) and the pathognomonic histological finding of crypt abscesses is highly diagnostic of Ulcerative Colitis (UC) .

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A 50-year-old woman presents with recurrent episodes of sudden heat sensation associated with profuse sweating and flushing over the past several months. She has irregular menstrual cycles suggestive of the menopausal transition. Which of the following is the most appropriate confirmatory investigation?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Serum FSH level

In women with vasomotor symptoms (hot flashes, flushing, night sweats) and irregular menstrual cycles suggestive of the menopausal transition, the most useful laboratory test—if confirmation is required—is serum FSH. Ovarian follicular depletion leads to reduced estrogen production, causing loss of negative feedback and a rise in FSH (typically >25–30 IU/L, though levels fluctuate during perimenopause).

High-Yield Points

• Most menopausal women do not require laboratory confirmation if they are >45 years with typical symptoms.
• If testing is indicated (e.g., younger women or uncertain diagnosis), FSH is the preferred investigation.
• FSH ↑, LH ↑ (less marked than FSH), Estradiol ↓.
• Progesterone is not useful for diagnosing menopause.
questions.learning: Serum FSH level — In women with vasomotor symptoms (hot flashes, flushing, night sweats) and irregular menstrual cycles suggestive of the menopausal transition, the most useful laboratory test—if confirmation is required—is serum FSH.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Identify the clinical sign seen around the 8th week of pregnancy that results in the characteristic appearance of the vagina as shown in the image.
questions.explanation: The clinical finding of a bluish or purplish discoloration of the vaginal mucosa and cervix during the 8th week of pregnancy is known as Chadwick's sign (Option B). This discoloration is caused by the increased vascularity and venous congestion within the pelvic organs that occurs shortly after conception. Palmer's sign (Option A) refers to regular, rhythmic uterine contractions felt during a bimanual examination in early pregnancy. Hegar's sign (Option C) is the softening of the uterine isthmus, typically assessed between 6 and 10 weeks of gestation. Osiander's sign (Option D) refers to an increased pulsation felt in the lateral vaginal fornices due to the hyperdynamic pelvic circulation. While all these signs are "presumptive" indicators of pregnancy, the specific visual change in color described and shown is the hallmark of Chadwick's sign
questions.learning: The clinical finding of a bluish or purplish discoloration of the vaginal mucosa and cervix during the 8th week of pregnancy is known as Chadwick's sign (Option B).

questions.subject: Community Medicine
questions.text: All are live vaccines except
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Hepatitis B

Hepatitis B is a recombinant vaccine, not a live vaccine.

Live attenuated vaccines are prepared from organisms that have lost their capacity to induce full-blown disease but retain their immunogenicity and are contraindicated in pregnancy unless the risk of infection exceeds the risk of harm to the fetus. Varicella, Mumps, BCG, Measles, and Rubella vaccines are examples of live attenuated vaccines.

Recombinant protein vaccines are prepared by recombinant DNA technology by expressing protective protein antigens in yeast cells like the hepatitis B vaccine. They are generally better purified from cultured microorganisms resulting in cleaner vaccine preparations with a better safety profile.

Inactivated or killed vaccines are prepared by growing the organism in culture media and inactivating them with heat and chemicals (usually formalin). They are usually safe in pregnancy. Examples include cholera, rabies, and polio (IPV) vaccines.

Toxoid vaccines are a type of subunit vaccine prepared by detoxifying the toxins produced by organisms like tetanus bacilli. In general, they are highly efficacious and safe immunising agents.

questions.text: A 25-year-old female patient with diagnosed recurrent migraine despite Sumatriptan, has 3-5 episodes/week and presents with features of anxiety and palpitations. There is no clinical neck swelling, no history of coronary artery disease; however, there is a family history of CHD. She reports experiencing chest tightness after taking the medication. This patient has frequent migraines (≥3–5/week) requiring prophylactic therapy.

Propranolol, a non-selective beta blocker, is effective for migraine prevention and also helps anxiety and palpitations.

Chest tightness with sumatriptan suggests triptan intolerance, so adding another triptan or ergotamine is inappropriate.

Topiramate is an alternative, but beta blockers are preferred here given associated anxiety and autonomic symptoms.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.text: A young patient presents with a large retroperitoneal hemorrhage. He also gives a frequent history of intermittent swelling of knees on strenuous exercise. There is no history of any mucosal bleed. Which among the following clotting factors is responsible for the above-mentioned condition?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Factors VIII and IX

The diagnosis based on the given clinical scenario hemophilia A. The clotting factors responsible for the above-mentioned condition are factors VIII and IX.

Hemophilia A is an X-linked recessive disorder. It occurs due to a deficiency of clotting factor VIII, which causes inadequate thrombin generation and results in the inability to form a tight fibrin clot to support the platelet plug.

Symptoms include easy bruising, intramuscular hematomas, hemarthroses, hematuria, and bleeding from minor traumatic lacerations of the mouth can persist for hours or days. Retroperitoneal hemorrhages can accumulate large volumes of blood and may cause a hypovolemic shock.

Laboratory findings in hemophilia A:

• Factor VIII - reduced
• Partial thromboplastin time (PTT) - prolonged
• Platelet count - normal
• Bleeding time - normal
• Prothrombin time - normal

Mild cases of hemophilia are treated by the administration of desmopressin acetate. Moderate to severe cases need the replacement of deficient clotting factors (factor VIII in hemophilia A). Monoclonal antibody emicizumab can restore activated factor VIII activity in patients with hemophilia.

Other options:

Option B: Factors XI and XII - Deficiencies of these factors are not associated with the clinical presentation described in the question. Factor XI deficiency (hemophilia C) can cause mild bleeding disorders, but it is generally not associated with severe hemorrhages or joint swelling. Factor XII deficiency is typically asymptomatic and not associated with bleeding disorders.

Option C: Von Willebrand factor - A deficiency in von Willebrand factor results in von Willebrand disease, which can cause excessive bleeding similar to hemophilia. However, von Willebrand disease usually presents with mucosal bleeding (e.g., epistaxis, menorrhagia, and gum bleeding), which is not described in this case.

Option D: Lupus anticoagulant - This is an acquired condition seen in antiphospholipid antibody syndrome (APS), which can cause thrombotic events rather than bleeding. It is not associated with retroperitoneal hemorrhage or joint swelling upon strenuous exercise.
questions.learning: Factors VIII and IX — The diagnosis based on the given clinical scenario hemophilia A. The clotting factors responsible for the above-mentioned condition are factors VIII and IX.

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: Which of the following are the predictive factors for Fetal Growth Restriction (FGR)? I. Low level of maternal 1st trimester Beta hCG II. Abnormal uterine artery Doppler at 20–24 weeks of pregnancy III. Fetal echogenic bowel on ultrasound IV. Maternal medical disorder Select the correct answer using the code given below:
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: D. II, III and IV

The following are important predictors of FGR:

• II. Abnormal uterine artery Doppler at 20–24 weeks of pregnancy: Increased uterine artery resistance, persistent notching, or elevated pulsatility index indicates impaired placentation and is a strong predictor of early-onset FGR and preeclampsia.
• III. Fetal echogenic bowel on ultrasound: Echogenic bowel is associated with FGR, congenital infections (especially CMV), chromosomal abnormalities, cystic fibrosis, and fetal bowel pathology.
• IV. Maternal medical disorder: Maternal conditions such as:

• Chronic hypertension
• Preeclampsia
• Diabetes with vascular disease
• Chronic kidney disease
• Autoimmune disorders (e.g., SLE, antiphospholipid syndrome) significantly increase the risk of FGR.

Why is I incorrect?

• I. Low level of maternal first-trimester β-Hcg: Low β-hCG is not an established predictor of FGR. More useful first-trimester biochemical markers include low Pregnancy-Associated Plasma Protein-A (PAPP-A) and low Placental Growth Factor (PlGF).

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: A G3P1A1 woman is admitted to the labor room at term with a cervix dilated to 4 cm, intact membranes, and the fetal head palpable at 3/5 per abdomen. After 4 hours, a repeat examination shows the cervix dilated to 5 cm with an unchanged station, and the cervicograph remains on the right side of the alert line. Which of the following statements about the progress of labor is correct?
options: The head was engaged at the time of presentation
The cervicograph status suggests that intervention is likely to be required
The cervicograph on repeat examination would touch the action line
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: C. The cervicograph status suggests that intervention is likely to be required

A partograph (cervicograph) is used to monitor the progress of labor by plotting cervical dilatation against time. Important lines on the partograph:

• Alert line → represents expected normal cervical dilatation
• Action line → placed 4 hours to the right of the alert line and indicates need for intervention if crossed

In this patient:

• Cervical dilatation progressed only from 4 cm to 5 cm in 4 hours
• Fetal station remained unchanged
• Cervicograph lies to the right of the alert line

This indicates abnormal or slow progress of labor and suggests that intervention may soon be required (eg, augmentation or operative delivery).

Additional concepts:

• “3/5 head palpable per abdomen” means the head is not fully engaged
• Engaged head usually corresponds to ≤2/5 palpable abdominally
questions.learning: The cervicograph status suggests that intervention is likely to be required A partograph (cervicograph) is used to monitor the progress of labor by plotting cervical dilatation against time.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.text: A 50-year-old man presents with complaints of vertigo, tinnitus, and hearing loss. An audiogram is provided for evaluation. Based on the audiometric findings shown, what is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The clinical triad of episodic vertigo, tinnitus, and progressive hearing loss is characteristic of Meniere's disease. The provided audiogram shows a low-frequency sensorineural hearing loss (the line is lower on the left side of the chart), which is pathognomonic for the early stages of this condition. BPPV (Option A) causes brief, position-triggered vertigo but no hearing loss or tinnitus. Vestibular neuronitis (Option C) causes sudden, severe, prolonged vertigo but hearing remains normal. Presbycusis (Option D) is age-related hearing loss that characteristically affects high frequencies (the right side of the chart) and is always bilateral. Meniere's disease is caused by endolymphatic hydrops—excess fluid pressure in the inner ear. Episodes typically last minutes to hours and are often preceded by a feeling of ear fullness. Management involves a low-salt diet, diuretics, and medications like betahistine to reduce the frequency and severity of attacks. Accurate audiometric assessment is essential for confirming the sensorineural nature and specific frequency pattern of the hearing loss

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.text: Which of the following types of amino acids are present in the transmembranous part of the membrane receptor?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: B. Hydrophobic

The transmembranous part of the membrane receptor consists of hydrophobic amino acids.

A membrane protein can be either integral protein (spans the thickness of the cell membrane) or peripheral protein (attached to the peripheral side of the membrane). The membrane-spanning segment of integral proteins are usually hydrophobic alpha-helices.

The central core of the cell membrane is hydrophobic. Integral proteins have their hydrophobic portions usually in the interior of the membrane and the hydrophilic portions towards the surfaces. The presence of these hydrophobic amino acids in the interior is a special adaptation that allows the protein to remain stable in the hydrophobic milieu of the cell membrane.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.text: What is the most useful drug to treat doxorubicin induced cardiotoxicity?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Dexrazoxane

Dexrazoxane is the drug of choice to treat doxorubicin induced cardiomyopathy.
Doxorubicin is an anthracycline group of anticancer antibiotics that acts by inhibiting topoisomerase II, and is known to cause cardiotoxicity. Dexrazoxane is a cardioprotective iron-chelating agent that is indicated for use along with high dose doxorubicin to avoid cardiotoxicity.
Dexrazoxane is currently approved to prevent or reduce anthracycline-induced cardiotoxicity in women with metastatic breast cancer who have received a total cumulative dose of doxorubicin of 300 mg/m2 .

Doxorubicin-induced cardiomyopathy takes two forms:

- Acute: pericarditis-myocarditis syndrome, arrhythmias, ST and T wave changes in ECG. Occurs within the first 2–3 days, is transient and in most cases asymptomatic.
- Chronic: Dose dependendent dilated cardiomyopathy associated with heart failure.

Doxorubicin, daunorubicin and epirubicin share similar cardiotoxicity profile. Idarubicin has least cardiotoxicity when compared to other anthracyclines.
Endomyocardial biopsy showing vacuolar degeneration and myofibrillar loss is seen in cardiotoxicity due to anthracyclines.
Difference between cardiotoxicity due to anthracyclins and trastuzumab:

Anthracyclins
Trastuzumab

Irreversible
Reversible

Dose-dependent
Not dose-dependent

Biopsy shows myocyte destruction
Biopsy does not show myocyte destruction

Anthracyclines like doxorubicin can result in a radiation recall reaction, where erythema and desquamation of skin are observed at sites of previous radiation injury. The risk of cardiotoxicity also increases with previous irradiation. Therefore, careful monitoring and dosage adjustments are required for doxorubicin.
Other options :
Option B, C and D : Dexamethasone, aprepitant and amifostine are not used in the management of anthracycline induced cardiotoxicity.
questions.learning: Dexrazoxane Dexrazoxane is the drug of choice to treat doxorubicin induced cardiomyopathy. Doxorubicin is an anthracycline group of anticancer antibiotics that acts by inhibiting topoisomerase II, and is known to cause cardiotoxicity.

questions.subject: Surgery
questions.text: A patient with a previous history of trauma now presents with diplopia, epistaxis, and restricted ocular movements. Based on these clinical features and the findings shown on the CT scan, what is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The clinical and radiological findings are pathognomonic for an Orbital Blow-out Fracture. This injury occurs when blunt force to the globe increases intraorbital pressure, causing the thin inferior orbital wall to fracture. The provided CT image shows the definitive "teardrop sign"—the herniation of orbital fat and the inferior rectus muscle into the maxillary sinus. This herniation leads to the patient's limited eye movements (specifically upward gaze) and resultant double vision (diplopia). Epistaxis (nosebleeds) occurs due to the associated fracture of the sinus walls. Le Fort fractures (Option A) involve broader facial bones in specific patterns. Isolated maxillary (Option B) or zygomatic (Option C) fractures would present with different patterns of facial instability. Because the pathology is strictly localized to the floor of the orbit with entrapment of contents as shown on CT, blow-out fracture is the definitive diagnosis

questions.subject: Obstetrics & Gynaecology
questions.text: In which of the following cases is the drug given below contraindicated?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Malpresentation of fetus

The drug given in the image is Oxytocin, and it is contraindicated in the malpresentation of the fetus.

The smooth muscle contraction seen with the use of oxytocin is physiological, i.e., it causes fundal contraction and cervical relaxation that helps in the delivery of the fetus, and makes oxytocin a good agent for the induction of labor.

Uses of oxytocin:

* To accelerate abortion and to stop bleeding following evacuation of the uterus

* Used as an adjunct to induction of abortion along with other abortifacient agents (PGE1 or PGE2)

* To induce labor by ripening the cervix before induction

* Augmentation of labor

* Following the expulsion of the placenta as an alternative to ergometrine.

* In active management of the third stage of labor

* To minimize blood loss and control postpartum hemorrhage.

* Oxytocin is involved in the regulation of preterm and term labor, but the exact mechanisms are not fully understood.

Contraindications of Oxytocin-

* Hypersensitivity to the hormone itself or any part of its synthetic version

* Vaginal deliveries that are in themselves contraindicated. These include:

* Active genital herpes infection in the mother,

* Vasa previa,

* Complete placenta previa,

* Invasive cervical cancer

* Abnormal position (most notably including a transverse lie)

Other options:

Option B- Recent studies have shown that induction of labor with a modified oxytocin infusion is a safe and effective alternative for selected gravidas with heart disease where elective delivery is warranted.

Option C- Oxytocin is used to induce or augment labor, including in some cases of premature labor when delivery is necessary. It's not contraindicated in this situation.

Option D- There's no specific contraindication for oxytocin use in hypothyroidism. Thyroid disorders don't typically interfere with oxytocin administration during labor.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.text: Corticospinal tract crosses at?
questions.explanation: The corticospinal tract is the primary descending pathway responsible for voluntary motor control. The axons originate in the motor cortex, descend through the internal capsule, midbrain (basis pedunculi), and pons. Upon reaching the medulla, they form the pyramids. The critical anatomical event, the decussation of the pyramids, occurs in the lower medulla. Approximately 80-90% of the fibers cross to the opposite side to form the lateral corticospinal tract, which descends in the lateral white column of the spinal cord. The remaining uncrossed fibers form the anterior corticospinal tract. This decussation is the reason why a lesion in the motor cortex on one side of the brain results in motor deficits on the contralateral (opposite) side of the body. Understanding the level of crossing is vital for clinical localization of spinal cord and brainstem lesions. Lesions above the lower medulla cause contralateral hemiparesis, while lesions below this level in the spinal cord result in ipsilateral motor deficits
questions.learning: The corticospinal tract is the primary descending pathway responsible for voluntary motor control. The axons originate in the motor cortex, descend through the internal capsule, midbrain (basis pedunculi), and pons.

questions.subject: Radiology
questions.text: Which of the following radiological interventions are used in the management of cerebral aneurysm?
questions.explanation:
Correct answer: A. Coiling

Coiling is the radiological intervention used in the management of cerebral aneurysm.

Aneurysms occur at the bifurcations of the large to medium-sized intracranial arteries. Rupture is into the subarachnoid space in the basal cisterns. Approximately 85% of the aneurysms occur in the anterior circulation, mainly on the circle of Willis.

Most unruptured intracranial aneurysms are completely asymptomatic. When the aneurysm ruptures, 45% of cases present with sudden onset severe headache, described as the worst headache of the patient's life. Other features include neck rigidity and transient loss of consciousness.

Diagnosis -

CT shows hyperattenuating material filling the subarachnoid space. CT angiography has a high sensitivity for aneurysms and AVMs, but digital subtraction angiography remains the gold standard.

Treatment -

Early aneurysm repair prevents re-rupture. At many centers, definitive repair is carried out within 24 h of the bleed in all patients who are stable enough to tolerate the procedure. An aneurysm can be “clipped” by a neurosurgeon or “coiled” by an endovascular approach.  Surgical repair involves placing a metal clip across the aneurysm neck, thereby immediately eliminating the risk of rebleeding. This approach requires craniotomy (option D) and brain retraction, which is associated with neurologic morbidity.

Endovascular techniques involve placing platinum coils within the aneurysm via a catheter that is passed from the femoral artery. The aneurysm is packed tightly to enhance thrombosis and over time is walled off from the circulation.

Intracranial pressure should be measured and the cerebral perfusion pressure targeted at 60–70 mmHg.

Delayed cerebral ischemia remains the leading cause of morbidity and mortality following aneurysmal SAH. Treatment with the calcium channel antagonist nimodipine (60 mg PO every 4 h) improves outcome, perhaps by preventing ischemic injury rather than reducing the risk of vasospasm.

The image below is an arteriogram showing a coiled aneurysm (indicated by yellow arrows) of the posterior cerebral artery with a residual aneurysmal sac.

Other options :

Option B - Sclerotherapy is used in the management of venous insufficiency.

Option D - Stenting is employed mainly for stenotic vascular lesions.
questions.learning: Coiling Coiling is the radiological intervention used in the management of cerebral aneurysm. Aneurysms occur at the bifurcations of the large to medium-sized intracranial arteries.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.text: Which of the following is not a type of superior mediastinal tumor?
questions.explanation: The superior mediastinum is the space in the thoracic cavity above the plane of the sternal angle (T4-T5). Common tumors in this region often originate from structures normally located there. Retrosternal thyroid goiters (Option B) frequently extend into the superior mediastinum. Lymphomas (Option C), particularly Hodgkin's disease, commonly present with superior mediastinal lymphadenopathy. The thymus (Option D) is a classic superior mediastinal structure, and thymomas or thymic cysts are typical tumors found here. While ectopic parathyroid tissue can occasionally be found in the mediastinum, parathyroid tumors (Option A) are fundamentally neck lesions. Even when ectopic, parathyroid adenomas are more commonly found in the "anterior" mediastinum rather than the superior compartment. Therefore, among the choices provided, a parathyroid tumor is the least typical "type" of superior mediastinal tumor compared to the well-recognized thyroid, thymic, and lymphoid pathologies. Clinically, a superior mediastinal mass often presents with Superior Vena Cava (SVC) syndrome or tracheal compression
